22:37:00 KST

An attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 failed only because a detonator wire snapped, leaving approximately 1.8 kilograms of Semtex concealed in a vegetable tin can unexploded, German newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported.
According to investigators, the plot involved three unmanned aerial vehicles. Two drones crashed during launch due to unexplained technical failures, while the third successfully reached the Ukrainian cargo plane inside the airport’s security perimeter but did not detonate.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Investigators assessed that an explosion would have caused catastrophic structural damage to the transport hub, noting that the Antonov transport plane held roughly 25,000 liters of jet fuel at the time of the incident.
German security agencies have identified two primary suspects: Belarusian national Andrei K. and Russian citizen Oleg L. Investigators assessed that Oleg L. coordinated logistical operations on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence service, the Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU).
Logistics, entry route, and GRU connections
Investigation records show that Oleg L. entered Germany through Berlin-Brandenburg Airport via Turkey before traveling to Serbia and subsequently returning to Russia.
Although German security agencies possessed preliminary intelligence regarding his potential ties to the GRU at the time of his arrival, authorities did not establish physical surveillance on him during his stay in the country.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Command Posts and Supply Depots
Forensic investigators traced the suspects through DNA evidence recovered from work gloves abandoned near a radio antenna used to operate the drone. The DNA profile matched records held in Lithuania and Finland, where Andrei K. had prior documentation linked to petty criminal offenses.
Polish prosecutors have separately tied Andrei K. to a major summer 2024 arson attack on a home improvement hypermarket in Łódź, which Polish authorities formally classified as an act of state-sponsored sabotage directed by Russian intelligence services.
Investigators determined that the Semtex used in the Leipzig plot was smuggled across Europe through Bulgaria and Serbia hidden inside hollow vehicle compartments of commercial freight trucks.
Upon arrival in Germany, the explosive charges were buried in ground caches in areas surrounding Leipzig/Halle Airport. German federal police later located several hidden caches after analyzing telemetry and GPS data retrieved from a vehicle rented by the suspects.
Diplomatic expulsions and mutual facility closures
The investigative disclosures follow diplomatic fallout between Berlin and Moscow over the attempted airport sabotage.
On Sept. 1, the German federal government attributed the Leipzig/Halle incident directly to Russian intelligence agencies, accusing Moscow of deploying contract operatives to target critical logistics infrastructure utilized by NATO and Ukraine.
In response, Berlin ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate general in Bonn – mandating the departure of roughly 60 Russian diplomats and staff by Sept. 18 – and terminated its intergovernmental operating agreement for the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
German intelligence officials assessed that approximately one-third of the personnel at the Bonn consulate were affiliated with Russian intelligence agencies.
On Sept. 7, the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched reciprocal measures, ordering the closure of the German Consulate General in St. Petersburg and terminating all branches of the Goethe-Institut cultural organization in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Yekaterinburg.
Russian authorities ordered German consular staff in St. Petersburg to vacate the country by Sept. 18 and gave the Goethe-Institut until Sept. 13 to shut down operations.
Western allies have characterized the airport incident as a major escalation in hybrid warfare against European aviation and critical infrastructure, with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warning that allied nations will respond to attacks on European territorial integrity and democratic stability.

Charity Commission acts on complaint against Board of Deputies

Charity Commission issues regulatory guidance to Board of Deputies of British Jews after ICJP complaint
The UK's Charity Commission has issued regulatory guidance to the Board of Deputies Charity Foundation's trustees over claims made about protests against the "Great Israeli Real Estate" event held at Edgeware United Synagogue in June.
The move comes after the International Centre for Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) filed a complaint to the commission, highlighting that the Board of Deputies of British Jews had claimed that the protests had taken place on "bogus grounds".
The protests against the real estate event took place due to the organisers' advertising of illegal settlement land for sale - a matter highlighted by rights groups, including Amnesty International.
The Board of Deputies characterised the anti-settlement protests as an attempt to "harass and intimidate members of the Jewish community".
The ICJP highlighted that material distributed at the event referred to several illegal settlement developments on Palestinian land -- a fact acknowledged by the organisers, who later apologised.
The pro-Palestine legal group raised the complaint after the Board of Deputies did not correct its statements.
“The Board of Deputies dismissed a lawful protest against the marketing of property in illegal Israeli settlements as being based on “bogus grounds”. But the evidence proved otherwise: promotional materials for properties in illegal settlements were distributed at the event, and the organisers were subsequently forced to apologise," Shaima Dallali, ICJP’s Legal Researcher, said.
“Palestinians are being driven from their land while that same land is marketed to buyers abroad, including in the UK. These are not ordinary property exhibitions. They are part of the economic infrastructure that sustains Israel’s unlawful occupation and settlement enterprise. Those who protested were challenging precisely the activity that the UK government is now moving to prohibit," she added, saying that the Board of Deputies must "correct the public record".
In its guidance, the Charity Commission noted that the claims about the protesters appeared to have been made by The Board of Deputies of British Jews Limited, rather than the charitable foundation, however deemed it appropriate to issue the guidance to the charity's trustees.
According to the ICJP, the Commission reminded the trustees of a charity being, "or perceived to be, closely associated with a company, particularly in relation to public statements and communications".
The regulatory action comes as the UK moves to impose sanctions on Israel's illegal settlements and ban trade from them. The sanctions, announced by UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Tuesday, was welcomed by pro-Palestine groups and sections of the UK Jewish community.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said it viewed the announcement with "deep regret", saying that it will be "felt particularly acutely by British Jews".

Trump says he'd like to see Ireland 'reunified' as he meets Taoiseach Martin in two-day official visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:33:48 KST

The US president criticised Europe over trade, energy and immigration, and called relations with European allies "disappointing" over their response to his Iran war efforts
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a two-day visit to a major tournament at his private Irish golf course.
At a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the UK’s Northern Ireland.
“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.
“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”
Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it's Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous US presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong ancestral and emotional ties to Ireland.
When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbour Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.
Northern Ireland was split between two main communities, nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British.
Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles, unwinding three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.
A 1998 peace accord that Washington was instrumental in brokering largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.
The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it.
Newly-appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said point blank on Wednesday that there won’t be another referendum on reunification unless there is an evident desire for one.
“I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one,” said Burnham.
Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address US and Irish business leaders at the US ambassador's official residence, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open golf championship.
Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected head of state, which is a largely symbolic and ceremonial position.
A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she has in the past criticised US policy in the Middle East and called the Republican president a “bully” in his dealings with other states, pressuring of them and approach to foreign policy and bilateral relations.
The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence in Dublin. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the US national anthem and inspected an Irish Army guard of honour.
Trump rebukes European allies
The US president also lashed out at European allies as he spoke in a joint press conference with Martin following the meeting, slamming them for what he says has been a notable decline in their societies.
"I hate to see what's happening with Europe. I hate to see what's happening on trade, energy, and immigration," he said. "Ooh... that immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves."
He also criticised Washington's relationship with European allies as "disappointing" following many nations' unwillingness to help the Republican president with his Iran war efforts, and the chaos that ensued with the closure of a strategic waterway, the Strait of Hormuz.
The US president however said that his country is maintaining a working relationship with all its allies in the continent.
Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.
Trump plays golf about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organising some of them in ways that benefit his family business.
His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.
The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.
Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire.
During that visit, he held talks with the then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss his controversial global ‘reciprocal’ tariff policy.

US Space Command Should Always Be Led by a Guardian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:33:00 UTC
22:33:00 KST

General Stephen Whiting took command of U.S. Space Command in January 2024, and if customary three-year tenures hold, his tour would end in January 2027. The question now before the President and Senate is who should follow him?
Whoever they choose, it has to be a Guardian—and so should every successor thereafter.
The reason is operational, not parochial: Guardians are the military professionals best prepared to integrate spacepower into global, multi-domain operations, and the Space Force exists to generate the nation’s combat-ready space forces.
Space is no longer an uncontested domain, merely enabling others; it is a warfighting domain and capable of delivering decisive effects. U.S. Space Command’s job is to secure space superiority to preserve access to space capabilities, and plan, execute, and integrate military spacepower into multi-domain global operations. Its commander therefore must be more than familiar with space-enabled capabilities. The position demands mastery of orbital warfare, space domain awareness, command and control, electromagnetic and cyber dependencies, counterspace threats, and the integration of space effects across every geographic combatant command. Guardians are the only service members who train from accession through senior command around that full mission set.
By law, the Space Force must provide freedom of operation for the United States in, from, and to space; conduct space operations; and protect U.S. interests in space. That statutory responsibility matters. Other services have space expertise to support their missions, but Congress made the Space Force uniquely responsible to organize, train, and equip forces for prompt and sustained space operations.
A Guardian commanding U.S. Space Command brings both the depth to fight for space superiority and the breadth to lead Soldiers, Sailors, Airmen, Marines, and allied forces as a joint team. Jointness is not achieved by rotating a command among services for the sake of balance; it is achieved by selecting the officer best prepared to accomplish the assigned mission.
When U.S. Space Command was re-established in August 2019, President Trump selected General John “Jay” Raymond, soon to be the first Space Force Guardian, as the commander. But this was a temporary one-year arrangement, as Gen. Raymond was also named the first Chief of Space Operations after the Space Force was created four months later. President Trump selected Army General James Dickinson to lead U.S. Space Command from August 2020 to January 2024. When Gen. Dickinson assumed command, the Space Force was still in its first year. No pool of seasoned Guardians existed to compete for the position.
That’s no longer the case. In 2023, President Biden nominated and the Senate confirmed Gen. Whiting for the position. Since then, the Space Force has continued to develop Guardian leaders with the critical operational experience, expertise, and an unparalleled understanding of space as a warfighting domain. Gen. Dickinson’s selection was a sound transitional exception, not a precedent for an enduring Army-Space Force rotation.
The Space Force now has multiple positions and pathways to prepare its senior leaders for the responsibilities of Commander, U.S. Space Command.
First is Combat Forces Command, which traces its lineage to Space Operations Command and Air Force Space Command, where Gen. Whiting and Gen. Raymond, respectively, commanded before taking the reins of U.S. Space Command. Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon is, the current commander of CFC. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. David “Rock” Miller, is still serving, now as Deputy Chief of Space Operations, Strategy, Plans, Programs and Requirements on the Space Force staff.
Second are the Space Force’s component commands, which present the service’s forces to different combatant commands. These component commanders range in rank from colonel to 3-star general in Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood at Space Forces-Space. These positions build essential experience in integrating space effects into combat operations and provide Guardians with a distinct expertise in integrating space effects with those of all domains to achieve national objectives terrestrially and in orbit. That pipeline now produces leaders who have both commanded space forces and integrated their effects across the U.S. military, the precise combination U.S. Space Command requires. 
The Army’s June 2026 decision to create its own Space Operations Branch, along with U.S. Space Command’s relocation to Huntsville will understandably fuel an Army case to lead Space Command in the future. But neither development changes the underlying command requirement: to deliver space superiority in support of national objectives in all domains.
The Army branch is designed to improve Army component access to space-enabled capabilities at the tactical edge; it does not displace the Space Force’s responsibility for space warfare or its much broader mission set.
Likewise, while Redstone Arsenal’s Army space expertise will be valuable to U.S. Space Command, that expertise is both technical and geographical. It has little to do with governance. Locating a combatant command on an Army installation does not justify an Army claim to command it.
Some might argue that a Guardian commander would somehow make U.S. Space Command less joint. This is specious. The command will continue to employ capabilities and personnel from every service and work with the intelligence community, allies, and commercial partners. But to ensure space superiority, the officer heading U.S. Space Command must be able to make time-critical decisions to protect, defend, and employ space combat power under attack. At that level, the domain expertise inherent to Space Force Guardians is not a mere parochial preference; it is an operational warfighting requirement. Jointness does not require rotation for rotation’s sake. It requires the right commander for the mission.
The President should make the institutional logic explicit: future commanders of U.S. Space Command should come from the Space Force. The Senate should reinforce that standard in confirmation.
Doing so would align operational command with the service Congress created to protect U.S. interests in space. It would also sharpen accountability for space superiority and preserve, rather than diminish, the command’s joint character.
The move to Huntsville should deepen U.S. Space Command’s and the Space Force’s partnership with the Army, but should not blur responsibility for leading the nation’s space warfighting enterprise. Gen. Whiting’s successor should be a Guardian. So should every commander who follows.

Are the UK sanctions on Israel real progress, or more illusion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

The United Kingdom, joined by Canada and France, announced this week that they are taking action against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. It’s an announcement that is at once groundbreaking and insufficient.
Specifically, the UK said it would suspend export licenses for weapons materially supporting Israel’s illegal occupation; ban imports of Israeli settlement goods, and; sanction private companies providing services–including financial services–that enable settlement expansion.
Those are, without a doubt, positive steps. They break with the long-standing western practice of empty condemnations of settlement activity without establishing any consequences if Israel continues that activity.
The fact that the sanctions the UK announced could include firms that provide services that support the expansion of settlements is also a meaningful and groundbreaking step. It widens the scope of actions that can be taken to prevent settlement expansion to areas that are much easier to influence than Israeli settlers themselves, especially in the field of finance.
In explaining these sanctions to the House of Commons, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband bolstered accusations of war crimes against Israel and even described its actions on the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing.”
That is perhaps the most important development here. A major ally of Israel, one which is often said to have its own “special relationship” with the United States, is supporting the decision of the International Court of Justice that declared Israel’s occupation of the West Bank and Gaza illegal.
That could profoundly change the international discourse regarding the politics around not just settlements but the occupation as a whole.
These are unquestionably good things, and represent real progress, coming from a sector that has been so complicit with Israeli crimes and so hypocritical in ignoring the yawning gap between British rhetoric on the issue and its actions.
But the enthusiasm in some quarters over this announcement is overblown. There is a need to pump the brakes and prepare for a much greater push that can capitalize on this promising first step, address its shortcomings, and create something impactful.
What’s missing in the UK statement
Obviously, we cannot expect the United Kingdom to go from a regressive, genocide-enabling policy to one that promotes real justice and hope in one day. Since that is too much to ask, we need to be clear-eyed about what is still needed, not to chastise Miliband or his new boss, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but to encourage and push them to go much further.
The exclusive targeting of settlements means that expansion will be more costly for Israel and that settlement enterprises themselves would face barriers to their income.
That’s great, but it is also already international law and, ostensibly, the policy of both the UK and the European Union. The problem is not the rules, it’s their enforcement.
The sanctions on settlements will not go into effect for six to nine months, and we can be sure that legal and political challenges will be mounted by Israel and its British supporters to maximize the delay.
During that time, the momentum and political urgency driven by this announcement could fade. If it becomes less politically convenient to enforce the sanctions, it would be very much in keeping with long-standing British and European practice to ignore them.
Then there is the matter of the efficacy of sanctioning only the settlements, not the state.
Back in June, the Global Echo Litigation Center released an illuminating report detailing the many ways settlement products evade regulations on labeling their point of origin accurately, making it more difficult to police their sale. It’s a system that is easily gamed.
As I reported at the time, “For years, it’s been widely known that Israel exports products, chiefly agricultural, from its settlements on the West Bank and the Golan Heights under a ‘Made in Israel’ label. It does so even though it is legally required by the European Union and the United Kingdom to label such products as being from settlements.”
Given the volume of world events and the speed of the news cycle these days, it is easy to imagine that, in nine months or more, the burden of policing false labeling and other deceptive practices would be more than the UK would want to undertake.
It’s also important to note that the ban on weapons is somewhat selective. One of the most crucial items Israel imports from the UK, albeit indirectly, are components of the F-35 fighter jet, a plane commonly used for airstrikes in Gaza. Those components were excluded from the weapons ban.
Indeed, Miliband’s wording on weaponry in general was very vague. “We will now also refuse all license applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation…”
Like cutting off money to the settlements, arms sales are fungible. Many arms Israel uses in military operations which are not covered by this ban are also used in the settlements. Such laws, which already exist in the UK, the EU, and the United States, have not been barriers to Israel arming itself to the teeth through western largesse. Nothing in Miliband’s statements indicates a fundamental change in that travesty is certain.
The false separation between the Israeli state and Israeli settlements
Israel has long since stopped trying to pretend that the settlement project is not fully part of state activities. The Israeli army openly escorts settlers on their pogroms. The Knesset retroactively legalizes so-called “outposts” that settlers simply put up on Palestinian land. Indeed, the military regularly confiscates Palestinian land, labeling them “closed military zones” or some other title before breaking ground on new settlements there.
Yet Miliband insists on limiting the penalties to the settlements themselves. He intends to sanction ”particularly violent settlers,” but not the Israeli leaders—up to, and including, the prime minister—who enable their activities.
His speech to the House of Commons explaining this “reset” in UK policy toward Israel was prefaced by a long-winded exposition of his love for Israel. But more concerning was his explicit refusal to target the state that is, after all, intentionally pursuing the policies that are bringing these sanctions.
“The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel,” Miliband said. “We will continue to support important and valued trade with green line Israel precisely because we support the two-state solution, including security and prosperity for Israel. For this reason, I wholeheartedly oppose the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions or BDS campaign.”
That strategy is doomed to fail. Beyond the question of enforcement of these new rules, sanctioning the settlements simply doesn’t have much impact. Settlement exports are a very small part of trade between the UK and Israel.
In 2025, according to the UK government’s reports, trade between the two countries totaled approximately $8.1 billion. While it is impossible to know exactly how much trade was done with the settlements because of the evasion practices discussed above, UK records show only about $8 million of imports from Palestine, which includes the West Bank, whatever drips out of Gaza, and the settlements.
Clearly, the trade from settlements is tiny. But the fact is that the settlements are not isolated from Israel. Many firms operating in the settlements are simply parts of larger Israeli companies. Most financing for those companies isn’t specifically sent to a “settlement” business.
Settlers themselves are not worried about this. They know they can find alternative recipients for their goods or, failing that, other ways to make a living. The unending support of the state reassures them, and they’re right to feel that way.
Limited vision
Miliband’s fear of this UK action being seen as a contribution to the BDS movement is also irrational. Whether he likes the movement or not, these are the sort of sanctions BDS activists want to see put in place, although they certainly want them broader, targeted at the state, and with more bite.
His approach to presenting these sanctions reflects another potential flaw in their implementation.
The sanctions were prompted not by a realization that years of UK policy in Palestine and Israel had dismally failed to make any progress toward ending the occupation or stabilizing the region.
No, they were prompted by Israel pushing the envelope, as it has so often done. The government of Benjamin Netanyahu knows well that construction in the E-1 corridor—which would, if completed, bisect the West Bank and shatter the last remaining illusion that a two-state solution is possible—is a red line for the Europeans, and would be so for a more rational American government as well. They also know that the escalated settler violence has prompted negative reactions around the world.
Netanyahu and his cronies are trying to see what they can get away with. Issuing tenders for construction in E-1 is something Israel has threatened to do for decades. They’ve always been forced to back off.
But they have, in the last few years, been able to get away with actions they had previously thought too provocative, such as the complete destruction of Gaza and the genocide of the people there. They have even managed to finally talk the United States into a suicidal war with Iran.
So why not see if they can finally get away with cutting the West Bank in half and putting paid, once and for all, to any Palestinian aspirations for a state?
These sanctions are Britain’s response to that. Even the United States, which routinely screams almost as loud as Israel at any hint of pressure on its Israeli ally, has been relatively quiet about this.
While the Christian Nationalist Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee threatened potential consequences, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who actually matters in this regard, sounded a more conciliatory note: “We heard their arguments as to why,” Rubio said. “But look, we share the goal of stability. We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region. But beyond that, as of this moment, we don’t have any further comment.” Neither he nor Donald Trump have said anything more.
This indicates that they are waiting to see if Israel backs off of the construction in E-1 in response to British pressure. There’s a good chance that this will happen, and, if it does, an equally good chance that the UK will back off from its sanctions.
That’s by no means inevitable. By invoking the ethnic cleansing of the West Bank and stating its support for the ICJ’s 2024 ruling, on top of recognizing the State of Palestine last year, the UK has made real progress.
But it’s not irrevocable progress, and Miliband’s own words contain both the promise that something can really change here, and the possibility that Britain will back off, especially if Israel agrees not to take any more steps in E-1 for a while and confines its killing and terrorizing of Palestinians to its security forces instead of the settlers.
Supporters of Palestinian rights—in the UK, the United States, and Europe—can all contribute a lot to pushing the Burnham government forward rather than back. One thing this recent announcement does show is that having been supported by Canada and France, if the UK does take more positive steps, they will be magnified by others.

EU Eastern Border Irregular Crossings Drop 47%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:25:00 UTC
22:25:00 KST

Irregular crossings into the EU via the bloc’s Eastern Land Border route fell by 47% in the first eight months of 2026, the EU’s border agency said, as eastern member states continue to fortify their frontiers.
Frontex recorded just over 4,000 detections along the route between January and August, according to preliminary data released on Friday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The route covers parts of the EU’s eastern external frontier, including Poland’s borders with Belarus and Ukraine.
Ukrainians, Afghans and Estonians were the three most commonly detected nationalities on the route, Frontex data showed.
The sharp decline came as irregular migration into the EU fell across almost all major routes, with nearly 75,000 crossings detected in the first eight months of the year, down 35% from the same period in 2025.
Frontex did not provide a specific explanation for the decline on the Eastern Land Border route. It linked the overall fall across the EU to sustained cooperation with partner countries and preventive measures in key departure states.
Eastern borders reinforced
The fall comes as Poland and other countries on the EU’s eastern flank continue to strengthen their borders amid concerns over irregular migration and security threats from Russia and Belarus.
Poland has extensively reinforced its border with Belarus in recent years, adding physical barriers and electronic surveillance systems following a migration crisis that Warsaw, Brussels and its allies have accused Minsk of deliberately orchestrating.
Most Ukrainian Refugees in Poland Plan to Return Home, Survey Finds
The country is also building East Shield, a 10-billion-złoty (€2.3 billion) defense program designed to fortify roughly 800 kilometers of its eastern and northern borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave, respectively.
Other countries along the EU’s and NATO’s eastern flank, including the Baltic states and Finland, have also moved to reinforce their frontiers with Russia and Belarus.
How other routes fared
Across the EU, the Eastern Mediterranean remained the busiest migration route, with more than 24,200 crossings recorded in the first eight months of the year, down 25% year-on-year.
The Central Mediterranean recorded around 19,400 detections, down 55%, making it the second-busiest route.
The Western African route saw the sharpest decline, with detections down 58% to around 5,100.
The Western Mediterranean, which includes routes toward mainland Spain and its Balearic Islands, was the only major route to record an increase, with detections rising 34% to around 15,900.
The figures exclude the large-scale movement of people from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July, as Frontex said many of those who crossed returned to Morocco without being registered.
Despite the decline in arrivals, more than 1,800 people have died in the Mediterranean so far this year, according to the UN migration agency, IOM.

Train derailment in France injures 44, police suspect sabotage
Authorities suspect sabotage caused a train derailment in northwestern France that injured 44 people after a piece of rail was found on the track.
The regional train was carrying 186 passengers from Rouen to Caen when it derailed Friday evening in Cleon. One carriage tipped onto its side while four others left the tracks.
An 18-year-old woman was among the injured and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen University Hospital, police said.
A spokeswoman for the French national police communications service, known as SICOP, told The Associated Press the piece of rail found on the track was "probably" linked to the derailment. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn't authorized to be publicly named in line with police policy.
"The reasons for its presence are unknown and will have to be determined by the investigation," Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois said, according to Agence France-Presse.
Investigators were working to establish whether the circumstances were accidental or involved sabotage, the service said. The prosecutor's office remained cautious about drawing conclusions, according to police.
Cleon Mayor Melanie Delacour said the victims were "in a state of shock."
"The windows of the carriages that remained upright shattered, and because of the train's speed, stones flew into the carriages," she told AFP.
France's previous rail disasters include the July 2013 derailment at Brétigny-sur-Orge, south of Paris, which killed seven people.
In November 2015, a high-speed TGV train carrying out tests derailed at Eckwersheim, near Strasbourg, killing 11.
More recently, a crash involving two high-speed trains at Adamuz in southern Spain killed 46 people and injured more than 100 in January, according to the Andalusian regional government.

Drone attack on Leipzig: clues apparently point to Russian intelligence service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:21:30 UTC
22:21:30 KST

German security services are still investigating the foiled drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport. Leads point to two suspects, one reportedly linked to Russia's GRU military intelligence.
Previously undisclosed investigative files have emerged in connection with the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport, reports the newspaper Welt. The information is based not only on the documents themselves, but also on details from security circles.
In the course of the investigation, the identities of the two suspects and details of their journeys to and from Germany apparently became known. The findings compiled in the process are said to have been crucial in prompting Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) to publicly hold Russia responsible for the attack at a joint press conference around a week and a half ago.
At the centre of the investigation are the Russian citizen Oleg Le. and the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. While, according to German security authorities, Le. is believed to have organised the logistical preparations, Ka. is suspected of carrying out the drone attack.
Drone came to rest next to a Ukrainian aircraft
The incident took place on 4 August at Leipzig/Halle Airport. A drone fitted with explosives approached a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. The device was detected and later rendered harmless.
Two other drones are believed, according to current findings, to have failed or been destroyed even before the actual attack: investigators found corresponding debris in the vicinity of the airport.
What makes the attempted attack particularly explosive is the potential blast. According to information from the investigation, a total of around 1.8 kilograms of Semtex was to be used. At the time, the targeted Antonov is said to have been fuelled with around 25,000 litres of kerosene.
In the end, the explosive charge did not detonate, as the detonator apparently became detached, according to current findings. CCTV footage is said to show the drone coming to rest directly next to the aircraft.
DNA trace: possible link to sabotage cases across Europe
The Leipzig case is apparently not being viewed in isolation by European security authorities, Welt reports. Investigators are looking into possible links to other sabotage operations in which drones, explosives or so‑called disposable agents are thought to have been used.
In the investigators' view, a recurring pattern is that individuals with a criminal background are recruited for specific jobs, while the real masterminds remain in the background.
A DNA trace apparently plays a key role in the search for the suspected perpetrators. Investigators found remnants of a glove on an antenna construction that was presumably used to control a drone.
The traces secured there are said to match DNA data already known from Finland and Lithuania. This brought the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. into the focus of investigators.
Ka. is said to have already come to the attention of the authorities in both countries for ordinary criminal offences; in Finland he is reportedly linked, among other things, to property crimes.
Polish authorities are also said to have mentioned his name in connection with a fire at a DIY store in Łódź. The incident in the summer of 2024 is being investigated there as a possible act of sabotage.
Investigators suspect professional planning
The German authorities apparently assume that the attack was not carried out on the spur of the moment. Hints of multiple drones, possible hiding places for equipment and the use of different launch points all point, in the investigators' view, to a pre-planned operation.
Ten days after the attack, investigators reportedly came across another drone and a fire site in Kabelsketal, a municipality in Saxony-Anhalt not far from the airport. Specialists are said to have secured around 50 grams of Semtex there. Semtex is a powerful, malleable explosive developed, among other things, for military and industrial blasting operations.
Potential hiding places were also examined south of the airport: near Schkeuditz, investigators are said to have identified several locations where, in their view, material or explosives could have been stored.
The search was driven forward, among other things, by the analysis of a hire car believed to have been used by the suspects.
Russian intelligence service under scrutiny
Particular importance is attached to Oleg Le. According to German security authorities, he is associated with the Russian military intelligence service GRU and is believed to have been responsible for the logistical side of the operation.
Le. is said to have entered Germany via Turkey. He later left the country via Berlin-Brandenburg airport, initially travelling on to Serbia. According to the available information, he is now back in Russia.
In the investigators' assessment, the German authorities were already aware when he entered the country that he could be linked to the GRU environment. Nevertheless, he was apparently not placed under permanent surveillance.
Political fallout
The dispute has now also had concrete diplomatic repercussions. The federal government has already responded to the allegations and initiated measures against Russia. These include the decision to close the Russian consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. The Russian ambassador was also summoned to the Foreign Office. Further steps, including additional measures at European level, are being examined.
Moscow responded in turn with countermeasures, closing the German consulate general in St Petersburg and also announcing the closure of the Goethe-Institutes in Russia.
The Russian government holds Berlin responsible for the escalation and continues to reject the accusations in connection with the drone attack. From Moscow's perspective, there is insufficient evidence of direct involvement by Russian state bodies.
For the German security authorities, the priority now is to further substantiate the evidence gathered so far and clearly identify those responsible as well as any possible masterminds. If the suspicion of an operation orchestrated by Russian actors is confirmed, the case could have further consequences for German security policy and its policy towards Russia.

20–30 minutes on the battlefield: The Defence Intelligence Directorate spoke about the life expectancy of Russian recruits
Russia is suffering significant losses on the front, while the average life expectancy of a recruit after arriving on the battlefield may be between 20 and 30 minutes. This was reported by Lieutenant General Oleh Ivashchenko, Chief of the Defence Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, in an exclusive interview with the British newspaper The Times, UNN reports.
Details
He noted that Russia recruits about 1,000 service members every day, and sometimes this figure reaches 1,200 people. At the same time, according to him, the losses of the occupation forces are significantly higher.
Russia recruits approximately 1,000 people every day, sometimes 1,200. But look at these losses. Yesterday — 1,410, the day before yesterday — 1,551. Of these, 835, about 60%, were killed in action
— Ivashchenko noted.
According to him, the average life expectancy of a Russian recruit after arriving on the battlefield is between 20 and 30 minutes.
Ivashchenko also spoke of the low morale of Russian service members and the unwillingness of a significant portion of the population of the Russian Federation to fight.
The enemy's morale is very low because no one wants to fight. And the state of Russia's population is the same: most people actually do not want war
— said the Chief of the Defence Intelligence Directorate.
What the Defence Intelligence Directorate says about a new mobilization in the Russian Federation
The generals of the Russian occupation army asked the Kremlin to mobilize 800,000 people after the so-called elections in September. At the same time, Russia is suffering significant losses on the front, while the average life expectancy of a recruit after arriving on the battlefield may be between 20 and 30 minutes. This was reported by Lieutenant General Oleh Ivashchenko, Chief of the Defence Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine, in an exclusive interview with the British newspaper The Times, UNN reports.
According to Ivashchenko, Russia's military leadership appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to mobilize 800,000 people after the September elections.

Houthi advance in Yemen puts U.S. in a new bind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:16:18 UTC
22:16:18 KST

Houthi advance in Yemen puts US in a new bind
WASHINGTON - A lightning offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis has put the militants in a position to control a crucial Middle East waterway, creating a major new problem for US President Donald Trump as his war with Iran grinds on in its seventh month.
Widening the Middle East conflict, Houthi fighters have advanced south along Yemen’s coast, increasing their ability to choke off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait - the “Gate of Tears” at the mouth of the Red Sea - giving Tehran potential leverage over both of the region’s main oil-shipping corridors.
The militants reached the island of Perim on Sept 11, in the middle of the strait between Yemen and Africa.
That is bad news for Saudi Arabia, which has been shipping much of its oil from Red Sea ports since the war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
It also comes at a difficult time for Trump, who is already grappling with record-low approval ratings and searching for a way out of the conflict, most recently by announcing an economic pressure campaign designed to force concessions from Iran’s government.
High US gasoline prices driven by the conflict have jeopardised his Republican Party’s chances of keeping control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Iran remains defiant despite being hurt militarily and economically.
“Just weeks ago, Trump adopted a strategy of squeezing Iran’s economy while keeping military conflict at levels too low to squeeze the American economy,” said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
“The Houthis have shattered Trump’s plan.”
Danger of joining the fight
The US administration can’t afford to have the Houthis close the strait, driving up energy prices and disrupting global trade.
But at the same time, entering a fight with a foe that has withstood previous attacks by Saudi Arabia and the US would be a dangerous new mission for a US military already stretched by the fighting in Iran.
Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, phoned Trump on Sept 10 and asked for US military help fighting the Houthis, three sources told Reuters. He was told Washington would not intervene directly for now, but would help with intelligence, the sources said.
Trump confirmed on Sept 12 that he had spoken to the crown prince, and said the Houthis had also phoned his administration and asked for Washington not to become directly involved in the conflict.
A senior Trump administration official declined to address specific questions, but said the US is focused on national security interests such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea “while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges”.
Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Houthis did not respond to a request for comment.
Iran’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Sept 10 that the Yemen conflict could not be solved by blockade or military action against the Houthis and called for dialogue, without addressing Iran’s own role.
A second key strait
Iran responded to US and Israeli attacks earlier this year by disrupting the Strait of Hormuz, the outlet to the Gulf through which around a fifth of global oil supplies flowed before the war.
If the Houthis close the Bab el-Mandeb, that would deal another economic blow, constraining another 7 per cent of global petroleum supplies and about 12 per cent of global trade.
“This was always the worst-case scenario, that the Iranians exert control not only of Strait of Hormuz but Bab el-Mandeb, two of the leading energy choke points in the world,” said David Schenker, who served as assistant secretary of state for near east affairs during Trump’s first term and is now at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think-tank.
“It’s an enormous amount of leverage that (the Iranians) have in hand.”
Analysts and former officials say Trump now faces a choice: devote US forces and scarce air-defence munitions to pushing back the Houthis, or leave Saudi Arabia and its allies, a Yemeni government based in the south, to confront them alone.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital 12 years ago, and a Saudi-led military intervention has failed to dislodge them since.
Taking on the Houthis would effectively end a deal Trump struck in 2025 in which the US would stop bombing the group in exchange for a halt to strikes on Red Sea shipping. That would be likely to expose US forces to missile attacks from Yemen.
A stretched US military
It would also be another burden for the US military.
US officials say a fight with the Houthis could require significant naval and aerial resources and divert US intelligence assets, given the need to pinpoint Houthi positions that have changed since 2025.
If US Navy vessels and aircraft have to start shooting down Houthi drones and missiles, it could also worsen diminished stockpiles of US munitions and air-defence interceptors.
The senior administration official denied that the US was concerned about its resources being stretched.
“The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the commander-in-chief’s strategic goals and beyond,” the official said.
Tim Lenderking, who served as US special envoy on Yemen under former president Joe Biden and is now a principal at law firm Squire Patton Boggs, said that with Trump signalling an unwillingness to get directly involved militarily against the Houthis, the US needs to do more to share intelligence with the Saudis for their air campaign and step up diplomatic and material support for Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
“This administration came in asking the question, ‘What can Yemen do for us?’” Lenderking said, during a webcast sponsored by the Middle East Institute think-tank in Washington.
“Well, Yemen can spoil our day.” REUTERS

Quzlu: A stepped village offering a glimpse of rural Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:15:34 UTC
22:15:34 KST

Quzlu: A stepped village offering a glimpse of rural Iran
TEHRAN - The stepped village of Quzlu, nestled in the mountainous landscape of northwestern Iran, offers travelers a chance to experience traditional rural architecture, unspoiled nature and a time-honored cultural heritage.
Located in Zanjan province, Quzlu is among the rural settlements that reflect the longstanding relationship between human habitation and the natural environment. Its hillside homes, built into the mountain landscape, provide a distinctive setting for visitors seeking an alternative to conventional tourist destinations.
Quzlu’s most striking feature is its stepped architecture, in which the roof of one house serves as the courtyard of the home above it. The arrangement follows the contours of the mountainside and creates a compact settlement that blends with its surroundings.
Traditional construction materials, including stone and wood, are part of the village’s architectural character. The buildings and their relationship with the surrounding landscape offer visitors an opportunity to observe a form of rural architecture rooted in local conditions.
Preserving this architectural fabric could help maintain Quzlu’s identity while creating opportunities for heritage tourism and traditional-style accommodation.
The landscape surrounding Quzlu adds another dimension to a visit. Mountain scenery, green pastures and springs are among the natural features described as attractions of the area.
The village and its surroundings offer potential for nature-based activities, including walking, photography and exploring the rural landscape. Seasonal changes in vegetation and scenery provide different experiences throughout the year.
For travelers interested in quieter destinations, Quzlu presents an opportunity to spend time in a mountainous environment away from the bustle of major cities.
Quzlu is part of Mahneshan county, an area known for its distinctive geological formations and historical sites.
Among the region’s notable attractions are the formations known as the “Jinn’s Chimneys,” volcanic rock structures that rise dramatically from the landscape. The ancient Behestan Castle, also known as Takht-e Div or the “Devil’s Throne,” is another landmark that adds historical interest to the area.
The combination of unusual geological features, ancient fortifications and traditional villages gives Mahneshan potential for both geotourism and cultural travel.
Experts say development of tourism in Quzlu could also create opportunities for the local community. Proposals include restoring traditional homes for use as eco-lodges, improving walking routes and providing training for residents who wish to host visitors.
Such initiatives could help introduce travelers to local food, handicrafts and agricultural products while creating additional sources of income for villagers.
The development of rural tourism, however, would need to be managed carefully to ensure that visitor numbers and new infrastructure do not undermine the village’s architectural character or natural environment.
Stepped villages: where architecture meets the mountains
Iran’s stepped villages offer travelers a rare chance to experience places where architecture, nature and traditional life have developed together over centuries. Built into hillsides and mountain slopes, these settlements are more than scenic destinations. They are living examples of how communities adapted to challenging landscapes while preserving their cultural identity.
One of the best-known examples is Masuleh in Gilan province, northern Iran. Its distinctive houses rise one above another along the green mountainside, creating a remarkable architectural landscape. In many parts of the village, the roof of one house serves as the courtyard or passageway of the house above it. Narrow lanes, stone steps and traditional buildings give Masuleh a character that is difficult to find elsewhere.
The charm of stepped villages lies partly in their close relationship with the surrounding environment. Steep slopes, flowing streams, forested mountains and changing weather create a constantly shifting backdrop. Mist drifting through Masuleh, for example, can transform its streets and rooftops into an atmospheric landscape.
Other Iranian villages, including Kandovan in East Azarbaijan and Abyaneh in Isfahan province, offer different interpretations of traditional mountain settlement. Kandovan is known for its homes carved into volcanic rock, while Abyaneh is recognized for its historic architecture and distinctive red-earth buildings.
These villages also provide opportunities to discover local customs, handicrafts, regional food and traditional ways of life. Walking through their lanes allows visitors to see how residents have maintained a connection with their surroundings.
For travelers seeking more than conventional sightseeing, Iran’s stepped villages offer a rewarding experience. They combine striking scenery with history, architecture and cultural heritage, making them valuable destinations for those interested in discovering the country’s diverse landscapes and living traditions.

Iranian women showcase traditional crafts at BRICS exhibition in New Delhi
TEHRAN – A group of female Iranian artisans highlight skills at a handicraft’s exhibition being held on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi.
The five-day exhibition, titled BRICS Bazaar, runs from Sept. 10 to 15. It brings together handicrafts from BRICS member countries in an effort to strengthen cultural and artistic cooperation, as well as broader economic and political ties.
The exhibition was designed as a symbol of cultural links among the participating countries, according to IRNA’s correspondent in the Indian capital.
At the entrance, handmade carpets from member countries are arranged in a circle in a range of colors, highlighting the cultural, ethnic and religious diversity of the BRICS grouping.
Talking to IRNA, Ameneh Sedighi, an artisan from Iran’s northern Gilan province, said her participation aimed to introduce Iranian traditional embroidery, particularly Rashti-doozi, to international visitors.
She said the craft dates back between 330 and 550 years before Christ and was historically practiced by men, but is now carried out by women.
Rashti-doozi is produced using natural silk thread from Gilan and a special hook, Sedighi, who teaches the craft, said.
“We were able to showcase the distinguished art of Rashti-doozi and our country’s traditional arts to visitors at this exhibition,” she said.
Sedighi said foreign visitors, particularly Indians, had shown strong interest in Iranian handicrafts and praised the host government’s cooperation with Iranian artisans.
The exhibition also highlights the similarities between the handicrafts of Kashmir and Iran. A representative from Kashmir attributed the resemblance to the close cultural ties between the two peoples, IRNA said.
The BRICS grouping, whose name derives from its original members Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, was established in 2009. It has since expanded beyond its founding membership.

ECB rate hike could push loan payments higher next spring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

ECB rate hike could push loan payments higher next spring
The European Central Bank's latest rate hike is already reflected in the six‑month Euribor that shapes most Estonians' loan payments, meaning borrowers are unlikely to see higher monthly costs this year — but a spring increase could still push payments up.
Financial markets currently believe that Thursday's ECB rate hike to 2.5 percent will not be the last this year.
"Market expectations put euro‑area base rates at around 2.8 percent by year‑end, and by next spring they are expected to rise to about 3.2 percent. Euribor, which moves mainly according to market expectations, stands at 2.8 percent today," said Rain Leesi, head of investments at Avaron, an investment management firm.
Since the six‑month Euribor affecting Estonians' loan payments is already at 2.8 percent, the next rate hike is considered priced in and should not raise loan payments. A further rise in Euribor is more likely later on.
"If we look at the level at which Euribor can be fixed for the next five years, today it can be fixed at 3.5 percent — the same high rate as in 2023, when ECB interest rates were around four percent," Leesi said.
Most Estonian home‑loan contracts use floating Euribor, meaning any rise in Euribor directly affects monthly payments.
"If today the six‑month Euribor is 2.8 percent and it rises by half a percentage point, then for a €100,000 loan balance the monthly payment increases by €30, and for €150,000 by €45," said Sille Hallang, head of retail banking at SEB.
So far, rising Euribor has not dampened Estonians' appetite for home loans.
"We do not see a decline in borrower activity — quite the opposite. The home‑loan market is very active and growing compared with last year, so there is no visible direct impact at the moment," Hallang said.
According to Hallang, SEB's volume of new home loans has grown more than 10 percent over the past year.
Ülo Kaasik, governor of Eesti Pank and member of the ECB Governing Council, said he understands why markets expect further rate hikes, noting that they depend on global developments and energy‑price movements.
"Whether we need to raise rates further depends on how future developments unfold and how inflation pressures play out. The main concern now is that risks are increasing, especially geopolitical risks, where events can shift in either direction at any moment," Kaasik said.

On Sept. 8, Russian attack drones struck a Kyiv-Sumy passenger train in the Sumy region. Early warnings enabled approximately 90 passengers and crew members to evacuate before the locomotive was hit and caught fire; two injured women later died in the hospital.
On the same day, an evacuation was ordered for a Dnipro-Zaporizhzhia passenger train before it was hit, though a female attendant was killed after re-entering the train.
Later on Sept. 8, consecutive drone strikes hit a suburban diesel train in the Sumy region, injuring 10 civilians. On Sept. 9, Russian jet-powered drones struck a passenger electric train at a railway station in the Izium district of Kharkiv region, injuring eight people and setting two passenger cars ablaze.
Pertsovskyi previously described the systematic assaults as a deliberate campaign against passenger rail traffic. Rail operations have served as the country’s primary transportation backbone since Ukraine closed its civil airspace following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Future Estonian defence minister: Fear of mistakes must not stop us helping Ukraine
Martin Herem, the candidate for Estonian defence minister, has said that the risk of mistakes in rapid arms procurement is inevitable, but fear of possible failures should not push the state into inaction.
Source: European Pravda, citing ERR, an Estonian public broadcasting network
Details: In an interview with daily morning radio programme Vikerhommik, given before news of his possible appointment as defence minister emerged, Herem said arms procurement for Ukraine in a critical situation requires difficult choices and involves risks.
"The only way not to fail is not to buy shells," Herem said, pointing out that refusing to help Ukraine would seem criminal to him.
He said rapid procurement and a willingness to take certain risks can sometimes lead to failures. However, that does not mean decisions should not be made.
Quote: "It seems the only way never to make mistakes is to do nothing. In reality, that would put us on a path of even faster decline. I do not know in detail all the risks that existed there, but I know that the Estonian state and the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) acted out of a desire to help Ukraine quickly."
More details: Herem said that Estonia had acted quickly in helping Ukraine and had not fallen behind other countries. However, such a policy inevitably created situations in which risks materialised.
Speaking about responsibility for failed decisions, Herem mentioned Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur, who on 2 September announced his resignation, saying there was a need to take political responsibility for the National Audit Office's remarks on the activities of the Defence Forces and the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK).
Background: On 9 September, Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal proposed Herem for the post of defence minister. Herem accepted the offer.

Pinglu Canal to become operational on Sept. 16
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:13:06 CST
22:13:06 KST

This photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows vessels taking part in a comprehensive navigation drill on the Pinglu Canal in Qinzhou, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region will become operational on Sept. 16, according to a Monday press conference on the canal's opening.
The 134.2-km canal links the Xijiang River shipping route in the north with the Beibu Gulf in the south. It is China's first major river-to-sea canal project that has been planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949.
Designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal stretches along the country's New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic route linking China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets.
It is expected to shorten the shipping distance between China's southwestern hinterland and ASEAN by 560 km and reduce logistics costs by 18 to 30 percent, said Lu Xinning, vice chairperson of the regional government, in another press conference held in early September. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)

Economic Watch: Racing overseas, Chinese NEVs drive the world towards green, shared growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
21:13:06 CST
22:13:06 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 12 (Xinhua) -- Carlos Alberto Corro Martin used to work for Ebro, an iconic brand of Spain's auto sector that had once faded into memory after its factories fell silent and jobs disappeared.
In 2024, with Chinese automaker Chery partnering with Spanish automaker EV Motors, the legendary brand was revived. Electric models rolled off production lines, creating some 1,000 local jobs.
"I'm very happy to see it return to the market," said Corro Martin, now a Chery dealer. "I believe the cooperation can open even broader prospects for the Spanish auto industry."
Supported by battery technology advantages, intelligent systems and supply-chain efficiency, Chinese new energy vehicle (NEV) brands are not just winning the hearts of global consumers, but also generating greater spillovers beyond the market expansion -- creating local jobs, supporting industrialization, and making the green transition more affordable and achievable.
In the first eight months, China's total auto exports reached 7.153 million units, up 66.7 percent, including 3.435 million NEVs, a 1.2-fold increase, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
Rather than simply shipping cars, many Chinese automakers are building manufacturing and research facilities overseas. In South Africa, Chery inaugurated a manufacturing plant in Rosslyn in July, retaining all 692 employees, with expectations of creating nearly 3,000 jobs across the supply chain.
"Chery's investment will pave the way for technology transfer, automation, digitalization and advanced manufacturing systems," said South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile, adding that these developments will strengthen South Africa's industrial capacity.
In Brazil, Chinese automaker BYD is embedding R&D, production, sales, services and supply chains into the local economy. Its plant in the state of Bahia employed 5,500 direct workers as of July this year, 86 percent of them from Bahia. Once fully operational, it is expected to support 20,000 direct and indirect jobs, with the company aiming for local suppliers to account for over 50 percent of components by 2027.
The expanding footprints of overseas investment came along with the increasing popularity of Chinese NEVs across diverse markets. In Europe, new-car registrations of Chinese brands have for two consecutive months surpassed those of Japanese automakers. In Southeast Asia, consumers in Thailand and Singapore have queued for popular Chinese NEV models, while in the Middle East, Chinese brands have continued to gain traction even amid regional instability.
Chinese automakers are also tailoring vehicles to local demands. Chery, now present in over 130 countries and regions, optimized acceleration and hill-climbing for South America's mountains and strengthened interior sealing for the Middle East's deserts.
Chinese NEV brands are especially gaining market share in the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia and other parts of the Global South, according to Ron Zheng, senior partner of Roland Berger and Asia head of automotive practice.
"For consumers in these emerging markets, Chinese NEVs are not only affordable but also offer superior features," Zheng said.
In Malaysia, Zeekr, the premium NEV brand under Chinese automaker Geely, entered the market in December 2024. Within months, Zeekr vehicles were more visible on Malaysian roads.
"Previously, Malaysians may have associated Chinese cars mainly with affordability," said Zarul Fadzly, sales manager for Zeekr's KLCC and Johor Bahru outlets. "But with the entry of Zeekr and other Chinese brands, they have experienced firsthand the safety, performance and quality of the vehicles. Their perception has changed. Now they are more inclined to pursue the performance and quality of Chinese brands."
On the broader impact of Chinese brands entering Malaysia, Fadzly added: "They bring more advanced technology, so other brands will follow suit and compete. Eventually the biggest beneficiaries are consumers -- everyone is competing to improve technology."
Beyond cost-effectiveness and technological advantages, Chinese NEVs are also accelerating the global energy transition. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that the global electric vehicle fleet displaced about 1.7 million barrels of oil demand a day in 2025, with China accounting for roughly 1 million barrels a day.
The increasing cost-competitiveness of electric vehicles, along with tighter standards to cut carbon emissions, is poised to drive market growth, pushing up the share of electric vehicles in global car sales to around 50 percent in 2035 from 25 percent in 2025, according to an IEA report.
"China's NEV industry offers the world an alternative to the Western high-cost green transition path, making green transition no longer a privilege of developed countries, but an affordable development opportunity for all nations," said Zhu Yifang, deputy chief engineer at the China Automotive Strategy and Policy Research Center.
Still, Chinese automakers' overseas expansion is currently in its early stages, far from reaching the globalization level of traditional automotive powerhouses, Zheng from Roland Berger said.
Roland Berger forecasts that by 2030, overseas sales of Chinese passenger car brands will grow to about 10 million units, with local manufacturing accounting for more than 50 percent.
With that growth on the horizon, China stresses that its aim is shared progress, not dominance. Wan Gang, honorary president of the China Association for Science and Technology and a former minister of science and technology, said China is building its automotive strength to share its achievements with the global community.
"We strive to make the global auto industry strong as a whole and to solve the common problems we face -- oil, emissions, affordable mobility for ordinary people, climate and the environment, among others," he said. ■

Russian Military Slang Reveals the Reality of Life on the Front Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
13:13:00 UTC
22:13:00 KST

A research project titled The Ethnographic Dictionary of War was published in June by anthropologist Alexandra Arkhipova and psychologist Yuri Lapshin in collaboration with ECHO, the Russian Anti-War Committee.
They analyzed almost 7,000 letters, texts, and other communications between Russian servicemen and their relatives. The information had been accessed following a leak of information from the digital platform used to register appeals to Russia’s Human Rights Commissioner made between April and September 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The supposedly independent commission acts as an ombudsman to evaluate complaints from Russian citizens questioning the actions of state bodies and officials.
However, as the commissioner is appointed by the State Duma for a five-year term, many question its true impartiality.
Details of the study
The study found that almost three-quarters of the applications submitted to the commissioner were related to Russia’s war in Ukraine. It also unearthed nearly 80 examples of “modern trench slang,” a combination of former USSR euphemisms, prison jargon, mockery of authority, soldiers’ irony, and technical metaphors. Among the terms recorded were “200” for a soldier killed in action, “sent on a business trip” for deployment to the front line, “ptichka” (bird) for a drone, and “ptichnik” (bird keeper) for a drone operator.
AFU Gains Ground, Kuban Gets Pounded, NATO Trains Hard and Gives Russian Drone Free Pass
The development of informal language within the military helps soldiers cope with stress, bond with peers, and make sense of complex systems. However, this is not a new phenomenon – every army of every age has its own.
The new slang that has emerged on the Russian front lines in Ukraine reveals the truth of life as a member of the Kremlin’s “meat grinder” way of war fighting that makes a mockery of the sanitized version fed by the official line to the media, schools, and the population at large.
The effect on Russian society
Additionally, what these researchers found as being noteworthy in the communications they reviewed was the widespread use of the language by mothers, wives, sisters, and children.
They argue that the language used shows that the war in Ukraine is impacting all of Russian society, transforming the language everybody now uses. Words born on the frontline have now become part of everyday speech.
These documents describe everyday life – in the trenches, in hospitals, during training, and in camps. They detail the often adverse relationship between commanders and soldiers, particularly in terms of humanitarian violations, corruption, torture, humiliation, and fraudulent payments.
The main thrust of the dictionary is not merely to show the meaning of a slang term but to illustrate the reality of the world in which the participants in the war live.
Its analysis suggests that soldiers and families alike consider the war in Ukraine to be more than the “business of death” and that the language of war is a language of logistics.
Analysis of letters show the “meat” (soldier) as simply a disposable resource that moves along a conveyor belt to death or injury.
Stories of conscripts being forced into signing military contracts, only to have their enlistment bonuses extorted, their ration cards confiscated, and their payments ending up in their commanders’ accounts, are widespread.
The economy of Putin’s war
There are frequent references to the payment of “otkup” (ransom), which is a bribe paid to influence a soldier’s fate, whether to avoid a “meat-grinder” assault, obtain leave, or receive medical care. Fines are often levied for battlefield losses. A “ptichnik” whose drone is shot down may be required to purchase a replacement at his own expense.
The letters contain stories of life and death behind the scenes. Mobilized soldiers are referred to as “mobiks,” though families often refer to them as warriors who went to fight not for money, but in “aid of the Motherland.”
Nevertheless, much of the communication is concerned with cash. There are many inquiries as to why compensation (combat or mortuary credit) for a wounded or killed soldier has not been paid and how it can be acquired.
The bodies of those killed invariably remain on the battlefield as there is too much logistic effort and risk to recover them. Therefore, it can be six months (or more), along with court approval, before a soldier is declared missing in action (BO), with many listed as deserters (SOCH), preventing payments to families.
Soldiers taken prisoner are merely considered to be part of the “exchange fund” when sufficient numbers are captured or lost to justify their release. They remain as simply missing (BP) until freed.
The authors conclude that something more is happening in Putin’s war than the simple acquisition of slang. They conclude that not only do the Russian authorities view their soldiers as dehumanized and disposable, but the language they and their loved ones use seem to accept that status too.
Ultimately, death on the battlefield is no longer a “noble calling” but simply the outcome of their participation in the logistics of war.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
