-  Perm region, Azot chemical factory, FP-1, daylight, no air defense, Sept. 11
                                                                                                                                                                         
The final item in this section as always is the hit list for the week. Here’s a graphic from Istribin showing the gap between how much oil Russia could produce and export, based on OPEC estimates, and how much it is actually producing and exporting. Right now the price of oil is at a near-record high. Russia really could use the money. But Ukraine’s drone strike campaign is cutting into that, visibly and significantly.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Real and fake serious countries – true arsenals of democracy
On Monday the news came out that Britain would donate £100 million ($135 million) to Ukraine for the purchase of Patriot interceptors, other air defense systems and ammunition, artillery shells and munitions, and other stuff. The interceptors are supposed to arrive “by winter.” On Tuesday the UK Defence Secretary said that beyond that, London will supply Kyiv with 120,000 drones this year. If you are wondering where Ukraine is getting all these excellent long-range drones, there’s a suspect for you.
On Tuesday Germany announced it will transfer PAC-2 missiles for Patriot to Ukraine from Bundeswehr stocks, along with increased supplies of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, because now the Ukrainian F-16s are running out of those as well. Ukraine meantime has ordered “several thousand” excellent German IRIS-T missiles (probably Ukraine’s best medium-range ground-to-air missile) via the European loan/frozen Russian assets facility, news reports in Berlin said.
And on Tuesday afternoon, Ukraine’s Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara announced Ukraine is signing contracts with partners, paid for by EU “frozen Russian assets loans” for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot interceptor missiles that will arrive in 2027 and 2028. Khmara went on to say now Ukraine is asking allied states to transfer Patriots from existing stocks in exchange for new missiles once the Americans produce them. For practical purposes, if the transfer takes place, it will be Greece and Spain giving up the missiles, and frankly that seems unlikely to happen. Later on in the day the EU said it would make an exception in its rules that normally mandate EU loans can’t buy non-EU weapons like Patriots. Ukrainian financial media said the next loan tranche €3.2 billion ($3.7 billion), might be transferred on Friday.
On Thursday President Volodymyr Zelensky, in Oslo, met with the Norwegian leadership to discuss joint production of the missile interceptor Freyja. This is a much more viable option, but interceptor missiles are complicated and even the usually ridiculously optimistic people at Fire Point are saying a test version without the difficult bit – the seeker – might be launched next month. Short term, none of this is likely to help Ukraine this winter. Still, responding to an air defense problem about a year and a half into the problem, is better than not responding at all.
Final foreign affairs note, this week the clown duo Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff went to Moscow, then went to Kyiv “to promote peace because Trump wants the killing to end.” They then told reporters everything is great, the talks were excellent, and the peace process is moving forward.
This is hogwash. Neither side budged, the Americans wasted everyone’s time. In fact, the only thing the American delegation did – not making this up – was serve as couriers to deliver toughened Russian terms to Ukraine, they literally did the Kremlin’s bidding. Here is an article about that utterly shameful American behavior and yet another case of ignorant US officials getting hoodwinked into pushing Russian narratives by Moscow. It should be condemned, and if you ask me this is all impeachable negligence.
The Ukrainians told the Americans they really appreciated the diplomatic engagement and Donald J. Trump’s sincere interest in peace. Translated from Ukrainian means “go away you morons and let the adults get back to work.”
When training maybe SHOULDN’T be NATO’s top priority
                                                                                                                                                                         
On Tuesday, as noted above, there was a big Russian missile+drone strike that blew stuff up and killed and injured Ukrainians, in an actual war.
The same day, two other things happened in NATO-land. First, a Russian jet-powered drone flew across half Ukraine, into Romania, flew around Romania in NATO air space for a half hour, and then returned to Moldova. The expedition covered about 500 kilometers (310 miles). It was quite the excursion, almost to the Carpathian Mountains.
NATO launched a pair of Spanish F-18s. No intercept. We don’t know why, but, last review courtesy the Polish media, we learned that the previous time NATO failed to intercept a Russian attack weapon flying in NATO air space – this happened to be a cruise missile – the Polish F-16s that should have carried out that intercept had trouble, because the spiffy high tech data link with the NATO AWACS “flying radar” watching every meter the Russian cruise missile flew, wasn’t working so ground controllers had to try to vector the pilots to the missile. It didn’t work. The malfunctioning data link system is called Link16, unsurprisingly first developed for the US Air Force. So maybe that was a problem for the Spaniards.
The other, even more humorous (some might say shocking) NATO development that day, was that Romania and NATO were simultaneously conducting two (!) major air exercises requiring air watch and so forth. It’s not like the drone flew into Romania and all of NATO’s air watch stuff was elsewhere. Based on Ukrainian sources, at minimum, the air operations training involved six NATO fighter jets, an AWACS, two fuel tankers, a recon drone, and a maritime search plane.
This produced the, I don’t know, ironic, maybe entertaining, and according to some probably negligent situation of all manner of NATO aircraft zooming and buzzing above eastern Romania and practicing defending NATO air space against any and all air threats, while, at the exact same time, about a 15-20 minute F-16 flight to the north (faster if on afterburner) an actual Russian drone with an explosive warhead was putt-putting across central Moldova and then well into central-eastern Romania, dozens of kilometers inside NATO air space, without anything stopping it. Here’s a link to a detailed article on that fiasco.
As an afternote it’s worth mentioning that all this seemingly almost intentional NATO air force energy spent not actually doing its job and defending NATO air space, over southeast Romania and the western Black Sea, took place simultaneously with the first day of the punishing Ukrainian drone raids against the Anapa, Sochi and other points in the Kuban. Some Russians might say the exercise was just a cover for nefarious NATO data-gathering on targets for the Ukrainians. I think that’s silly but the theory is out there.
Next day, so second day of those strikes, NATO flew a deep reconnaissance mission over the Black Sea that did a fairly close fly-by of Crimea and flew suspiciously close to Russia’s Black Sea coast where, as we knew, only hours before a salvo of Ukrainian Neptune anti-ship missiles had hit and to all appearances pretty solidly damaged tree to five Russian warships in the vicinity, including two missile launch platforms. The NATO recon mission, flown by an RAF Rivet Joint spy plane, had every appearance of NATO checking out the degree to which the beating the Ukrainians had laid down on the (remains of) the Russian Black Sea Fleet, would be long-lasting.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Those darn Russian “Partisans” and long Ukrainian memories
The probable SBU/HUR bloggers that are probably masquerading as a Russian partisan movement on Tuesday put out a list of claimed assassinations for the past month. Only one murder could be confirmed by other sources, but the list is worth taking a look at. This won’t affect the course of the war overly, but again, anyone thinking the war can just be ended by a neat ceasefire after which everyone goes back to playing nicely and buying cheap Russian energy, has no understanding how vicious the Russians have been in Ukraine and how dead set the Ukrainians are on hunting down responsible individuals and killing them.
- On July 27 SBU assassins in Donetsk killed Oleg Shutov, an assassin himself employed by the special services division of the DPR. The Ukrainians had been after him for the June 27, 2017 murder, in Kyiv, of Maj. Gen. Maksym Shapoval, commander of the 10th special forces detachment. Shutov also reportedly was involved in a March 31, 2017 murder, in Mariupol, of the head of the counterintelligence department of the SBU in the Donetsk region, Col. Oleksandr Kharaberyush. Some of us remember that. The SBU said it surveilled Shutov for several days before blowing up his car. The SBU announced the assassination this week.
                                                                                                                                                                         
- On July 29, in Tula, Andrei Cherezov, head of the Russian Air Transport Laboratory and a fairly high profile supporter of the invasion as well as a player in Russia’s drone manufacturing effort, was ambushed in the entryway of his apartment building and shot and wounded with a pistol. Word is he was seriously wounded and is unlikely to recover. The shooter escaped. This was reported in some media.
- On Aug. 5, in Sverdlovsk, Vladimir Tkachuk, another drone manufacturer and simultaneously host of a rah rah Russia Telegram channel called “Obsessed with War,” was blown up in his car. He survived but lost limbs and the function of major organs, reportedly he’s in a local hospital in vegetative state. The bomber wasn’t caught. Part of this was reported in some Ukrainian media.
- On Aug. 27, Aerospace Forces Lt. Col. Sergei Sechkov died in a car bombing in St. Petersburg. Reportedly the woman who planted the bomb escaped to Moldova via Turkey, and traveled onwards. The Russian police supposedly know the identity she crossed the borders with, but not much else. This was pretty thoroughly reported in Ukrainian media and even mentioned by Russia milbloggers.
- On Sept. 3, Aerospace Forces Maj. Gen. Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of a long-range bomber division, was shot near his home as he was getting into his car in Engels. This is the home base of bombers that launch cruise missiles at Ukraine; by almost any logic he is the senior officer signing off on the strikes. A motorcyclist driving up to his car shot him twice, once in the face and once in the stomach. He survived and reportedly was airlifted to Moscow for intensive care. The motorcyclist escaped. According to Russian media the general was possibly injured in an accident.

‘I didn’t want a hero, I wanted a father’: Daughter of Argentina’s disappeared confronts the past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:59:51 UTC
20:59:51 KST

In 2020, shortly after leaving her job at the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, Noni Kofman dreamed one night that she and her mother were at the airport in Buenos Aires. Her mother was holding an old slide viewer containing a black-and-white photograph of a young man in a floral shirt, staring directly into the camera.
“It was the last photograph of my father,” Kofman says. “It was taken at a Museum in Tucumán, in northern Argentina, and sent to my mother shortly before all trace of him disappeared.” The last thing the family learned was that Jorge Kofman had been taken off a bus at a military checkpoint.
“That was on June 10, 1975,” she says. “His fate, like that of tens of thousands of people who disappeared during that era in Argentina, remains unknown.”
The photograph still sits framed in her mother’s study beside the computer. “In the dream, my mother positioned me and pointed the slide viewer at me so that I could be seen next to my father,” Kofman says. “In reality, we never met.”
She woke with an unsettling feeling and decided to write down the dream. That became the foundation for her first novel, Shkufiot (slides), a historical suspense novel rooted in both family history and imagination. It combines mystery, memory and documentation while focusing on the people condemned to live in the shadow of an absence that never ends.
Born into hiding
“I was born into a reality in which my father was already missing,” says Kofman, 51, who lives in Kfar Saba with her husband and two children and works as a sales consultant for startups.
She was born in Córdoba, Argentina, two years after her older brother, to Beatriz Gerber and Jorge Kofman, both 23-year-old Jewish students, Zionists and political activists. “They grew up in Hashomer HaTzair and eventually moved from social activism into political activism,” she says.
In 1973, when Gen. Juan Perón began his second term as president of Argentina, the country descended into chaos. Numerous political organizations on both the right and the left were seeking to overthrow the government and replace the existing regime, and each underground group had its own ideology.
“My parents were active in the People’s Revolutionary Army. The organization’s underground newsletter was printed in their home, and my father took part in various operations, including breaking into a prison to free political prisoners.
“In 1975, he joined the movement’s armed wing in northern Argentina, against my mother’s wishes. By then she already had a toddler and was pregnant with me. Both of them were wanted and were forced to move from place to place.
“In June 1975, after two months in the north with very little communication between them, he decided to return home. His bus was stopped at a military checkpoint, and he was taken off along with a priest who was later found dead. My father disappeared without a trace. My mother only learned several weeks later that he was missing. When she gave birth to me in hiding, she still didn’t know.”
Her mother named her Patricia after an underground activist who had been killed, but the nickname Noni stuck.
“For the first two years of my life, my mother was mostly on the run, without us. She was wanted, and by then it was already known that the authorities were abducting the children of regime opponents and placing them for adoption with people connected to the government.
“My brother and I spent most of that time with my father’s parents. My maternal grandparents had another daughter who was active in the underground and had been arrested. When she was temporarily released, they took the opportunity to leave with her for Israel in 1976.”
The search for Jorge was led by Kofman’s grandmother, Celina Kaufman, a retired school principal who became active with the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo organization, formed by mothers searching for children who had disappeared. Their decades-long protest became an international symbol of nonviolent human rights activism, helping pave the way for many of those responsible for the abductions to face trial after democracy returned to Argentina.
No secrets
Kofman arrived in Israel at age 2½ with her mother and brother. They had been hidden before eventually being smuggled out of Argentina, she says, “thanks to my mother’s resourcefulness, courageous people and a lot of luck.”
Her earliest memory is from a home in Be'er Sheva, sitting on the shoulders of Ari Kumpel, her mother’s second husband, himself originally from Argentina. “He is the first and only father I know,” she says. “He is my children’s grandfather.” Her sister was born when Kofman was seven. 
“We were an immigrant family,” Kofman says. “We spoke Spanish at home and listened to Spanish-language music. My mother, who had studied medicine in Argentina, started out working in nursing in Israel and eventually became head of the infection prevention unit at Meir Medical Center. She still works there as a retiree.”
When Kofman was eight, the family moved to Barcelona to join friends living there. Three years later, they returned to Israel, this time settling in Kfar Saba.
When did you learn that Ari was not your biological father?
“The Argentine story was always there. There were no secrets. I always knew Ari wasn’t my father. He came into my life when I was four.
“It was important to my mother that I know the real story. When I was six, she sat me down and told me about my father, that they had tried to build a better world and that he was missing.
“We had other friends from Argentina whose father had been active underground and was murdered, and another father raised them. But they had a grave. The obvious advantage is that they had certainty. There were no questions. They knew where he was. My father’s absence and that constant sense of a divided identity followed me throughout my life.”
After graduating from high school, where she specialized in French, Kofman served in the IDF as an education instructor. “It was difficult for me to wear a uniform because I felt that my father had been killed by people in uniform, but I did it with my family’s support and encouragement,” she says.
After completing her military service, she traveled through South America, spending most of the trip in Argentina. “It wasn’t my first encounter with the country where I was born. I had been traveling there to visit family since I was 15, and I speak Spanish. In 1999, during one of those visits, my mother, my brother and I decided to travel north to the area where my father disappeared. We also visited the last place where he was photographed before he vanished.”
How did you feel standing in the last place where he was known to have been?
“I thought I would be emotional, but I didn’t feel anything. At the time, heroic stories were still being told about him by relatives in Argentina and human rights organizations. My mother, on the other hand, never built a heroic narrative around him. I knew she had also taken part in underground activity, but she didn’t support taking up arms.
“She didn’t believe the country could be liberated through weapons, and she didn’t want to kill people. He believed that was the only way.”
Who am I?
Kofman first married at 24 and moved with her husband to the United States. They divorced four years later.
“We lived in Michigan, where I worked for an Israeli high-tech company and studied Latin American literature for both my bachelor’s and master’s degrees. I did very well academically, received scholarships and was on track for a doctorate on street theater in Argentina in the 1930s.
“I deliberately stayed away from the more politically explosive period. I felt I didn’t want to carry my parents’ burden on my back. In Michigan, I volunteered as head of the university’s Amnesty International chapter and was involved in human rights issues, but at some point I felt I had to find out who I was without this story.
“After six years in the United States, I came to Israel for an extended vacation and never went back. After my divorce, I met Guy Tabarovsky, my current husband and the father of my children. Around the same time, I began working in staff positions at the Prime Minister’s Office.
“During my 13 years there, I had my two children and Guy founded a successful startup. Five years ago, I left, returned to high-tech and completed an MBA in entrepreneurship at Reichman University.”
When, if ever, did you begin to feel angry with your father?
“At 30, after I returned to Israel, I started thinking more seriously about the choices I had made in life. I asked myself whether I was living through the story of my missing father, and how much my decisions were shaped by the expectations of a father who was no longer there.
“That was when I realized there is a kind of cult around the hero who goes off to fight for his ideals, while the real heroism belongs to those left behind to deal with the consequences. My grandmother, for example, devoted decades of her life to the Mothers’ struggle, right up until her death. And then there was my mother, who was left in an extraordinarily difficult position and had to fight the battle of everyday life.”
“There’s something a little naive about going off to fight for your ideals and believing that society will take care of your children if something happens to you. It feels good to believe you’re on the side of the good guys, fighting for freedom and willing to sacrifice yourself for everyone else, but there is a family left behind, carrying the burden and paying the price in pain.
“By the time I was 30, I found it hard to relate to that innocence. I realized I didn’t want a hero. I just wanted a father. Once I allowed myself to be angry, I also felt a sense of release, to the point that I found myself going to work in Israel’s security establishment and actually enjoying it.”
Are you still angry with him today?
“Not anymore. I don’t judge him. His ideals and intentions were good, but he and his friends didn’t fully understand the forces they were up against. I think he was naive. At 23, it’s hard not to be naive and idealistic. From his perspective, he genuinely believed he was trying to do something good.
“And I don’t think that at that age you have the perspective to understand the void you might leave behind, while still believing completely that you are not abandoning the people you love.”
When did you decide to write a book connected to his disappearance?
“Months after that dream, I opened the file again and decided to continue the story from the moment the dream ended.”
And did it become a memoir?
“No. It’s fiction, with fictional characters, though some of what happens to them is real. I looked at the final photograph of my father and asked myself: Why would a wanted revolutionary enter a museum and pose for a photograph in the middle of a conflict? Was he trying to send his wife a clue?
“That is where the plot begins. The book’s protagonist and her mother return to Argentina to solve the mystery and decipher the clues he supposedly left behind.”
Did you consult your mother while writing it?
“I told her I was writing it and emphasized that it wasn’t our family story. She was happy and encouraged me. While I was writing, she read it and liked it. In the first draft, she told me that the daughter needed to be angrier. I changed the story accordingly. She is angry at her mother because her father isn’t there to absorb that anger.”
Are the main characters based on you and your mother?
“The daughter is very different from me and from who I am, although we share a similar sense of cynicism and humor. The mother is also very different from my own. In the book, she hides the full story from her daughter, which creates a deep sense of mistrust. My mother, by contrast, never hid anything from us. She has no regrets, but she has always been critical in ways she expressed both at the time and later.
“My mother is the real hero of our family story. At 25, with two small children, she secretly got us out of Argentina, arrived in Israel with nothing, built an extraordinary career and created a life for us. Alongside her work, she is also a swimmer and has a house full of medals from masters competitions. She has lived a full life defined by optimism and humanism.”
How long did you work on the book?
“Three years, on and off. The wonderful editor Hagar Yanai came on board after I finished the second draft of the book. My goal was to bring this difficult story to readers unfamiliar with it in a way that was accessible and engaging, without turning it into something didactic.
“Judging by the reactions, I feel I succeeded. My mother loves the book and is proud of it. I think she needed people here to know this story. She may be Argentine by birth, but she has been Israeli since she was 25. Israelis love Argentina and tend to associate it with soccer, Maradona, Messi and alfajores, but they know much less about this side of its history.”
What does your family think of the book?
“My daughter is reading it now, my son tells everyone about it, and my husband is waiting for the TV series that will be made from it.
“There will also be a Spanish translation, and all our relatives in Argentina are already waiting for it with curiosity.”
Do you see the book as a kind of closure with your father?
“Yes. I created my own private sense of closure because the chances that he will ever be found, or that we will discover exactly how he died, are almost nonexistent.”
Given what happened in Argentina at the time, do you see circumstances in Israel that could lead to a similar civil conflict?
“I think some of the things that happened in Argentina are already happening here. The divisions are so deep and significant. I am definitely concerned, because things like that can happen anywhere.”

Afghan woman removed from US on orders of 'terror court'

Unknown Publisher

Breadcrumb
Afghan woman removed from US on orders of 'terror court'
An Afghan woman accused of supporting a plot to carry out a mass shooting in the United States has been sent back to Afghanistan in the first case heard by a special US terror court, the Department of Justice said Friday.
Nazira Haji Zada, 47, a Texas resident, was removed from the United States on 25 August on the orders of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC) in Washington, the department said in a statement.
The ATRC was established by Congress 30 years ago but had never previously been used.
It allows for the presentation of classified evidence whose public disclosure the government believes would endanger national security.
The Department of Justice said that Zada, who came to the United States in 2018, "conceded that she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order."
"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
"This first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country."
Zada's son, Abdullah Haji Zada pleaded guilty - alongside a co-conspirator, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi - to plotting an attack on US election day in 2024 on behalf of the Islamic State.
Abdullah Haji Zada, who was 17 at the time of his arrest, was sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2025. Tawhedi is awaiting sentencing.
According to court documents, the pair purchased two AK-47 rifles and 500 rounds of ammunition from an undercover FBI employee to carry out a "mass-casualty attack."
The Department of Justice's public announcement of Zada's removal was made on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 Al-Qaeda attacks on New York and Washington.

Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'

Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'
September 12, 2026
US President Donald Trump has said he would "love" to see the Republic of Ireland, an EU member, unite with British-run Northern Ireland as he faced reporters' questions on a range of issues on Saturday.
Trump is taking the weekend trip largely to watch the Irish Open golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country’s Atlantic coast, but he met as well with the Irish president and prime minister, or taoiseach.
The US leader also spoke optimistically about his country's war with Iran and its trade conflict with Canada, among several other topics.
What did Trump say about Ireland?
After a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in the capital, Dublin, Trump said he very much supported what he said would be the eventual unification of the two parts of the island of Ireland.
"Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters.
"The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing," he added.
"Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing."
The British government responded swiftly to the remarks, with Prime Minister Andy Burham's office saying that in his view, there was no majority public support for a referendum on the issue and that there would not be another one until that changed.
Previous US presidents have avoided touching on the subject in view of the delicate nature of the issue, with Northern Ireland seeing decades of of deadly sectarian violence in the 20th century over the question of whom it should belong to.
What did Trump say about the Iran war?
Trump also said that the US war with Iran, which began on February 28, would "end very soon" — a view he has frequently expressed in the past, but which has not yet materialized.
He also said that the end of the conflict would mean that the price of oil, which has soared as a result of the war, would "come tumbling down."
However, he vehemently defended his decision to mount the military operation against Iran.
He said that the US attacked because "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon", adding: "They were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."
"If they had it, they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East, and they would have hit some [...] in my opinion, [of] Europe's cities and beyond cities, and they would probably hit us soon before we put out the fire. But they cannot have a nuclear weapon."
The war with Iran is not supported by a majority of the US population, particularly in view of promises made by Trump on the campaign trail to keep his country out of foreign "forever" conflicts.
What did Trump say about Canada?
The president sounded a similarly optimistic note regarding the US trade war with Canada.
He said Canada was keen to make a deal and that one could be struck "fairly soon," while reiterating his claims that Canada had treated US farmers unfairly with its tariffs.
"Canada wants to make a deal very badly," he said.
"Canada has to treat our farmers better. They can't charge our farmers tariffs," he said, adding: "You'll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon."

The world was supposed to begin phasing out coal in 2026, but Trump and Russia’s war against Ukraine have changed the forecast

The world was supposed to begin phasing out coal in 2026, but Trump and Russia’s war against Ukraine have changed the forecast
Kyiv • UNN
After a record-breaking 2025, coal demand was expected to decline in 2026. Russia’s war against Ukraine and Trump’s policies are casting doubt on the forecast.
Global demand for coal, which was finally expected to begin declining after reaching a record high in 2025, may remain high for longer than forecast. Among the reasons are the energy consequences of russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine and the policies of US President Donald Trump, BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
Coal remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the energy sector. That is why phasing it out was considered one of the key ways to implement the Paris Climate Agreement and curb global warming.
The situation changed after russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Cuts in Russian gas supplies to Europe and a sharp rise in energy prices forced a number of countries to use coal more actively again as an alternative fuel.
2026 was meant to be a turning point
The trend continued through 2025, which set a record for global coal demand. The International Energy Agency expected the situation to change as early as 2026 and consumption to begin declining.
However, as BBC notes, these forecasts came into question after Donald Trump’s return to the White House and a shift in US energy policy.
Thus, the expected phaseout of one of the most carbon-intensive fuels is being delayed, despite international commitments to reduce emissions and combat global warming.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war against Ukraine during bilateral discussions held on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the Hindustan Times reported.
During their meeting, Modi reiterated New Delhi’s longstanding diplomatic stance, emphasizing that “dialogue and diplomacy are the path to resolving conflicts” and affirming that India remains prepared to support international peace efforts.

According to the Indian Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the two leaders reviewed regional and international security developments, focusing specifically on conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region that have disrupted maritime commerce and imperiled merchant crews.
The discussions regarding maritime security follow recent drone and missile strikes on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, which resulted in the deaths of at least five Indian seafarers in recent weeks.
The incidents prompted official diplomatic protests from New Delhi to both Moscow and Kyiv, with Indian authorities characterizing attacks on commercial maritime personnel as unacceptable.
Consecutive appeals following Bishkek summit
Saturday’s exchange marks the second time in less than two weeks that Modi has directly called on the Russian leader to halt military operations.
On Aug. 31, during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Modi urged Putin to transition from an “endless war to ending the war.”
Russian Ballistic Missiles Strike Zaporizhstal Steel Plant, Injuring 4
Addressing Putin during their opening remarks in Bishkek, Modi emphasized that prolonged warfare imposes severe setbacks on global stability, stating that every day of conflict moves humanity backward while steps toward peace provide renewal and hope.
Modi framed his appeal through India’s traditional foreign policy principles, remarking that “the land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha has only one message – peace.”
India has maintained close strategic, defense, and economic ties with Russia, significantly expanding imports of discounted Russian crude oil over the course of the full-scale invasion while declining to join Western sanctions against Moscow.
However, New Delhi has consistently avoided endorsing Russian military actions, maintaining dialogue with Kyiv and advocating for a negotiated settlement based on international law.
The bilateral engagement in New Delhi follows a diplomatic mission by Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar to Kyiv in early September, during which President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed appreciation for India’s commitment to diplomatic engagement.
BRICS summit diplomacy amid regional conflicts
The discussions between Modi and Putin took place as leaders gathered in New Delhi for the two-day annual BRICS summit, which opened Saturday amid complex geopolitical divisions across its expanded 11-member bloc.
The summit marks Chinese President Xi Jinping’s first official visit to India since 2019, reflecting gradual diplomatic stabilization between the two Asian powers following deadly 2020 border clashes along their disputed Himalayan frontier.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also arrived in New Delhi for talks, placing ongoing conflict in the Middle East and energy transit security high on the multilateral agenda alongside representatives from the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt.

Small parties face steep deposit hurdle in bid for Riigikogu seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Small parties face steep deposit hurdle in bid for Riigikogu seats
Parties outside parliament are weighing bids for next spring's Riigikogu elections, with some already committing and others still undecided, but all face the same major hurdle: raising the candidate deposit required to get on the ballot.
The board of the Estonian Nationalists and Conservatives (EERK), founded in 2024 by former EKRE members, decided unanimously a few weeks ago that the party will participate in the March Riigikogu elections with its own list. EERK chair Rein Suurkask said the plan is to field lists in all electoral districts.
"The goal is to clear the electoral threshold — five percent. That is the main objective, and there's no room for doubt. We are of the view that we won't settle for less; that five percent is very important for us," Suurkask said.
EERK is currently assembling its lists, and the campaign is being prepared. The entire program will be based on the party's core principle that the state exists for its people, Suurkask added.
The Estonian Greens will also definitely participate in the Riigikogu elections, said party co‑leader Rasmus Lahtvee.
"For a political party, the most important goal is to participate in elections, gain a mandate, and then implement decisions based on its worldview," Lahtvee said.
However, Lahtvee sees the deposit requirement — which must be paid to register candidates — as a major challenge. The deposit equals one Estonian minimum monthly wage per candidate. According to initial calculations, the Greens may need around €120,000 if they run a full list.
"A party that is not funded by taxpayers must pay this amount itself, and if it doesn't get elected, it loses the money. In the European Parliament elections, the Greens went to court and received interim relief. There is still no final decision from Europe, but for those elections, the European Commission said the amount was clearly excessive," Lahtvee noted.
The Estonian National Liberals–Free Party has also recently contacted the Chancellor of Justice regarding the deposit issue. Party chair Märt Meesak said political competition should be more open.
"Half joking, if you don't have a rich mother‑in‑law handing you money from a cupboard or a wealthy uncle in America, it's pretty difficult. I think this is a serious problem for Estonian democracy, because this way we never get new people or new ideas. Right now, we're not checking the seriousness of candidates — only the thickness of their wallets — and that's not good for democracy," Meesak said.
Meesak added that although the party has become more active recently, the board will likely make a final decision on participating in the Riigikogu elections in November. By then, the Chancellor of Justice's response on the deposit issue should also be available, he said.
Last autumn, there was talk that Plan B might enter the Riigikogu elections as a party, but that plan has since collapsed. Plan B's Narva representative Urbo Vaarmann said the group will not participate with its own list. However, members may run as independents or on another party's list. Vaarmann added that Plan B aims to counter excessive party power and supports rethinking the party system.

At least 11 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv strikes Russia's 'shadow fleet'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:49:26 UTC
20:49:26 KST

The strikes hit several regions, with Odesa suffering particularly badly. At the same time, Kyiv is pursuing an operation against Russia's "shadow fleet", aiming to choke off a key source of war funding
At least 11 people were killed and 96 injured across Ukraine in overnight Russian attacks between 11 and 12 September.
The Odesa region was hit hardest, but strikes also targeted, among others, the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson regions.
According to Ukraine's Air Force, Russia used 129 drones of various types, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, eight Kalibr cruise missiles and six guided Kh-59/69 missiles. Around half of the drones deployed were fitted with jet engines.
Ukraine's air defences destroyed or disrupted 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S-8000 Banderol cruise missile launched from a drone and 101 unmanned aerial vehicles.
Attack on Odesa
One of the main targets of the overnight attack was Odesa. At around 5.30 a.m., Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian cruise missiles were heading towards the city from over the Black Sea.
A multi-storey residential building was damaged in the strike. "The enemy attacked the city. A multi-storey residential building has been damaged," said Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper.
The number of wounded in the Odesa region rose as more information came in about the aftermath of the attack. In the end, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old baby and a 17-year-old. Some of the victims required hospitalisation.
Russian attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region
Russian forces also attacked the Dnipropetrovsk region. In Dnipro, drones, artillery and air-dropped bombs damaged an industrial facility, residential buildings, garages and vehicles. One person was killed and 19 were injured.
During the night another Russian strike hit an industrial plant in Kryvyi Rih. One person was killed and three were wounded. A 54-year-old man was taken to hospital in a serious condition.
In total, two people were killed and at least 22 wounded in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including a child, governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Russian attacks also hit the Zaporizhzhia region. Over the past 24 hours, Russian forces have carried out strikes on 45 towns and villages, including five missile attacks on Zaporizhzhia city. Two people were killed and 11 injured in the region.
In the Donetsk region, four people were killed and five wounded. Two people died in Sloviansk, one in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka, governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the Kyiv region, one person was killed and three were injured, including a child. Russian attack drones struck five districts: Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil and Vyshhorod. Fifteen facilities were damaged, including seven houses, vehicles, warehouses, hangars and a power line.
In the Sumy region, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community. In a separate attack on the Novoslobidske community, a 64-year-old man was wounded. Over the course of the day, Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks on 25 localities there, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aerial vehicles and guided air-dropped bombs.
In the Kharkiv region, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, and a 19-year-old man was wounded elsewhere in the region. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and seven other localities, using guided air-dropped bombs and various types of drones.
In the Kherson region, 18 people were wounded. Russian attacks targeted residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure. Fifteen residential buildings were damaged, along with shops, a petrol station, a service station, an ambulance and vehicles.
Attack on Russian plant
Ukraine's defence forces confirmed that during the night of 11 to 12 September they carried out a strike on the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara region. The factory supplies products used by the Russian military-industrial complex.
The attack sparked a fire on the plant's premises. "The scale of the damage is still being assessed," Ukraine's General Staff said.
The plant produces, among other things, synthetic rubber, monomers, fractions and additives for high-octane fuels. The Ukrainian military stresses that synthetic rubber is used, among other purposes, in the production of solid fuel for short-range missiles and ballistic rockets.
Earlier, "Ukrainska Pravda" reported a strike by Ukrainian forces on the Machine-Building Plant in Snizhne, located in Russian-occupied territory of the Donetsk region. The plant manufactures components for gas turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades.
Ukraine targets Russia's "shadow fleet"
As Russia was carrying out its overnight bombardment of Ukraine, Ukrainian forces continued operations aimed at the country's economic backbone.
On 12 September, Robert "Brovdi" Browdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, announced further attacks on Russia's so-called "shadow fleet", used to transport Russian oil in circumvention of some sanctions.
According to Browdi, since the operation began around ten weeks earlier, Ukrainian forces have attacked a total of 285 vessels belonging to Russia's "shadow fleet" operating in the Azov and Black Seas.
The highest number of attacks was recorded in July: 215. In August, a further 54 vessels were struck, and between 1 and 11 September another 16.
Browdi claims that the Ukrainian strikes have almost brought traffic by Russia's "shadow fleet" in the Sea of Azov and the Kerch Strait to a halt. He says the operation has also seriously impeded its activity in the northern and north-eastern parts of the Black Sea.
The commander released footage which, he said, shows an attack by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces on a sanctioned Russian tanker belonging to the "shadow fleet". The ship was reportedly being escorted by a Russian helicopter.
Browdi stressed that revenues from Russian oil exports are one of the sources of funding for the war against Ukraine. Attacks on vessels involved in transporting Russian oil are therefore intended as part of broader efforts to limit Moscow's financial capabilities.

Russia has set a record payment for recruiting foreigners to fight in the war against Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
In the Irkutsk region, 1.5 million rubles will be paid for each foreigner recruited into the Russian army. The payment for Russians from other regions has been doubled.
The authorities of the Irkutsk region have set Russia’s highest reward for recruiting foreigners into contracts with the Russian Defense Ministry — 1.5 million rubles per person recruited. The Moscow Times reports this, citing Verstka and a decree by the region’s governor, UNN writes.
Details
Governor Igor Kobzev signed the corresponding decree on September 10. The reward will be paid to those who facilitated the conclusion of a contract with Russia’s Defense Ministry by a foreigner or stateless person.
At the same time, the Irkutsk region doubled the payment for recruiting Russian citizens from other regions — from 400,000 to 800,000 rubles. Foreigners were singled out as a separate and most expensive category for the first time.
Recruitment rewards are rising sharply
The Irkutsk region has been paying for the recruitment of contract soldiers since at least April 2026. Previously, the maximum reward was 400,000 rubles, regardless of the recruited person’s citizenship.
Other Russian regions are also expanding similar programs. In the Smolensk region, the payment was increased from 115,000 to 1 million rubles for recruiting a person, while in the Ryazan region it rose from 575,000 to 805,000 rubles for a foreigner from a country outside the CIS or a Russian citizen from another region.
According to Verstka, efforts to recruit foreigners into the Russian army began to intensify in early 2025 amid a decline in the flow of Russian volunteers. The outlet also reported cases of foreigners being forced to sign contracts and threatened with deportation.

Left with nothing, people in Gaza are forced to rent generators by the hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:43:28 UTC
20:43:28 KST

Left with nothing, people in Gaza are forced to rent generators by the hour
Israel’s destruction of homes and infrastructure in Gaza has left few working household items and expensive services for daily chores.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – For more than four hours, Hajj Rabhi al-Fairi, 79, has been standing outside his home in Gaza City with his children and neighbours waiting their turn to use a small generator.
The generator’s owner pours in the fuel, starts a timer and switches on the machine.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
- list 2 of 4Shift in British policy on Israel is palpable
- list 3 of 4Israeli academia accused of systemic apartheid against Palestinians
- list 4 of 4Israeli strikes devastate homes, displace families across Gaza
Each family gets a few minutes to operate a pump that pushes water up to a storage tank on the roof, before the generator moves on to the next house.
For al-Fairi and his neighbours, this is how they get water.
“We have an old water pump, but there is no electricity to run it. We have to rent a generator,” al-Fairi tells Al Jazeera.
Since the family returned to their home in October 2025, after fleeing a month earlier during Israel’s assault on their neighbourhood, the generator has become a familiar sight on the streets of Nassr.
When it arrives, residents gather around it, each carrying a jerrycan of diesel to operate the machine, which they have to pay for themselves.
“We came back and found the place a tragedy,” he says.
Their neighbourhood and home were badly damaged from years of Israeli bombing, with no municipal electricity or water supplies functioning. The family depends on an old pump – but without electricity, it cannot bring water up to the rooftop tank.
Each family needs only about seven or eight minutes to fill up their tanks, but with the number of flats in their building, the generator needs to be rented for about an hour.
The cost has also risen. Al-Rabhi says families used to pay about 80 to 90 shekels ($26-30) to rent a generator for an hour. At different times, the price has risen to about 100 or 120 shekels ($33-40) an hour, excluding the cost of diesel.
A generator on wheels
Khalil Abu Ouda, 39, takes a machine mounted on a horse-driven cart from one house to another. The generator’s metal body is covered in black soot and grease, and white smoke rises from the engine when it operates.
At each house, Abu Ouda connects long electrical cables to the water pump. The cables stretch across the street as neighbours gather around the machine to wait their turn.
“Go on, switch it on,” someone calls.
For Abu Ouda, this machine is both a service for the neighbourhood and an essential source of income for his family.
He says there are very few small, mobile generators, like his, left in working condition in Gaza. Many have broken down, while spare parts are difficult to find or too expensive to source due to Israel’s siege.
Mechanics are also expensive to hire, while fuel and engine oil are increasingly scarce and costly.
“If I could, I would lower the price as much as possible,” he says.
At the same time, demand has never been higher.
“People are under pressure and they need water. If I stayed working until morning, I would keep working,” Abu Ouda says.
To cope with the demand, he often works for 10 to 12 hours a day, putting pressure on himself and the machine.
“But this is our livelihood. There is no alternative,” he said.
When the home stops providing
With most Palestinians in Gaza having no home or losing their possessions due to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, they have to rent or hire items or services for the most basic household chores.
This includes washing clothes, something once done at home but now impossible to do with no power.
Earlier in the war, Abeer Ghorab, 52, used to wash everything herself. Now she gathers clothes from her tent and takes them to a nearby laundry, where they can be washed and dried in far less time and with less effort.
“When these laundries started opening, they gave us some relief,” Ghorab said.
The difference is particularly important in winter, when heavy clothes, blankets and bedding can take time to dry.
“In winter, the tracksuits are heavy. They need another day to dry,” she said. “When I bring them here, they wash and dry them for me, and I get them back clean and dry. That really helps.”
But due to a limited income, Ghorab cannot afford to use this laundry service every day.
Before the war, Ghorab had a washing machine, a refrigerator and regular electricity at home.
“Things we once took for granted have become dreams. Now we have to pay for every little thing we used to do at home.”
The loss of the household
Across Gaza, the infrastructure that once allowed families to carry out everyday tasks at home has been severely disrupted.
A recent United Nations assessment found that 91 percent of surveyed households experienced moderate-to-high water shortages in early August.
A separate damage assessment by the authority found that 107,941 of the 178,632 housing units inspected – about 60 percent – were severely damaged, destroyed or otherwise considered uninhabitable.
Water systems, electricity, sanitation and household appliances, which families relied on to manage daily life, have also been disrupted.
For families living in damaged homes, tents or makeshift shelters, everyday tasks must be paid for.
A laundry adapting to shortages
Fadi Abu Shawarb, 23, has worked at his family’s al-Hurriya laundry for six years.
Before the war, the business relied on large, 50kg (110lb) washing machines for carpets, blankets and other heavy loads. But due to the high cost of operation, these machines are far too expensive to run.
“We started replacing the 50kg machines with 25kg ones because there is not enough electricity,” Fadi says. “There are no solar panels, no reliable power, and the generators are always breaking down.”
Most of his customers are displaced families who lack electricity, water or washing machines at home.
The laundry now handles about 20 to 30 loads a day, with clothes-washing among the most in-demand services.
A load costs six shekels ($2) when the laundry can use solar power and 12 shekels ($4) when it relies on a generator.
But even that is hard for people to pay. “People’s situation is difficult,” he says.
For Ghorab, the laundry is only one of the many expenses she now has to budget for.
“I feel like I’m going through a difficult time,” she says. “I have to pay for every little thing in my day, and with how difficult things are, it’s hard to keep up with everything.”

Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled negotiations to find a solution to the conflict, Europe's deadliest since World War II, with US negotiators recently visiting Kiev and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks on the conflict over the phone.

Russia's finance minister has already attended one G20 meeting, causing discomfort among some of Ukraine's allies, and a Russian diplomat said on Saturday that Moscow will also send some officials to a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week.

Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Putin and Trump also discussed the war earlier in the week in what the Kremlin termed an "extremely frank" and constructive hour-long phone call.
Diplomatic efforts intensify

"It's respect to our people," he said.

Kiev has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was "too early" to discuss a venue or dates.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kiev have shifted their positions.
Both Moscow and Kiev have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Zelenskyy also repeated his call for Ukraine's allies to provide more interceptor missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.
"Russia produces... today 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need 280... You will never have 280 missiles per month," he said.
It was a "huge challenge" to have 100 a month, he said.

Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row

Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
September 12, 2026
Uganda has concluded a nine-day period of mourning for King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, with a funeral for the Tooro Kingdom's late monarch due to take place in the western city of Fort Portal on Saturday.
Oyo, who once held the unofficial title of the world's youngest king, ascended the throne as a young child in 1995 and died last month of cancer aged just 34, with his death prompting a bitter succession dispute.
How is Oyo to be laid to rest?
The casket carrying the king's body, which was draped in the blue-and-yellow Tooro flag, was carried by hearse from the royal palace in Fort Portal in a procession accompanied by royal guards dressed in orange tunics and beating wooden sticks.
The ceremony in St. John's Cathedral was to be attended by hundreds of mourners, including senior Ugandan government officials.
After the service in the cathedral, Oyo was to be buried at the site of the royal tombs.
At the burial ceremony, tradition dictates that the successor should throw nine coffee berries into the grave.
Dispute over Oyo's successor
However, the question of that successor has aroused considerable controversy, and it was in doubt until late on Friday who would carry out that rite.
On Wednesday, a committee made up of members of the royal clan announced it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, as the new king.
Kijanangoma, 54, is a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC.
But the immediate family of the late king said that the latter's will had called for a son who was born out of wedlock and has yet to be identified to succeed him.
Additionally, there have been claims on social media that there are at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo's children.
Those supporting Kijanangoma say Oyo's family has so far failed to come up with concrete information on the alleged son, while traditionalists also favor the choice of an adult as new monarch.
A source with knowledge of crisis talks on the matter said authorities had managed to get Kijanangoma officially accepted as successor on Friday.
Beloved traditional monarchs
Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined the family's ability to mourn the king's death.
"I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: Please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."
Although Uganda is led by an elected head of state, it still possesses several kingdoms that were restored in 1993 after being banned for some three decades following the country's independence from British colonial rule.
The monarchs of such kingdoms are often beloved but hold no formal power. Instead they are seen as guardians of traditional identity and heritage.

Ukraine’s parliament changes how military budget is cleared, and freezes money behind one of war’s cleverest supply schemes, defense-industry council says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:40:49 UTC
20:40:49 KST

New changes to the legislation from Ukraine's parliament have jammed the money in one of the war's cleverest supply schemes: the system that lets frontline units turn confirmed kills into new weapons. Under the program, known as eBaly, a military unit can earn points for verified strikes on Russian targets and spend them on Ukrainian-made drones and other gear, which the makers deliver first and get paid for later. The makers have kept delivering. The payments have stopped, according to Ihor Fedirko, who runs the Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry.
The freeze is real money to real firms. Fedirko says the companies are owed between $540,000 and several million dollars each for equipment already handed over and have gone roughly two months without payment. It matters because eBaly is not a fringe experiment: units have ordered and received more than 181,000 drones, robots, and electronic-warfare systems through it in 2026, choosing the gear that performs best in combat.
The Ukrainian Council of Defense Industry brings together more than 300 private manufacturers and key associations of Ukraine’s defense-industrial sector.
A budget change froze the money
The problem, Fedirko said, affects every delivery made through eBaly. Under the updated 2026 budget, the split of Ukraine's military income tax stayed the same: 60 percent to the Defense Ministry, 30 percent to the state communications service, and 10 percent straight to military units.
But the ministry's and the communications service's shares now have to be signed off by the Ukrainian National Security Committee.
"Now, the committee approves not individual payments or deliveries but the general directions of spending," Fedirko wrote.
It is unclear what is causing such delays in obtaining signatures on committee decisions and what is lacking to enable swift decision-making.
It is worth noting that the Ebaly system reduces the risk of ministries approving procurement through “their own” companies, since hundreds of companies participate in it and are selected by hundreds of commanders.
Small firms feel it first
For the largest defense companies, a delay of a million or two dollars is a manageable cash-flow gap, Fedirko said. For small ones, the same money was meant to cover wages, buy components, and fund the next production run.
"Some enterprises have already run into problems paying salaries," he wrote.
Producers have spent about two months appealing to the responsible institutions to clear the debt for gear already delivered, without result.

'Our Loves' is a film about people, not October 7, Israeli filmmaker Avi Nesher tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
11:40:29 UTC
20:40:29 KST

‘When something horrible happens to you, you can succumb to the tragedy and get swallowed by the abyss – to paraphrase Nietzsche – or you can say, ‘OK, what do we do now? What do we change?’” said Avi Nesher, whose latest movie, Our Loves, is a beautiful and moving film about ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances. It’s suspenseful, sad, and sometimes even funny, the kind of movie that can change the way you see the world – and yourself. It tells the stories of a group of people “who think they are having the worst day of their lives on October 6, 2023” and who go on to spend much of the movie fighting to survive the attack that begins a day later.
Our Loves will have its world premiere on September 13 at the Toronto International Film Festival, in the prestigious Centerpiece section. It will then open the Haifa International Film Festival on September 26 and will be released in theaters throughout Israel on October 15, prior to an international release.
It is Nesher’s 22nd feature film and probably the most anticipated movie he has ever made. He became one of Israel’s leading directors decades ago when he released the now-classic movies The Troupe (Ha-Lahaka) and Dizengoff 99, back-to-back in the late ’70s. After their success, Hollywood called, and he spent over a decade making genre films there. But he just couldn’t quit Israel and came back in 2001, releasing an extraordinary series of diverse and quintessentially Israeli movies over the last two decades, such as Turn Left at the End of the World (2004) and The Matchmaker (2010).
Now in his early 70s, he might be expected to be winding down his career, especially after his family suffered a tragedy in 2018, when his son Ari was killed in an accident at the age of 17. His daughter, director Tom Nesher, made Come Closer in 2024, a movie about a young woman who loses her brother that was clearly inspired by Ari’s death, but Nesher prefers to make movies that explore his emotions without delving too closely into his biography. Following his loss, he chose to keep working and made some of the best films in recent years, including Image of Victory, a drama about young people on a southern kibbutz during the Independence War.
A film about October 7?
After the Hamas massacre took place on October 7, 2023, it seemed obvious to many that Nesher would want to make sense of the tragedy by creating a film about it, although he didn’t quite see it that way at first.
“I was at home, horrified. Horrified,” he said, when I asked him about his experience on that day. “It was something that couldn’t possibly have happened. It seemed like, somehow, we were getting it all wrong, because this cannot happen. Yes, we can get some missiles shot at Tel Aviv. OK. We can have a few Hamas people penetrating the border. OK. But we cannot have Hamas people inside the kibbutzim. That’s not Israel. That’s not the Israel I grew up in, and it’s not part of my sense of safety living in this country. Hamas people in all those kibbutzim? Unbelievable. People on the roads, people in Ofakim. Oh God, this cannot be happening. And then you go: Where is the government?... No one knew anything.”
The shock brought back memories for him of an earlier war, in which the IDF and government were similarly blindsided. “I’m a veteran of the Yom Kippur War, so I know about impending doom,” he said.
Nesher, who spent much of his adolescence in New York, where his family moved because of his father’s career, and who attended Columbia University, came back to Israel to join the army. He initially served in the elite Sayeret Matkal unit until he sustained an injury and was an intelligence officer when the Yom Kippur War broke out.
“October 7 was even worse, because in 1973, I was a soldier. I had something to do,” he said.
In the weeks following October 7, as he reeled in shock along with the rest of the country, it didn’t cross his mind to make a movie about the attack.
“Early on... there’s just trying to survive, trying to bounce back, grieving. I know a thing or two about losing dear ones. My heart breaks every day,” he said.
The fact that he could empathize so deeply with those who had lost family on October 7 initially made him feel less, rather than more, inclined to make a movie about it. “People asked me if I wanted to make a movie about October 7, and I said, ‘No, no, no. You can’t make a movie about October 7. It has to be done by historians.’”
An unexpected and deeply moving experience soon led him to change his mind, which was connected to the release of his film The Monkey House, a literary mystery/comedy, a week before October 7. It received rave reviews and sold over 100,000 tickets – until the war broke out and the theaters closed.
“But I thought: Who cares about that? There’s so much horror around.” Then he got a call from a man from one of the kibbutzim that was decimated in the massacre, who told him he and his wife had bought advance tickets for the movie and had been looking forward to seeing it on the evening of October 7. Housed in a hotel at the Dead Sea following the massacre, he asked if Nesher could bring them the movie and show it there.
'My last memory of myself as a human being'
Nesher was a bit bewildered by the call. “But then this man said, ‘It’s my last memory of myself as a human being. The last time I remember myself just living my life, just buying tickets. So, please bring your movie.’ I said, ‘Of course I’ll get you the movie. No problem.’ And he says, ‘And I want you to come and talk about the movie.’
“But I said, ‘This I cannot do.’ Because when I had that awful time, with what happened to Ari, if somebody had talked to me about cinema, I would have slapped him. What the f***? And he said, ‘No, no, we’re not like that.’ I told him my own story, which he knew, and he said, ‘No, it’s different. Please come.’ Of course, you cannot say no. I came there, and I went up on stage and apologized. And he said, ‘Please, Mr. Nesher, let’s see the movie.’ They screened the movie, and they laughed. A lot. And they clapped at the end. A lot. I got up on stage, and it was the longest Q&A I’ve ever done in my life.”
It ended so late that he stayed over in the hotel and spent more time with them, learning their stories.
At breakfast, they told him, “‘You see these two young people sitting in a corner? They met on October 7. Because he was running, he had no place to go, and she took a chance and opened her mamad [safe room] and let him in. And now they’re a couple.’ They fell in love. Can you imagine? With all this horror and bloodiness, can you imagine? Suddenly you feel these people are trying somehow to regain sanity. They’re trying to grab hold of what’s left. They kept telling me more about the way they got into October 7, more about what they were doing before October 7, than about October 7. And then someone jokingly said there were some people who actually thought October 6 was the worst day of their lives.”
A movie about the human spirit
This was a lightbulb moment for Nesher. “I said, ‘Really? Like who?’ Mostly people with severe romantic problems or family problems, they said. And I said, ‘Hmm. That’s interesting.’ I thought maybe I could make a movie not ‘about October 7’ – of course, you go into October 7 – but you make a movie about the human spirit, and especially the Israeli spirit, which ultimately triumphs. Then you can make a movie that will give hope.
“Because it seemed to me: You think October 6 is the worst day of your life, then you go through the horrible ordeal. You make it out alive somehow. And then you have to rethink all of your life. If I survived this, how do I make it better? It’s a movie about change… It has to do with a personal, possibly with the national, redemption. Things have to change. I thought that was really interesting.”
He turned to Emilio Schenker, the CEO of the Israel-based, global entertainment company, SIPUR. “Emilio completely understood the vision, which is rare – and they hired three wonderful researchers who scouted and found people who survived October 7 who had personal, romantic, parental, religious, and whatever other kind of problems.”
People opened up to him and his researchers, and he began writing. “My thing was basically to use only what they told me. Not to make anything up. It’s so interesting, because you make a movie whose first third will play almost like a romantic comedy, and then the sky will fall. Then you have to survive somehow. And then, when you come out, you have to reconsider everything, and you have to appreciate life. You have to say, ‘Life is a great gift, and I’m here.’ Again, I know about this stuff because this is pretty much what I went through myself, with Ari.”
Our Loves is true cinema
Our Loves presents a stark contrast to previous movies and television series that have focused on the attack, which were basically reenactments of the experiences of real people with actors. Instead, Our Loves is a carefully shaped dramatic story, true cinema, that features three-dimensional characters and even some darkly funny moments. It opens at a concert on the night of October 5, 2023, where most of the main characters happen to be, for different reasons.
These include a religious young woman, Sapir (Daniel Gimpel), who has just been dumped by a guy she hoped she would marry and who has decided to rebel by attending the Nova music festival, and who ends up running and hiding with a drug dealer (Leib Levin) who keeps his stash in his underwear. There’s also a retired general, Shabi (Shalom Michaelswilli), who is suing his ex-wife to force her to sell their house, which deepens the rift between him and his children, especially his young adult daughter (Noa Cohen). The latter storyline will remind people of several real-life stories of retired generals who grabbed a weapon and headed south when the attack began, but it has a twist.
“This guy was really a son of a bitch. He was a terrible father,” Nesher said. He managed to use this story to insert some comic moments into the film. Many of them involve four hopeless recruits, who have only been in the army a week – “the leftovers of the leftovers of the leftovers” – whom the retired general picks up along the way to help him in his quest.
“Now, in a way, this guy has to become their parent because he has to somehow make them into fighters.” One of the most moving and surprising aspects of the story is how, in the course of schooling these bumbling soldiers, the retired general is schooled as well.
“It’s easier being a hero than being a human being,” said Nesher. “I don’t mean to downplay heroism. But some of these people were amazingly flawed as human beings. And they did a heroic deed because it was the right thing to do. But then the event changed them... The trick was to make a movie about people caught in a situation, not about the situation.”
Eventually, he gave the script to Schenker. “Emilio read it and said, ‘This is great writing. It’s not a war movie. It’s about people,’” said Nesher. At a later stage, two important international producers, Danny Cohen, president of Access Entertainment, and Fernando Szew, president and head of FOX Entertainment Studios, signed on as co-producers. Moshe Edery, Nesher’s longtime collaborator, also co-produced the movie for United King Films.
Nesher has made movies about true historical stories in the past, but never before had he done a movie where the majority of the cast and crew had lost friends in the event, and the filming was an emotional roller coaster.
“Interestingly, in the crew we had two girls who were at Nova. They came to work for us in order to deal with the fear of going back. It was amazing to see them dealing with trauma,” Nesher said.
While it is hard to discuss specifics of the plot without revealing spoilers, Our Loves ends with a character uttering the line, “I’m not leaving.”
When asked what the line refers to, Nesher mentioned a moment in this character’s storyline but agreed that it could have a deeper significance as well. I asked whether, on some level, it is he who is making this affirmation, especially since he could have stayed in Hollywood and been sitting by his pool today.
He acknowledged that was true. “Obviously, it’s appropriate for this character to be saying this, but this message is my message… Yeah, I could have stayed in Hollywood and made American movies. Easily.”
The movie has gotten great word-of-mouth reaction from previews in Israel, and Nesher spoke with anticipation about showing it abroad. It will be the sixth time one of his movies has premiered at Toronto, although a few things will undoubtedly be different this time around.
“The great thing about the Toronto Film Festival is that they’ve always stood for great cinematic values. As opposed to other festivals that are about ideology – if you say the right word, they’ll get you in – Toronto was always about cinema. They have great taste. They have great people selecting films. I guess they just saw the movie and thought it belonged. That’s why they put it in Centerpiece, which has great movies. I salute these people, and I salute this festival and all the values it stands for,” he said.
Israeli movies in the current film industry
He is aware, of course, that many in the film industry have called for all Israeli movies to be boycotted.
“In the ’60s we knew how to protest – all these great antiwar marches. But they were against the US government. Against Robert McNamara. LBJ, against the Vietnam War... Nobody thought for a second of boycotting Hollywood. Nobody thought for a second of boycotting American literature or American music or Andy Warhol.”
Nesher is no cheerleader for the Israeli government and spoke openly about his hope that the elections will bring a change in leadership. Noting that at the time of the October 7 attack, about half of all Israelis were fighting to preserve and strengthen democracy against government interference, he said, “As always, at the forefront of every fight for democracy are people from the arts. So, you want to stay away from movies and culture and handicap the people fighting for democracy?... Either you are really stupid, which I don’t think you are, or there is a tinge of antisemitism in this, because you did not boycott Iranian art. You did not boycott the art of any other country when you disagreed with their government.”
He knows that there may be protests in Toronto against Our Loves, and he is ready for them. “For me, this conflict is not about land. The conflict is about story. The conflict is about narrative,” and he is eager to present this narrative to audiences.
He is also well aware that he is likely to be asked why the story is not told, at least in part, from the perspective of the Hamas terrorists.
“Actually, I got an offer from an Italian producer: If I would do Our Loves like Image of Victory [which features a major character who is an Egyptian photojournalist embedded with Egyptian troops], he would come in with an investment of a million euros,” said Nesher.
“I told this producer, ‘Sadly, I cannot do it.’ In Image of Victory, I could write the Egyptian side because the Egyptian side was just like us, only in Arabic,” he said. “But Hamas is a whole different thing. It’s like ISIS... I would not know how to direct Charles Manson, how to tell his story. I just would not know.”
When it comes to Hamas, “I do not know how to direct people who did these horrible things... I do not understand the guy who gets pleasure out of killing a baby, out of burning families alive. So, I did not take the money. And we made the movie anyway.”
Toward the end of Our Loves, some characters make it to a hospital, and the doctor in charge is an Arab physician, played by Hisham Suliman.
“Twenty percent of the population is Arab, and they’re going to remain here, and there has to be a way of making it work,” he said. “The truth is, it simply wouldn’t be realistic if I showed a hospital in Israel without Arab employees. But beyond that, it makes a point: Let’s not get confused. Arabs are not our enemy. Hamas is our enemy. It’s a whole different thing.”
The more he talks, the more it becomes obvious that he is the perfect director to tell this story right now: An Israeli who is equally comfortable in America, but also an ardent Zionist who cares deeply about what happens in Israel. It’s clear from his personal story that he empathizes with grieving families and can identify with all those who suffered loss on October 7 and since. And he wants to fight back with the most potent weapon he knows – story.
“That’s the beauty of cinema. Cinema gets you to accept a different normal than the one you’ve been told before… And again, there’s this Israeli spirit, which I have admired since young childhood. I think that’s why we all live in this country even though it makes no sense at all. We’re not going anywhere. We’re not leaving,” he said, echoing his movie’s last line.
