Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:00:24 UTC
13:00:24 KST

Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.
Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.
In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.
The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.
A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo.
The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said.
“Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.”
Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said.
The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym for chocolate-flavoured coffee.
Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.
Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck.
Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014.
By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. 
The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through.
But if the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.
The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.
The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.
“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.”
Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high.
This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide.
“Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.”
On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock.
“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”

====================================================================================================

Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:00:23 UTC
13:00:23 KST

A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order.
Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment.
With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period.
It is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany.
The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month.
“This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany,” he said on Monday.
Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces. Pivotal elections are due next year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland.
Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is the wrong man at such a consequential crossroads, calling him a ham-fisted and empathetically challenged leader who is erratic in his messaging.
Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University.
“The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutory pension and healthcare schemes.
The former chancellor Angela Merkel, Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, has criticised him publicly for his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes.
“This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.”
Speaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts.
Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’”
The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016 refugee influx, when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship.
Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government under Olaf Scholz. He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system.
His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems.
Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He had infamously accepted support from the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests.
As “irregular” arrivals of migrants have fallen sharply since Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain ground far beyond its eastern heartland.
The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the “firewall” strategy of shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change.
Biebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity.
As well as the threat from Russia, he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such as car manufacturing, and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports.
“None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebricher told public radio.
Merz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes.
The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice.
“Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich of Die Zeit newspaper.
“The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.”
Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder.
Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists have long disparaged as counterproductive.
Yet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent.
Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular.
During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out the threat it poses to German democracy, Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits.
He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair.
Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.”

From content creators to organised fan groups, state media and local authorities urge greater awareness of boundaries and restraint
Authorities in China are taking content creators, fan groups and online platforms to task as their aggressive pursuit of online traffic upends lives and public services across the country.
State media and local authorities have called on these parties to exercise restraint and stop attention-seeking behaviour from getting out of control.
The warnings followed a wave of public attention that hit a 75-year-old man and his wife in Shaoxing in eastern Zhejiang province this month.
Crowds of visitors, live streamers and photographers descended on the couple’s home to see seven gourds growing on their balcony, a scene reminiscent of Calabash Brothers, a popular Chinese animated series released in 1986.
The series follows seven magical brothers born from gourds and raised by their grandfather. Videos and images of the couple in Shaoxing and their gourds quickly went viral, with internet users dubbing the man “Grandpa Calabash”.
However, as more visitors began gathering outside the home, taking photographs, live-streaming, calling out “grandpa” and knocking on the door, what began as an expression of affection increasingly disrupted the couple’s daily life, eventually leading them to cut down all the gourds last Saturday.

When Indonesia burns, these women run towards the fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
04:00:08 UTC
13:00:08 KST

When Indonesia burns, these women run towards the fire
Meet the all-female volunteer brigade risking their lungs and lives to fight Indonesia’s devastating wildfires
Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick, yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home.
She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives straight into the impenetrable smog emanating from wildfires devouring the peatland and ancient forests of Borneo.
“I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother told This Week in Asia, moments before disappearing into the murk that has settled over the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan.
Irma, who like many Indonesians only goes by one name, is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit that heads out every day during the dry season to battle blazes smouldering deep beneath the island’s peatlands.
They fight fires lit, deliberately or otherwise, by the agricultural burning of poor farming communities clearing land the cheapest way they know how. This year, those fires arrived earlier and burned harder than most can remember, fuelled climate anomalies and drought conditions.
“We are the ones who feel its effects most,” said Irma, who is the group’s coordinator, explaining that it was women who were left to care for housebound children through increasingly long stretches of the year.

Taiwan’s Hsiao welcomed at conference in birthplace of European federalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
03:59:37 UTC
12:59:37 KST

Ventotene is a small island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, two hours by ferry from the Italian coast. In 1941, three anti-fascist prisoners confined there — Altiero Spinelli, Ernesto Rossi and Eugenio Colorni — wrote the manifesto that is usually taken as the founding text of European federalism.
On Friday, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) spoke at the second Ventotene European Conference for Freedom and Democracy, on a panel with European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, former Italian foreign affairs undersecretary Gianni Vernetti and journalist Antonio Talia.
She traveled with Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). Among the other guests were Yulia Navalnaya, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and 2022 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk.
Hsiao’s presence was kept quiet until the delegation had landed, a precaution Taipei has used before when senior leaders travel. Picierno, who convened the conference, announced it herself on the morning of the panel and explained why the announcement had waited.
“No one can decide who is hosted in Ventotene and who is not,” she said, adding that freedom of debate is not something to be negotiated with autocracies. Beijing lodged what its foreign ministry calls “solemn representations” with Rome and with the EU, and described the initiative as futile. The conference continued as scheduled.
Beijing’s reaction was predictable. What deserves more attention in Taipei is what the visit says about a relationship that has been growing steadily and with very little noise for the past three years.
Positioning
Relations between Rome and Taipei have always been conducted in a narrow space, and both sides have become very good at using it. When Italy recognized China in November 1970, the one point its negotiators secured was a matter of wording: the joint communique recorded a Chinese “declaration” on Taiwan rather than a “position,” and Italy took note of it.
Taiwan, for its part, declared relations ceased from the moment of recognition, keeping the initiative on its own side. That vocabulary has held for more than half a century, and everything built since has been built inside it — from the representative offices opened in the 1990s to the double-taxation agreement of 2015.
Four cross-party delegations have traveled from the Italian Parliament to Taipei in the past 20 months, more than in the previous decade. In January 2025, a group led by Marco Osnato, chair of the Chamber’s Finance Committee, met officials of the Mainland Affairs Council.
In September the same year, a second delegation attended Semicon Taiwan. In January, a third brought together members of six parties, from the governing coalition to the opposition, and toured Hsinchu Science Park.
In the first days of this month, 10 members of the Italy–Taiwan Interparliamentary Friendship Group — established in 1992 and chaired by Senator Lucio Malan — led by Senate Vice President Gian Marco Centinaio on his fifth visit, were received by President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) and opened the Italian pavilion at Semicon.
Lai thanked them for the Italian law that now protects Taiwanese artworks lent to Italian museums from seizure. Centinaio told him that supporting Taiwan means supporting the whole free world.
The exchanges run in the other direction too, and at a higher level each time. In October 2025, Foreign Minister Lin came to Rome as the guest of representative Vincent Y.C. Tsai (蔡允中) to inaugurate the renovated Taipei Representative Office. Nine senators and nine deputies from both the majority and the opposition attended, a few weeks before the Italy–China Intergovernmental Committee met in the same city.
Two-way trade
In June 2026, former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) spent several days in Italy for the Global Women Leaders Summit on Lake Como, meeting parliamentarians from across the political spectrum, scholars, students and business representatives.
She was received at Palazzo Madama, the seat of the Italian Senate, by Centinaio and Malan, whose group counts some 90 members, roughly 15% of the two chambers. This week, the vice president came, with the foreign minister beside her.
GlobalWafers has invested more than NT$11.0 billion (300 million euros) in Novara, in Piedmont, in what became last October the largest 300-millimeter silicon wafer facility in Europe. An Italian Chamber of Commerce in Taiwan was founded in 2025, and a second Taipei representative office opened in Milan in 2023 to serve the industrial north. Two-way trade reached NT$197.6 billion in 2024.
Vernetti, who shared the panel with Vice President Hsiao, went to Taiwan in 2007 while serving as undersecretary for foreign affairs. He went formally on holiday, because that was the only way to go.
Nineteen years later, he sat beside Taiwan’s serving vice president on an Italian island that Europeans regard as the birthplace of their union. The pair talked about how democracies defend one another. The formal framework has not moved an inch. Almost everything inside it has.

A Russian government official will attend next week’s G20 energy meeting in Houston, the White House confirmed Friday, just weeks after Moscow’s return to an in-person G20 ministerial gathering triggered protests from European officials over Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
The G20 Ministerial Meeting on Energy Abundance will run from Monday through Wednesday, Sept. 14-16, with US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright and White House official Jarrod Agen among those attending.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Energy officials from Europe and Asia are also expected at the three-day gathering.
The White House has not disclosed the identity of the Russian representative.
Europeans bristled at Russia’s G20 return
The Russian presence comes less than two weeks after the country’s Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended a G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina – the first time Russia’s finance minister had participated in person since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
His attendance angered European officials, who warned against any normalization of relations with Moscow while Russia continues its war.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil called the signal sent by receiving Siluanov as a regular participant “quite troubling” and said he would have preferred greater clarity from Washington that the Russian minister should not be treated as a normal guest.
Zelensky Warns of Global Food Crisis, Urges Faster Sanctions on Russia
European ministers and central bankers also opposed appearing alongside Siluanov in the traditional G20 “family photo.” Organizers ultimately took the photograph without the Russian minister.
The disagreement highlighted differing approaches toward Moscow as Washington maintains direct engagement with Russian officials while European governments continue pushing for stronger economic pressure over the invasion of Ukraine.
Russia sanctions vote could coincide with talks
The Russian official could arrive in Houston just as the US House of Representatives considers another sanctions package targeting Moscow.
The Senate has already passed the legislation 86-11. The measure would impose additional penalties on Russian officials and authorize tariffs against countries purchasing large quantities of Russian energy. The House Rules Committee is expected to take up the bill Monday.
The Trump administration imposed its first Russia sanctions over the Ukraine war in October 2025, targeting oil giants Rosneft and Lukoil by freezing assets and blocking transactions.
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he had recently held a “great” conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin and said the Kremlin leader wanted an agreement to end the war.
However, intelligence officials in the US, Ukraine and Europe remain skeptical that Putin is genuinely seeking to end Russia’s invasion, Reuters reported.
Houston on road to Miami G20 summit
The Houston gathering is among a series of ministerial meetings leading to the G20 Leaders’ Summit, scheduled for Dec. 14-15 at Trump National Doral near Miami.
Russia is expected to be invited to the leaders’ summit as a G20 member. The Kremlin said earlier this year that Putin may attend but had not decided whether he would travel to Miami. A US official told Reuters that Russia would be invited to G20 ministerial meetings and the leaders’ gathering.
Putin has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019, with his absence in subsequent years shaped first by the COVID-19 pandemic and then by the international fallout from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Drones attack Tolyatti and Taganrog in Russia, sparking fires at industrial sites – photos, videos

Source: Monitoring Telegram channels; Samara Oblast Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev
Details: Early reports from monitoring Telegram channels indicate that the KuibyshevAzot chemical plant in Tolyatti may have been targeted. Eyewitnesses posted videos showing a fire at an industrial site in the city.

Meanwhile, a series of explosions was heard in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, followed by several fires.
According to an Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) analysis by Russian media outlet Astra, one of the columns of smoke is rising from the area of Taganrog-Central air base, which is home to Russia's 708th Military Transport Aviation Regiment.
The 325th Aircraft Repair Plant is also located near the air base. It specialises in the repair of transport aircraft and the manufacture of components for them.
In addition, satellite images from NASA's FIRMS system have captured fires on the premises of TagAZ, an automotive assembly plant located in Taganrog. Monitoring Telegram channels reported that a storage tank had caught fire.
The site of the defunct car plant is used for various industrial and military purposes, including the assembly of strike drones.
Fedorishchev reported overnight that air defence had repelled a "large-scale UAV attack".
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported that operations at Kurumoch International Airport in Samara had been suspended.
At present, the nature and extent of the damage at the Russian facilities require confirmation. The editorial team is unable to independently verify social media reports in real time.
Background: Drones attacked the city of Tolyatti in Russia's Samara Oblast on the night of 3-4 April. Two chemical plants, Tolyattikauchuk and KuibyshevAzot, were hit.

Ukrainian forces struck multiple Russian military and industrial targets on Sept. 12, including the Tolyattikauchuk rubber plant in Samara Oblast and FPV-drone production and air-defense facilities in Taganrog, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Ukraine's military said.
Ukrainian long-range drones struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Samara Oblast and a fire broke out on its premises, according to Ukraine's General Staff. The extent of the damage was still being assessed.
"The Tolyattikauchuk plant specializes in the production of synthetic rubbers, monomers, fractions and high-octane gasoline additives," the General Staff said. "Synthetic rubbers, in particular, are used in the production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles."
Known as "Russia's Motown," Tolyatti is located about 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border and is home to Russia's largest state-owned car manufacturer AvtoVAZ.
Footage from residents of Tolyatti purportedly show Ukrainian drones flying over the city with a building on fire, billowing smoke. Other videos appear to show damage to a residential building caused by a downed drone, Supernova+ reported.
Previously, Ukrainian drones hit a rubber factory in Tolyatti on June 12. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the attack, as well as damage to the plant, the products of which are used in the "further production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles."
In Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, Zelensky said SBU forces struck an FPV-drone production facility, drone storage warehouses, an oil-products tank, a radar system, and a Pantsir-S2 air-defense system.
The city, on the coast of the Sea of Azov, is around 40 kilometers (25 miles) east of the Ukrainian border.
Resident footage from Taganrog show large fires, reportedly from an airfield near the city, according to Supernova+, with smoke plumes rising into the sky. NASA's FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) shows multiple fires burning in the city.
Zelensky also said Ukrainian long-range strikes over the past day hit another chemical industry facility in Russia's Perm region and a target in the Black Sea. He added that Ukrainian forces had destroyed a Su-33 aircraft and two Mi-8 helicopters in the Krasnodar and Rostov regions earlier in the week, and struck an oil facility in Perm.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the damage.
The strikes come amid Kyiv's continuing long-range drone campaign against Russian manufacturing plants aiming to cripple industries supplying the nation's military.
On Sept. 9, Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept. 1 warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drones.

Mexican law enforcement has said it rescued eight people who had been forcibly recruited by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of the country’s most powerful and violent drug trafficking organisations.
The eight people were found at a clandestine clinic on a farm in the municipality of Tecalitlan, in the western state of Jalisco, roughly 160 kilometres (100 miles) from Guadalajara, the AFP news agency reported.

I apologize for the wording; let’s put it in quotation marks.

Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

King Oyo, once world's youngest monarch, buried in western Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12

King Oyo, once world's youngest monarch, buried in western Uganda
KAMPALA, Sept 12 - Ugandan king Oyo Nyimba, long the world's youngest monarch, was buried on Saturday among the tombs of his royal forebears as his Tooro Kingdom looked to put a bitter succession battle behind it.
Oyo's appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at age 3. Images of the toddler king donning a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.
He died last month at 34 in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.
Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the British colonial era and are seen as bulwarks of traditional identity and heritage.
At a church service before the burial, Oyo, who became a U.N. goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and AIDS, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.
"Although he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun," said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.
Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo's casket through the streets of the kingdom's capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.
ARCHBISHOP CALLS FOR UNITY AFTER SUCCESSION BATTLE
The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo's coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.
A committee consisting of members of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.
But the late king's immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom's prime minister said he had a son in the statement announcing his death.
Supporters of Kijanangoma's succession say Oyo's family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.
A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma's succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.
The Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kazimba Mugalu, called for unity.
"Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict," he told mourners. "It can even destroy the legacy of the king we are mourning."
LATE KING WAS CHAMPION OF FIGHT AGAINST HIV, FRIEND OF GADDAFI
Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.
In addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning against HIV and AIDS, Oyo cultivated close ties with former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.
The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a lower profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.
Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

'Who Is American?' Exploring the complicated history of Jewish citizenship in the US - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
03:02:48 UTC
12:02:48 KST

Citizenship confers “the right to have rights,” philosopher Hannah Arendt wrote in 1951. “Remove that priceless possession, and there remains a stateless person, disgraced and degraded in the eyes of his countrymen.”
In Who Is American? Belonging and the Question of Jewish Citizenship, Prof. Lila Corwin Berman (professor of American Jewish history at New York University), author of Metropolitan Jews, challenges the widely held assumption that, in contrast to Europe, Jews in the United States were granted citizenship routinely and without controversy.
Amid periodic “stress tests” of “legal belonging,” Berman demonstrates that judges, legislators, and litigants often revisited classifications of Jews as “a race,” “nationality,” and “religion,” to determine their status and the status of other groups. And the founding of the State of Israel informed the adoption of dual citizenship.
Immensely informative, Who Is American? provides a timely reminder that, perhaps inevitably, legal definitions of citizenship are contested and often unsettling works in progress.
Throughout the 19th century, Berman indicates, Jews cited George Washington’s complimentary 1790 letter to a Jewish congregation in Newport, Rhode Island, as evidence that they had been – and should be – accepted as citizens of the US.
But as pressure to restrict immigration mounted in the early 20th century, lawyers representing the American Jewish Committee lobbied a congressional committee to remove “Hebrew” from the racial classifications in the reporting of immigration statistics. Since Jewishness indicated a religious identity, they argued, Jews should not be separated from annual summaries of the numbers of emigrants from the nations in which they had resided.
Jews granted 'extraordinary exception' for citizenship
In 1909, after the Federal Naturalization Service denied citizenship to four Armenians because they were not “free white persons,” a federal judge opined that in this respect the Armenians did not differ from Jews, “a true race,” whose “origins were Asiatic.” After noting as well that the Christian religion was “born in Palestine,” and that recently, Hebrews had “suffered most cruelly among all men on Earth from European hatred and contempt,” Judge Francis Cabot Lowell determined that until Congress clarified its definition of “whiteness,” the “extraordinary exception” of citizenship for Jews should become the rule.
Between 1924 and 1965, the federal government set nationality quotas for admission of immigrants to the US and grants of citizenship. Many legislators and judges doubted whether Jews had developed an allegiance to the country from which they had emigrated.
The Jewish nationalism, Zionism, and the establishment of the State of Israel, Berman writes, fed suspicions “that Jews constituted a separate nationality dedicated exclusively to their own political ideologies and inherently incapable of loyalty to another nation.”
Such concerns contributed to the enactment of laws defining behavior that could trigger a loss of citizenship: residence in an immigrant’s native country for two years; a woman’s marriage to a foreigner; oaths of fealty to, serving in the army of, or voting in a foreign nation. Jewish organizations declared that this legislation relegated naturalized citizens “to the status of second-class citizens.”
At the end of the 1970s, the Supreme Court affirmed that only citizens had the power to declare themselves expatriates.
Orthodox Jews, Berman reminds us, were among several religious groups that challenged laws requiring businesses to close on Sunday. Forced to lose revenue or give up their own belief in Shabbat, they implied that laws reflecting Christian values hindered them from exercising their rights as citizens.
In 1961, however, the Supreme Court affirmed the constitutionality of Sunday closing laws.
Nonetheless, antisemites declared the litigation had been driven by money, not religious conviction. Even justice Felix Frankfurter, a Jew, asked, presumably tongue-in-cheek, whether Orthodox Jewish shops marked their telegraph paper as kosher.
By contrast, efforts to persuade the Supreme Court to outlaw prayer in public schools were successful, though they contributed to the growth of a narrative of Christian victimhood, accompanied by anti-Jewish sentiment, that has recently resulted in a restoration of Bible readings and postings of the Ten Commandments in classrooms in some states.
Who is American? details intertwined issues surrounding Jewish citizenship
Who is American? concludes with a detailed analysis of debates surrounding a series of intertwined, controversial issues:
Are Jews among the “protected classes” covered by Title VI of the Civil Rights of 1964, which addresses discrimination in public accommodations, voting, and employment based on “race, color, or national origin,” but does not mention religion”?
Should Jews (who suffered from quotas in the past) join white and Asian applicants to college, claiming to be victims of illegitimate uses of Title VI, including affirmative action?
Should Jews accept race as a legitimate legal definition of Jewishness because Jews had been and continued to be discriminated against as if they were a separate race? Or should race – which US Supreme Court chief justice John Roberts deemed “an artificial category,” prone to manipulation, in a Supreme Court decision declaring affirmative action unconstitutional – no longer provide a foundation for any laws or policies?
As the 20th century ended, racial identity was increasingly regarded as “constructed,” Berman suggests, and legal categories affecting citizenship are now more “malleable” than ever.
In the 21st century, and more aggressively when US President Donald Trump was president in his first term, the Office of Civil Rights declared some speech or action related to Zionism and Israel a unique form of discrimination and intervened to protect Jewish students from rhetoric and behavior deemed antisemitic.
Once resistant to classifying Jews as a “protected class,” most Jewish organizations in the United States have accepted what, for the moment, seems popular and perhaps inevitable.
That said, Berman warns of the danger inherent in “moving law from principle to weapon,” operating, however well-intentioned, “as a targeted strike, advancing just one group, one political ideology, one right.”■
The reviewer is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin emeritus professor of American studies at Cornell University.
WHO IS AN AMERICAN? BELONGING AND THE QUESTION OF JEWISH CITIZENSHIP
By Lila Corwin Berman
Princeton University Press
258 pages; $32

====================================================================================================

'Sarah: Text and Presence' offers a 21st-century reimagining of traditional Jewish texts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
03:02:04 UTC
12:02:04 KST

Sarah: Text and Presence represents an electrifying vision of what can happen when we take traditional text – full of magic and mystery in itself – and, with our 21st-century sensibility, give it wings to soar. When two of Jerusalem’s powerhouse directors unite to dream up a new form of engagement, I want to see it with my own eyes, and I will.
Sarah: Text and Presence is the second collaboration between Theatre Company Jerusalem (TCJ) and Theater and Theology. Created and performed by their respective directors, Gabriella Lev and Yael Valier, it draws on materials from TCJ’s iconic Hebrew play Sara Take 2. This new project differs in a number of ways from the first collaboration, Shards of Laughter, which played to packed houses earlier this year.
Shards was conventional theater, solo and intimate, telling a personal story. In contrast, Sarah: Text and Presence, billed as “a performative beit midrash,” is an experimental interactive event featuring multiple genres and performers. Live music, biblical and midrashic texts, and contemporary writing are interwoven with performances of monologues by Aliza Elion Israeli and haiku poetry by Sara Tropper, along with special light design by John Krug.
What can ancient art tell us about living in modern times?
Lev explains what, for her, is the driving force behind this production: “As a theater artist living through the two great events of our decade – the pandemic and Oct. 7 – I keep returning to one question: where is theater in such a time and what is its duty? These are not small disturbances: what can this ancient art still do in the face of them?” For her, the answer lies in the genre’s most basic quality: “Theater depends upon presence. Deep human contact is becoming increasingly rare. In theater, people go to sit in a room with strangers and experience something together, to share the same time and air. That cannot be reproduced by a screen.”
Valier observes: “In Jewish tradition, learning is interactive. We’ve made the paired debate chevruta study model three-dimensional, bringing text into dialogue with actors and audience, and drawing also on imagination, humor, association, interpretation, and empathy.” She too makes the connection with our time: “I think the moment demands that we climb out of artistic boxes and use whatever performance, music, text, conversation, and imagination can give us.”
This collaboration is a dream come true for both women. Lev notes: “Despite our different theatrical histories, Yael and I are both interested in Jewish text as living material, moving beyond conventional theater and changing the relationship between performer, text, and audience.” This move required courage: “The challenge in this hybrid play and beit midrash form is that the artists surrender some control to the living energy in the room, so the form has to be strong enough to hold it,” says Lev.
Sarah: Text and Presence in the words of its creators
How does ‘Sarah: Text and Presence’ build on the earlier play ‘Sara Take 2’?
GL: It inherits a great deal – and yet this is not ‘Sara Take 3,’ it is a new event.
Sara Take 2 emerged from a lecture by Avivah Zornberg and a central question we were asking ourselves: how can we recover the woman’s voice within our ancient texts? That production included monologues by the late Aliza Elion Israeli and innovative vocal work from my sister Ruth Wieder-Magan. We also developed Theatre-Beit Midrash and Midrash-Bama, in which the audience first studied the texts and then encountered our theatrical derash. This work has now been fundamentally renewed in Sarah: Text and Presence.
Why Sarah?
GL: Sarah is a figure full of contradictions, and contradiction is inherently theatrical. And the midrashic association of Sarah’s cries with the shofar means that we can ask, ‘What is Sarah saying now, and what do we hear in her voice today?’ In the new work, she is also placed within the larger landscape of the hagim: beginnings, re-creation, gratitude and celebration.
What is exciting about this production?
YV: What excites me about this piece is the way it expands text learning through theater. The Talmud itself – especially in aggadic passages – often thinks poetically and associatively, allowing ideas to emerge through juxtaposition, image, and resonance. Many people have lost both the habit and the pleasure of learning this way. A performative beit midrash can help kickstart that mode of engagement. I hope that audiences, especially those used to more conventional theater, will take the plunge and come along with us.
GL: I’ve long wanted to create an event that is “unplugged,” without amplification, microphones, or lighting effects. I’m also excited by the meeting between very old material and the present moment, and by how the text’s meaning is changed through what surrounds it: candlelight, the shofar, celebratory haikus by poet Sara Tropper, and live acoustic music from composer-cantor Daniel Fox.
History changes meaning too. These words are being spoken after COVID and Oct. 7, in a society that has experienced profound rupture. The words may sometimes be identical. We are not.

Gulf bloc condemns drone attack on Saudi pipeline from Iraq
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
03:01:07 UTC
12:01:07 KST

Merve Aydogan
12 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) secretary-general on Friday condemned "in the strongest terms" a drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline in the capital Riyadh and Madinah regions, which Riyadh said originated from Iraq and caused injuries and property damage.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said the attack represents "a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its territorial integrity, and its vital installations," describing it as "a flagrant violation of the principles of international law."
He urged Iraq to intensify efforts and take "necessary, decisive measures" to prevent its territory from being used as a launchpad for such attacks.
Albudaiwi reaffirmed the council's "complete and steadfast solidarity" with Saudi Arabia, voicing "full support for all measures and actions the Kingdom takes to protect its security, stability, territorial integrity, facilities, citizens, and residents."
No retaliation ‘at this stage’ from Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia said earlier Friday that it had shut down the East-West Pipeline as a precautionary measure after several drones struck the oil pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions on Thursday morning.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said several people were injured and received medical treatment, while the attacks also caused damage to the pipeline. Emergency and technical teams were deployed to secure the facility and assess its condition.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the drones originated from Iraq. Riyadh said it had decided not to retaliate "at this stage" after Iraq's prime minister asked Saudi Arabia to allow Baghdad to take measures to prevent further attacks launched from Iraqi territory.
Saudi Arabia said it supported Baghdad's efforts but reserved the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security, and infrastructure.
Iraq condemned the attacks and said its territory and airspace "will not be a launching point for attacks against any country."
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, also commander-in-chief of the nation’s armed forces, ordered an investigation into the attacks and directed authorities to take legal action against anyone found to have been involved.
Rising tensions
Tensions between Riyadh and Baghdad had already risen in July after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted several drones launched from Iraq toward oil facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh region. Riyadh blamed Iranian-backed militias and urged Baghdad to prevent Iraqi territory from being used for attacks against the kingdom.
Iraq subsequently formed a joint security committee aimed at preventing unauthorized attacks on neighboring countries.
The dispute escalated on July 29, when US and Saudi forces carried out strikes on sites belonging to the Iranian-aligned Popular Mobilization Forces in Iraq. The PMF said 20 members were killed and 32 others wounded.
Saudi Arabia said the operation was carried out in self-defense following attacks from Iraq on its petroleum facilities.
The East-West Pipeline provides Saudi Arabia with a strategic alternative for exporting crude through the Red Sea as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted by the US war against Iran.

What is AGI? How China’s AI firms are catching up as OpenAI Astra sparks debate
A primer on what AGI means, where top Chinese AI developers stand, and how Chinese policymakers view the technology
As China races to close the gap with the US, leading Chinese AI companies are declaring their ambitions to pursue AGI, even as Beijing appears to maintain a cautious stance towards the concept.
Here is a primer on what AGI means, where top Chinese AI developers stand, and how Chinese policymakers view the technology.
What is AGI?
There is no single definition for AGI, though it broadly refers to systems that match or surpass human-level intelligence.
First coined by US physicist Mark Gubrud in 1997, the term was popularised in the 2000s by computer scientists Ben Goertzel – author of the book Artificial General Intelligence – and Shane Legg, co-founder of Google DeepMind.
Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have triggered new efforts to define it.
A widely cited paper in December by researchers – including Dan Hendrycks from the Center for AI Safety and Dawn Song from the University of California, Berkeley – defined AGI as AI matching the “versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult” across 10 cognitive components, such as reading and reasoning.

Iran obtained Chinese satellite images before deadly strike on US troops, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
02:59:47 UTC
11:59:47 KST

Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery from Chinese sources before carrying out a missile attack on a U.S. air base in Jordan that killed three American soldiers, U.S. officials familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal.
The officials described the finding as the clearest evidence to date that Chinese support for Iran has had lethal consequences for U.S. forces.
They said Washington had linked the imagery to the July 17 attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in northeastern Jordan, where Iranian ballistic missiles struck a residential compound housing U.S. troops.
Three American soldiers were killed and four others wounded. U.S. officials also told the Journal that Iran targeted manned and unmanned aircraft stationed at the base.
The officials did not identify the Chinese entities that supplied the imagery and did not accuse the Chinese government of direct involvement. Iran obtained satellite images both before and after the attack, they said.
The disclosure threatens to add another source of tension between Washington and Beijing less than two weeks before Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due to meet President Donald Trump at the White House on September 24.
U.S. officials have grown increasingly frustrated over what they describe as Beijing's refusal to address repeated warnings that Chinese companies have been supplying Iran with satellite imagery that could be used to target American personnel and military assets in the Middle East.
Senior U.S. officials raised the satellite imagery linked to the July 17 attack directly with Chinese counterparts, according to the Journal, but Beijing rejected the allegations and demanded evidence.
Chinese officials have repeatedly dismissed Washington's concerns and refused to acknowledge that Chinese companies were engaged in such activity, the report said.
China's Foreign Ministry accused "certain parties" of attempting to drag Beijing into the conflict. The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to the Journal's request for comment.
A strike that exposed a growing threat
The attack on Muwaffaq Salti was one of three separate missile strikes on the base within 24 hours and represented a significant escalation in the conflict.
The deaths were the first U.S. military fatalities since the April ceasefire and underscored the difficulty of protecting American personnel even at a heavily defended installation.
They also intensified concerns in Washington over Iran's improving ability to accurately strike U.S. targets.
Trump administration officials had spent months warning their Chinese counterparts that Chinese companies were providing satellite imagery Iran could potentially use to target American forces and assets in the region.
In May, the administration imposed sanctions on several Chinese companies, saying their provision of satellite imagery to Iran "poses a threat to U.S. and allied personnel."
Within three days of the July attack, Iran released high-resolution images showing damage in three separate sections of the Jordanian base.
The Wall Street Journal said its analysis of lower-resolution satellite imagery available to the public showed damage to more than 20 structures across those three areas.
Analysts and former officials cautioned that imagery from Chinese sources was likely only one part of the intelligence picture available to Tehran.
Iran's military also relies on its own satellites and human intelligence networks, while receiving intelligence and imagery from Russia, U.S. officials cited by the Journal said.
Trump seeks to avoid clash with Beijing
The revelations come at a particularly sensitive moment in U.S.-China relations.
Trump has told his team that maintaining a good relationship with China, and with Xi personally, is a top priority, according to the Journal.
U.S. officials have consequently sought to avoid public confrontations with Beijing that could overshadow or disrupt preparations for the September 24 summit.
A White House official told the newspaper that no outside assistance received by Iran had meaningfully improved its ability to attack the United States, without directly addressing the findings concerning the satellite imagery.
Senior administration officials have also publicly played down the significance of any Chinese assistance to Tehran.
Days after the July 17 attack, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.
Asked afterward whether China was supplying Iran with intelligence for targeting purposes, Rubio declined to answer directly, saying that "nothing China did altered in any way the course of the conflict."
The dispute nevertheless adds a new security dimension to the Trump-Xi meeting, as Washington weighs its desire to preserve ties with Beijing against mounting concerns that Chinese technology and commercial services may be strengthening Iran's ability to identify and strike American targets in the Middle East.

Australian scientists say they'll have a live Tasmanian tiger by 2036
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
02:58:12 UTC
11:58:12 KST

in brief
- Scientists are using advanced gene-editing techniques to bring the extinct Tasmanian tiger back to life.
- Researchers hope a living thylacine will walk the Earth by 2036 using surrogate dunnarts.
Scientists hoping to catch a tiger by the gene trail are on the verge of creating a live thylacine before the 100th anniversary of the death of the last-known specimen famously filmed in a zoo.
Using advanced genetics, international scientists are working to bring the legendary marsupial back from extinction.
This week marked the 90th anniversary of the death of the last Tasmanian Tiger in Hobart on September 7, 1936.
The marsupial, an apex predator that once roamed the Australian mainland, was wiped out in its last stronghold by European hunters, habitat destruction and disease.
Drawing on thylacine remains in museums and universities, researchers have already pieced together a full genome in a step toward reviving the species.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Given the progress, lead geneticist for the project at Melbourne University, Professor Andrew Pask, is very hopeful a live thylacine can walk the Earth again in 2036.
Four years ago, he teamed with Colossal Biosciences in the US, and now a large team of scientists is focused on bringing the tiger back, with the technology well advanced and pushing boundaries.
Genetic engineering and editing were now possible at scale, and artificial intelligence helped further, Pask said — the first scientist to put a thylacine gene into a mouse and make it work.
Finding a host mother
When a full genome is sequenced, it's a matter of finding the closest living relative to the extinct species.
In the case of the thylacine, that's a tiny marsupial called the Fat-tailed Dunnart, which is about 99.8 per cent genetically identical to the tiger.
Gene-editing tools are then used to change every bit of code where the dunnart differs from the thylacine, with cloning employed using an egg from a donor dunnart.
"That's part of the technology we're working on at the moment; how we clone, how we take a cell and create a whole animal from it in marsupials," Pask said.
"You build up over time, get closer and closer to live DNA cells of the thylacine. We're in that process now of making all of those edits."
Researchers were also becoming proficient at artificial DNA synthesis, meaning future gene editing could be bypassed, and a thylacine genome could be synthesised.
A dunnart would have no problem birthing a thylacine because the newborn tiger would only be about the size of a grain of rice, Pask said.
"It could probably survive in Mum's pouch for about two weeks so it would get that early milk ... then you would remove it and just hand-rear it from then on."
Undoing the mistakes of the past
Pask said thylacines with slightly different DNA would be produced to ensure diversity and a healthy breeding population.
The rewilded tigers would not need to be taught to hunt and mate as that was hard-wired into them.
Genetic tools are also being developed to protect endangered Northern Quolls from dying after eating cane toads, and Tasmanian Devils from a fatal facial tumour disease.
Rather than tampering with Mother Nature, Pask said scientifically reproducing a live thylacine was about righting human wrongs.
"We tampered with nature when we hunted the thylacine to extinction, and I think we have a moral obligation, now that we have the technology, to bring these animals back," he said.
"We're doing the good thing now of undoing some of the big mistakes that we know we made in the past."

‘Explosive’ planes and bioweapons: CIA declassifies pre-9/11 intel warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
02:51:16 UTC
11:51:16 KST

‘Explosive’ planes and bioweapons: CIA declassifies pre-9/11 intel warnings
The CIA has declassified dozens of presidential intelligence briefings revealing that US officials were warned years before the September 11 attacks that Osama bin Laden and his Al-Qaeda network were considering strikes on American soil involving hijacked or explosive-packed aircraft, while also pursuing biological, chemical, and nuclear weapons.
The agency released 71 President’s Daily Brief (PDB) products on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. The collection, totaling more than 100 pages, is the largest release of CIA presidential intelligence related to the attacks and covers assessments dating from 1998 through the immediate aftermath of September 11, 2001.
Among the most striking documents is a September 1998 memorandum on Bin Laden’s intentions. Intelligence indicated that his “preferred option” was to strike the US “on its own soil in Washington,” the CIA wrote, warning that his network “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city.”
To commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11, CIA released 71 President's Daily Briefs to give Americans a glimpse into our most sensitive intelligence from the years before and day after one of our Nation's darkest moments.https://t.co/Z2QIjcuvAjpic.twitter.com/N8ZoZ2OvtZ
— CIA (@CIA) September 11, 2026
Three months later, another briefing warned that Bin Laden and his allies were preparing attacks in the US, including a plan to hijack an American airliner during the holiday season.
The newly released material also shows persistent concern about unconventional weapons. A February 1998 assessment claimed Bin Laden and other extremists sought to procure unspecified chemical, biological, and nuclear substances. By May 1999, the CIA assessed that Bin Laden was pursuing “a variety of options” for developing these types of weapons. A subsequent briefing in June said trainees at an Afghan camp produced and tested “dozens of toxic chemicals and biological toxins,” and that operatives experimented with adding radioactive material to explosives.
The best-known warning came on August 6, 2001, when then-President George W. Bush received a briefing titled ‘Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US’. It said Bin Laden had wanted to attack the US for years, cited suspicious activity consistent with preparations for hijackings, and noted that the FBI was conducting around 70 investigations into possible Al-Qaeda-linked activity in the country.
By the summer of 2001, then-CIA Director George Tenet later recalled, the intelligence system was “blinking red.”
The 9/11 Commission found that many officials knew “something terrible was planned,” but failures in intelligence sharing, policy, and preparedness prevented the scattered warnings from being turned into action.
Bin Laden rose to prominence during the Soviet war in Afghanistan, when Washington poured billions of dollars into arming anti-Soviet mujahideen through Pakistan. US officials have denied directly funding Bin Laden, but the American-backed war helped create the militant infrastructure and environment from which Al-Qaeda later emerged.
The deadliest terrorist attack in US history, which killed 2,977 people, prompted Washington to launch the War on Terror, invading Afghanistan within weeks and Iraq less than two years later. At home, the PATRIOT Act vastly expanded the government’s powers to spy on its own citizens.

What is celebrated on September 12 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:44:52 EEST
11:44:52 KST

What is celebrated on September 12 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, September 12 is celebrated as Cinema Day and Physical Culture and Sports Day. Around the world, first aid, video games, and South-South cooperation are commemorated.
On September 12, Ukraine celebrates Ukrainian Cinema Day and Physical Culture and Sports Day; worldwide, under the auspices of the UN, South-South Cooperation Day and World First Aid Day are observed, as well as International Video Game Day. According to the new style, the church calendar commemorates Hieromartyr Autonomus and marks the Leave-taking of the Feast of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos; according to the old style, it commemorates Saints Alexander, John, and Paul, Patriarchs of Constantinople, UNN writes.
Ukrainian Cinema Day
An official professional holiday for cinematographers and admirers of domestic screen art, celebrated on the second Saturday of September in accordance with a 1996 decree of the President of Ukraine.
The date is dedicated to the rich history of Ukrainian cinema—from Alfred Fedetsky's first film shoots in Kharkiv at the end of the 19th century, and the silent-film masterpieces of Oleksandr Dovzhenko and the “poetic cinema” of Serhii Paradzhanov and Ivan Mykolaichuk, to contemporary national films that win awards at the most prestigious international film festivals in Cannes, Berlin, and Venice, as well as at the Oscars.
Physical Culture and Sports Day of Ukraine
An official holiday for teachers, coaches, professional athletes, and all supporters of an active lifestyle, celebrated annually on the second Saturday of September in accordance with a 1994 presidential decree.
The event highlights the importance of mass sports and physical education in preserving the nation's health, and also honors the achievements of Ukrainian Olympians and Paralympians, who represent athletics, boxing, swimming, football, and other sports disciplines on the world stage.
United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation
An official UN international observance established by the General Assembly in 2003 to commemorate the adoption on this day in 1978 of the Buenos Aires Plan of Action for Promoting and Implementing Technical Cooperation among Developing Countries.
The day is intended to highlight the economic, political, and social achievements of the regions of the Global South, as well as to promote the exchange of technologies, expertise, trade, and investment among the countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
World First Aid Day
A global medical and social observance established in 2000 by the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, traditionally held on the second Saturday of September.
The event is dedicated to raising public awareness of basic emergency first-aid skills that can save the lives of victims during the first critical minutes after accidents, disasters, or other emergencies.
International Video Game Day
An unofficial holiday for gamers, developers, programmers, and digital artists around the world.
The event celebrates the multibillion-dollar interactive entertainment industry and its historical evolution—from the first text-based games and arcade machines to today’s spectacular esports disciplines, virtual-reality systems, and complex game-design projects with deep storylines.
Leave-taking of the Feast of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers observe the Leave-taking of the Feast of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, concluding the eight-day period of afterfeast for this Great Feast.
On this day, they also commemorate Hieromartyr Autonomus, Bishop of Italy, who moved to Bithynia at the end of the 3rd century during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian, converted many pagans to Christianity, and built a church in honor of the Archangel Michael, where he later suffered a martyr's death at the hands of a pagan mob.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy hierarchs Alexander, John, and Paul, Patriarchs of Constantinople, who in the 4th–6th centuries selflessly defended Orthodox teaching against the Arian and Monothelite heresies. They also remember Saint Alexander of Svir, a prominent ascetic of northern Rus' and the founder of a 15th-century monastery, who became renowned for his ascetic feats, prayer, and strict monastic rule.

We asked teens what they thought of sweeping changes to child protection laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
02:44:29 UTC
11:44:29 KST

Tiwi Island teenagers reflect on changes to NT child protection laws
Surrounded by the ocean, where eucalypt forest stretches from the sand to meet the sky, the Tiwi Islands are a living library for the young people who call it home.
Etched into the landscape are guides on how to live off the land and language that describes their way of life, all of which has taught kids their traditional customs over generations.
The island and its community hold the knowledge that tells the story of each family and how they're connected.
But there are fears these connections to kin and culture are under threat.
These fears are acutely felt by 17-year-old Tiwi Island girls Shanina Kantilla and Tahni Thompson, who are cousins on their mother's side.
Even when they're hundreds of kilometres from home, the islands are never far from their minds.
Shanina recalls a happy childhood spent camping, hunting, swimming and fishing.
"It's very important, especially starting from a young age, learning about our culture, skin groups and also our country … where we inherit our tribes, the sacred sites, ceremony," she said.
Tahni also feels a deep connection to being Tiwi, having returned after spending part of her childhood in Darwin.
"It's like my safe place. Whenever I go to other places, I always feel homesick," she said.
Life on the Tiwi Islands
The Tiwi Islands is known for many things — vibrant artwork, secluded fishing spots and die-hard footy fans — with some of Australia's most renowned AFL players coming out of the region.
"We have a local league of AFL and it gets really hectic around those times," Tahni said.
Tiwi culture is also embedded in the girls' schooling, with weekly lessons on country.
But the real tutoring starts young and comes from within families — grandparents, parents, aunties and uncles.
Shanina's pride in her family traditions shines through as she explains how she's been taught to take wood from the local paper bark trees to weave into baskets.
"We scrape all the wood out and when we're done, we have to boil it and then we fold it, and let it sit for about two, three hours," she said.
"Once it dries up, we come back and start doing our traditional paintings."
Both girls are well aware past government policies prevented this cultural knowledge from being passed down.
"Since the missionaries came, they just changed everything," Tahni said.
"Some of the kids on the other island, [due to] the [Stolen] Generations, don't really speak Tiwi."
From the early 1900s, Catholic missions on the Tiwi Islands controlled much of daily life, influencing where people lived, who they married and the upbringing of their children.
For many families, the policies disrupted the transmission of language, cultural practices and traditional knowledge.
Today, cultural disconnection can take different forms.
Tahni knows this firsthand. Growing up away from her homelands, she felt as though a part of her identity was missing until she returned to the Tiwi Islands.
"I wouldn't want to be taken away from my family," she said.
"I would want to stay with them forever."
Deflating the 'political football'
On the other side of the territory's coastline, as thousands gathered for the Garma festival, First Nations people voiced fears of a renewed threat to kinship systems and culture.
Just weeks before, the Northern Territory government announced changes to child protection laws which critics said weakened the Aboriginal Child Placement Principle.
National Indigenous children's commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter was among those fearing it would lead to more children removed from their communities.
"I'm not here in a battle, I'm here to protect our children and make sure they're safe," she said.
"I feel like it's a bit of political football for everybody, and that's not what our kids should be."
The child placement principle aims to keep Aboriginal children connected to family, community and culture when they enter care.
It prioritises placing children with family in the first instance, then the child's own First Nations community and then other First Nations carers.
But under the NT changes, introduced after the death of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the government no longer needs to try to place a child with their community or a First Nations carer if they can't be placed with family.
Sue-Anne Hunter sees devastating echoes of the past.
"No-one is saying that our children need to be unsafe. If a child needs to be removed, then that's the fact. The thing is that culture is part of safety. It's their identity," she said.
"Maybe they [the NT government] need to have a discussion with some Stolen Generation people about how being disconnected affected their lives."
Ms Hunter spent much of her time at Garma hearing directly from young people, many of whom told her they were anxious about the changes.
"It's front of mind for youth as well," she said.
"We need to be investing in the front end. Family support, getting into families early, not waiting until we're ready to remove them."
A spokesperson for the NT government denied the changes were weakening protections for Aboriginal children.
"These reforms — designed after extensive consultation — created a Universal Child Placement Principle so the same strong provisions apply to every child," they said.
"Additional provisions have been retained for Aboriginal children that reflect their cultural needs and connection to family, community and country."
Child protection isn't the only policy change adding to Ms Hunter's workload.
In recent years the NT lowered the age of criminal responsibility and reintroduced spit hoods, the NT, Victoria and Queensland removed the principle of detention as a last resort for children, Victoria and Queensland brought in "adult crime, adult time" laws and nearly all jurisdictions tightened youth bail.
Ms Hunter said she wished the politicians who attended Garma, including NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, had asked the next generation what they thought of the changes.
"There are a whole lot of people here ready to give some solutions, have some discussions, but it just doesn't seem to be happening," she said.
"It would have been nice if [Ms Finocchiaro] was able to stay, maybe go into the youth forum and listen to the kids."
The NT government spokesperson said lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 10 was about "early intervention and community safety".
"Strong families, cultural connection and early intervention are the best way to break the cycle of youth crime, alongside clear consequences when offending occurs," they said.
'They are just little kids'
Inside the youth forum, Tahni and Shanina reflected on family and friends who had been caught up in the justice system or removed from their families.
"Those ones that are under Territory Families [in out-of-home-care], they don't know our culture much because they only come once a year for a visit around the community," Shanina said.
"It's hard for them to know who their family is, who they are, and their culture … I feel for them."
They were also worried about children as young as 10 being held responsible for crimes.
"Ten years old, they're not really teenagers yet, they are just little kids. They aren't mature enough [to understand]," Tahni said.
"Instead of sending them away, just discipline them on the island and that way they can learn from their mistakes instead of getting them sent off somewhere else.
"[Juvenile detention is] pretty traumatic, and they'll have to carry that trauma for the rest of their lives."
The cousins say there are deeper issues affecting young people and punishment isn't the solution.
"I think younger children have to do counselling, talk about their feelings … instead of getting frustrated. That causes a lot of problems," Shanina said.
As the youth forum began to wind up, Tahni shared her message for the NT government.
"Our voice matters," she said.
"We don't want [Stolen Generations] to happen again.
"If we didn't have culture, we wouldn't know our identity. That's why it's important for us to learn at a young age.
"[Otherwise] there might not be any Tiwi people left. There will just be lost generations."

Ni Gugu is a type of clay sculpture from Xunxian County that makes sounds when blown into. In 2006, it was inscribed on China's national intangible cultural heritage list.
In recent years, Xiyangqitun Village of Xunxian County has focused on the development of Ni Gugu, forming a full chain covering production, study tours, e-commerce and rural tourism. (Xinhua/Zhang Fan)
An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 6, 2026 shows the city view and the Pinglu Canal in Qinzhou City, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Pinglu Canal in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region will become operational on Sept. 16. The 134.2-km canal links the Xijiang River shipping route in the north with the Beibu Gulf in the south. It is China's first major river-to-sea canal project that has been planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949.
Designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal stretches along the country's New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, a strategic route linking China's inland regions with ASEAN and other global markets. For cargo from southwest China, the new route will shorten the inland waterway journey to the sea by about 560 km compared with the route via Guangzhou Port, with overall logistics costs estimated to fall by 18 to 30 percent. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)
