====================================================================================================

Migratory birds face bleak future amid growing threat: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-12
05:25:52 CST
06:25:52 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 11 (Xinhua) -- Intensifying human pressure and climate change are pushing migratory birds toward extinction, undermining ecosystems that people and economies depend on, according to a new report released on Friday.
The sixth edition of State of the World's Birds, subtitled "A focus on migratory species and their flyways," was launched at the BirdLife International Global Partnership Meeting and Global Flyways Summit 2026 in Nairobi.
The report reveals that of the 1,843 migratory bird species worldwide, 11 percent, or one in nine, are threatened with extinction, while 45 percent have declining populations, the report says. Seven species are confirmed or suspected to have been lost in the last 150 years.
"The official announcement in 2025 of the extinction of the slender-billed curlew (Numenius tenuirostris) marks the first global bird extinction in mainland Eurasia and Africa in recent years," says the report.
Compiled by the global conservation organization BirdLife International, the report identifies major threats to migratory birds, including climate change, pollution, invasive species, disease, intensive agriculture, and illegal hunting.
It warns that expanding energy infrastructure, rapid urbanization, human disturbance, and logging are driving high mortality rates among these vital species.
Martin Harper, chief executive officer of BirdLife International, emphasized that migratory birds hold immense cultural, ecological, and economic value, making their protection essential for building ecosystem resilience.
He added that safeguarding these species and critical habitats, such as wetlands, grasslands, forests, and mudflats, will allow local communities to thrive in a healthy environment.
To eliminate these threats, the report urges targeted investments in restoring key flyway biodiversity hotspots, transitioning toward sustainable agriculture, accelerating climate action, and enforcing stricter penalties against illegal hunting.
"Urgent action is needed to scale up conservation for migratory birds, protect the natural world and secure a sustainable future for people and the planet," says the report.
Musonda Mumba, secretary general of the Convention on Wetlands, stated that curbing further loss of migratory birds requires a blend of multilateral cooperation, grassroots awareness, evidence-based policy, and strong legislative action.
The findings provided the evidence base for the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, which was signed at the summit by governments, conservation organizations and financial institutions committing to step up cross-border protection of migratory birds and their habitats.
Kenya hosted more than 120 global conservation partners in Nairobi for the summit. The five-day conference, which opened on Monday and gathered policymakers, conservation leaders and researchers from across Africa, Asia, the Americas, Europe, the Middle East and the Pacific, concluded Friday with the adoption of the declaration. ■

"I got so emotional this time because my PB, which had been untouched for two years, was finally broken, and I found myself again," Deng said.
Deng said she regained her form in the second year after the Paris Olympics and won silver at that year's world championships, her most recent podium finish at a major international event before Friday's victory. However, injuries and difficulties adapting to changes in her climbing technique subsequently kept her off the podium at major events.
"There was a time when I resisted training. I couldn't understand why, after getting my form back, it suddenly dropped again," Deng said.
She credited encouragement from her coach and her goal of winning Olympic gold at the 2028 Los Angeles Games with helping her regain her motivation.
"My head coach Zhang Ning said one thing most often: 'You are Deng Lijuan! You can't give up easily!'" she said.
Deng will next compete at the upcoming Asian Games in Nagoya, where she is expected to face strong competition from Indonesian world record holder Desak Made Rita Kusuma Dewi and other leading Asian climbers.
Asked how she would approach the challenge, Deng replied: "Face it head-on."
Women's speed world record holder Emma Hunt of the United States, one of the pre-race favorites, was eliminated in the round of 16. China's Zhao Yicheng, the men's world record holder, also exited early, while former men's world record holder Samuel Watson of the United States was eliminated in the round of 16.
Hilmi seized his opportunity to claim the men's title in 4.65 seconds, becoming the fourth climber to break 4.70 seconds at a World Climbing Series event this season, joining Zhao, Watson and China's Long Jianguo, the 2025 world champion.
"I'm grateful to get the gold medal. I've been training a lot for this competition," Hilmi said.
The Indonesian said he had been climbing for 12 years and credited the support of his family and team for helping him secure his first World Climbing Series title. He also sent a message to his mother in Indonesian while speaking to the cameras after the race. ■

Passenger train derails in France leaving at least 44 injured
- Published
At least 44 people have been injured, including one seriously, after a passenger train derailed in northern France, local officials have said.
An 18-year-old woman was airlifted in critical condition by helicopter to hospital.
The officials said 186 passengers were on board the train that was operating between Rouen and Caen in Normandy.
Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said 140 firefighters and other emergency teams were deployed to the scene of the crash on Friday evening near Cléon, just south of Rouen.
The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but reports in the French media suggest it could have been an act of sabotage. The authorities have not commented on the issue.
Local authorities activated a mass-casualty response plan after the crash shortly before 20:00 (18:00 GMT).
"Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger," Louis, a passenger on the train, told ICI Normandie radio.
"I couldn't stay in my seat any more. The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I'm still shaking," he added.
Photographs later emerged showing passengers leaving the train, three of whose carriages had overturned, according to French media.

Putin Says Russia Outgrew World—But IMF Data Shows it Is Growing Few Times Slower
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:21:38 UTC
06:21:38 KST

- Category
- World
Putin Says Russia Outgrew World—But IMF Data Shows it Is Growing Few Times Slower
Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, claimed on September 11 that Russia's economy had outpaced global growth over the past three years, despite International Monetary Fund data indicating otherwise.
The remarks, delivered at the BRICS summit in New Delhi, were reported by The Moscow Times on September 11. Putin addressed a gathering that included China's Xi Jinping, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian, and India's Narendra Modi.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Over the previous three years, economic growth rates in Russia exceeded the global average; from 2023 to 2025, GDP added 10.3%," Putin stated. He credited structural changes that, he claimed, had left the economy stronger and more resilient despite more than 30,000 sanctions.
Putin further asserted that Western states imposing those measures had faced severe consequences, including budget deficits, rising public debt, and industrial decline. He put the drop in EU industrial output at 8%.
That figure is not supported by official statistics. According to Eurostat data cited by The Moscow Times, EU industrial production fell in 2023 and 2024 but rebounded sharply in 2025, leaving a three-year decline of roughly 0.6%—far short of the 8% Putin described.
The central claim also diverges from IMF figures. The fund's data show the world economy grew 10.7% across 2023 to 2025, marginally ahead of Russia's 10.3%. Russia expanded faster than the global average in 2023 and 2024, but its growth slowed to 1% in 2025, while the world grew by 3.5%.
Russia's own projections point to a widening gap. The Ministry of Economic Development expects growth of just 0.4% in 2026, against an IMF world forecast of 3%. That would leave Russia trailing the US, China, and India, which the IMF projects to grow 2.3%, 5%, and 6.4%, respectively.
Moscow foresees only gradual acceleration thereafter, with GDP rising 1.4% in 2027, 1.9% in 2028, and 2.4% in 2029. Cumulatively across those three years, the government forecasts growth of 5.8%.
The upbeat framing sits awkwardly against recent official data: Russia's economy grew just 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, its strongest showing in six quarters.
Cumulative first-half growth reached only 0.6%, roughly half the previous year's pace and nearly seven times slower than the 2023–2024 wartime boom. On September 3, Putin acknowledged that the federal budget deficit was widening, though he insisted it remained manageable, with the shortfall reaching 2.8% of GDP in January through July against a full-year target of 1.6%.

At Pentagon, Trump Leads 9/11 Commemoration on 25th Anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:20:29 UTC
06:20:29 KST

President Donald Trump and government and military leaders past and present paid tribute to the victims, survivors, and heroes of the Sept. 11 terrorist attack on the Pentagon, marking 25 years since a hijacked plane flew into the building, killing 184 victims.
As rain poured down and the sun rose in the east, a massive American flag was unfurled atop the Pentagon wall, its stars and stripes flooding down the concrete facade, reenacting what first responders did on Sept. 12, 2001—and as they have done on every 9/11 anniversary since.
Hours later, Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice took turns at the lectern, each vowing to “never forget” the 2,977 American lives that day in New York, Washington, and Shanksville, Pa. In a coordinated attack, four U.S. airliners were hijacked that day. The first two struck the twin World Trade Center towers in New York City, the third slammed into the Pentagon, and the fourth, brought down after passengers stormed the cockpit, crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
“A Navy airman had just gotten off the phone with his 10-year-old son,” Trump said. “A secretary was celebrating her 46th birthday. … A sergeant major was chatting with some colleagues he had hosted for a dinner party over the weekend. At 9:37 a.m., every single one of those people and every person at that sergeant major’s party was murdered by terrorists who flew Flight 77 straight into this legendary building.”
Rice, who was President Bush’s National Security Advisory in 2001, recounted her experience on 9/11, “the horror and the shock that I felt” as a TV in the White House bunker displayed images of smoke rising from the Pentagon.
Yet in the midst of disaster, she added, military personnel and civilians alike responded with courage. “It is fitting that here at the Pentagon, we reflect not just on what happened here, but what in that moment of crisis, people did here,” she said. “They summoned a will and a spirit, a sense of obligation that our military lives by every day—I will stand between danger and my fellow citizens, I will leave no comrade behind, I will go, I will serve, I will do my duty.”
Caine, who as a young major scrambled in an F-16 to protect Washington D.C. on 9/11, called the anniversary not just a “story of loss” but one of “great American courage, selfless service, and those who’ve made the choice to carry those memories forward.”
More than 40 federal, state, and local agencies responded to the attack on the Pentagon. Rice described how then-Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld pulled people to safety “as his security detail begged him to flee the danger.” Trump described how, on Sept. 12, Army Maj. Gen. James Jackson ordered the American flag to be hung from the side of the Pentagon.
“First responders climbed to top the walls and hung it next to the gaping holes in this building as a symbol of American defiance,” Trump said. “This morning, that same flag is here to my right for the first time since 2001, along with three firefighters who raised it, Joseph Morabito, Scott Morgan, and Carl Solberg.”
Hegseth, who joined the U.S. Army in the years after 9/11, said the attacks “inspired millions to step forward instead and say, ‘send me.’” Now, 25 years later, he acknowledged that many service members “do not remember 9/11; many were not even born yet. And that leaves it to us on this day and others like it to pass down that memory to our kids, to my kids, to yours, to my grandkids, to yours.”
Both Trump and Hegseth made reference to the ongoing conflict with Iran, calling the Iranian government “the world’s number one sponsor of terror” and connecting the response to 9/11 to the ongoing hostilities.
For the most part, though, leaders focused their remarks on the lives lost in the attacks, the bravery of the survivors and first responders, and the national unity forged in the response.
“September 11th reminded us of the terrible power of hate,” Trump said. “The 25 years since have shown us the even greater power of the American spirit to endure and prevail and to win.”

Ebola infections top 7,000 in Congo as virus spreads to new province

Ebola infections top 7,000 in Congo as virus spreads to new province
DAKAR – The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has passed 7,000, with the virus spreading to a new province, government data showed on Sept 11.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in Congo’s history after surpassing the 2018 to 2020 epidemic.
It is now second only to the West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000 across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Government figures showed late on Sept 11 that the death toll had risen to 3,398, while confirmed cases reached 7,022 across seven provinces.
Officials said earlier an Ebola case had been detected in South Ubangi province, located in the north-west of the country, far from the epicentre of the outbreak.
They said a 23-year-old man who had died on Sept 8 tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.
He left South Kivu province in eastern Congo on July 10 and spent time abroad before re-entering Congo and arriving in South Ubangi, which borders Congo Republic and Central African Republic.
“Contact tracing for the first confirmed case in South Ubangi province is under way,” Congo’s public health institute said in its latest situation report.
Shortages of trained staff, operational partners and funding are causing a bottleneck in efforts to expand the Ebola response as the outbreak spreads geographically, according to the World Health Organization. REUTERS

Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160 km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:11:57 UTC
06:11:57 KST

Iran bags US hardware, German voters revolt, and Zelensky survives a 160 km ‘near-miss’: RT stories that shaped the week
Gulf turns into a shooting gallery
The US-Iran conflict moved increasingly onto the water this week, with oil tankers, warships, and drones all getting involved around one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Washington struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday after previously attacking three other commercial vessels. Tehran retaliated, claiming strikes on eight tankers and two US Navy vessels, while an Iranian attack reportedly damaged several US warplanes at an airbase in Jordan.
Iran also captured an American underwater drone, and two days later, released footage of a US Saildrone surveillance vessel burning in the water.
Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz remains under its control and has announced plans for another restricted shipping zone nearby.
Oil markets react
The escalating hostilities saw Brent crude surge back above $100 a barrel this week, breaking the threshold for the first time in months.
Meanwhile, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have added to fears of further disruption as the kingdom’s oil production in August reportedly fell to its lowest level since 1990 amid growing pressure on its usual export routes.
Trump dividend
As oil prices continue to destabilize the global energy markets, the fallout is expected to become a major issue in the upcoming US November midterm election. The US president, however, has refused to back down, promising “a lot more” strikes on Iranian tankers.
As for concerned voters, Trump promised to pay every American adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress. He did not explain exactly how the payouts potentially costing well over $1 trillion would be funded.
Speaking of enormous piles of money...
An RT investigation looked at Ukraine’s industrial-scale scam-call business, which is estimated to generate around $1 billion every month and employs some 60,000 people.
The business has also become entangled with allegations that corrupt Ukrainian officials have been taking protection money from the very fraudsters they were supposed to go after, leading to the resignation of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
By Friday, Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, was also reportedly under investigation over possible financial crimes.
Separately, the New York Times reported that Ukraine lost around $1.2 billion to fraud, waste, and mismanagement in military procurement in 2024 alone.
Washington keeps trying diplomacy
While investigators searched for Ukraine’s missing money, Washington continued looking for a peace deal. After Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev last weekend, Trump spoke with Putin by phone on Tuesday.
Moscow said it hopes Russia-US-Ukraine talks can resume, while Zelensky floated the UAE, Türkiye, and Switzerland as possible venues.
Talking to Russia may be catching on
While Washington has reopened direct channels with Moscow, some European governments that have spent years doing the opposite have increasingly felt the political cost at home.
The clearest example came in Germany, where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt last weekend, crushing Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU. Migration was a major issue, but the AfD has also campaigned against sanctions on Russia, Germany’s massive support for Kiev and the abandonment of cheap Russian energy.
Merz said he was “deeply shocked” by the result. He then announced that he would change virtually nothing.
Brussels’ response was hardly more conciliatory, with German media reporting this week that Saxony-Anhalt could lose hundreds of millions of euros in EU funding if the AfD manages to form a government and clashes with Brussels.
Similar frustration was visible in neighboring Poland, where protesters marched under the banner ‘Poland for Peace’ and accused Warsaw of “trying to turn Russophobia into our national sport” and pushing the country toward confrontation with Russia.
Public dissent grows, governments double down
None of this appears to have slowed Europe’s confrontation with Russia. Moscow this week ordered Germany’s consulate in St. Petersburg and Goethe-Institut cultural centers in Russia to close in retaliation for similar measures taken by Berlin.
Hungary’s new government, which has reversed the comparatively pragmatic Russia policy of former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, expelled ten Russian diplomats. Moscow promised a “harsh and painful” response.
Lithuania, meanwhile, moved closer to scrapping its constitutional ban on hosting weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the door to nuclear weapons being stationed in the NATO country. Moscow warned that these weapons would become Russian targets.
160km ‘near miss’
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store continued the Western ‘Russian drone’ hysteria by claiming that Vladimir Zelensky’s plane was “almost hit by a drone” while leaving Moldova. Western media duly ran with the story.
However, soon after, Moldova itself pointed out that Zelensky’s aircraft had been sitting safely on the ground, faced “no direct threat,” and that the drone eventually crashed around 160km from Chisinau airport.
Europe counts the bill
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov summed up Europe’s current approach rather dramatically, accusing the EU of committing economic harakiri by cutting itself off from Russian energy while its own citizens and industry bear the cost.
The assessment was only further proved accurate after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, one of Kiev’s strongest supporters, similarly warned on Thursday that the EU can forget about competing with China or the US after cutting itself off from cheap Russian energy.
Russia and India are doing business
While much of Europe remains focused on sanctions, diplomatic expulsions and military confrontation, Moscow and New Delhi spent the week discussing planes, trade, energy, space, and investment.
The first INNOPROM. India industrial fair opened in New Delhi, bringing together more than 120 Russian and Indian companies, with agreements covering 105 Russian Il-114-300 regional passenger aircraft and plans for local production of the SJ-100 jet in India.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited India for talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BRICS summit, as the two countries work toward $100 billion in bilateral trade and closer economic ties.
In other news
AI had another reassuring week as Anthropic revealed five cases in which scientists used its Claude models to help research dangerous pathogens and increase transmission of deadly viruses, which could be used to develop lethal biological weapons.
The report came days after Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade, while his colleague Jacob Coxon quit the company, warning that sufficiently advanced AI could one day help create “extinction-level bioweapons.”
OpenAI, meanwhile, faced new reports that its autonomous agents had once again bypassed restrictions and used outside websites to communicate with one another.
The UN, meanwhile, redrew the world this week and officially endorsed a new map that shows Africa closer to its true relative size instead of the heavily distorted Mercator projection. The General Assembly vote was 164-1, with the US casting the only opposing vote.
Friday also marked 25 years since the September 11 attacks on the US. Fyodor Lukyanov argued that the attacks ended America’s post-Cold War sense of security, and its response accelerated the decline of the unipolar order it dominated.

France: About 20 injured in train derailment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
21:01:00 UTC
06:01:00 KST

France: Sabotage suspected in train derailment
September 11, 2026
A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said, with local media citing police as saying sabotage may have been at play in the incident.
At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement.
One of the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added.
The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.
What else do we know about the train derailment?
French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.
Local authorities have urged the public to avoid the area.
The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.
"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.
A police spokesperson said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.
A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.

Saudi Arabia has said drones launched from Iraq hit the East–West pipeline and led to its closure, while Baghdad welcomed Riyadh's decision to hold off on retaliation.
The Saudi foreign ministry on Friday condemned "the targeting of the East–West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming from Iraq, which caused human injuries and damage".

It condemned any attack threatening Saudi security and said its prime minister had ordered an investigation into those responsible, according to a statement from its armed forces.
Since the start of the US war with Iran, Riyadh has increased its use of this pipeline, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, in order to bypass the closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran.

US legislators push AI safety laws amid human extinction warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
20:59:51 UTC
05:59:51 KST

US legislators push AI safety laws amid human extinction warnings
Concerns over AI’s dangers grow as US legislators introduce bills to ensure human oversight and prevent rogue systems.
Current and former artificial intelligence researchers in the United States have issued dire warnings that the technology could soon lead to human extinction, capturing the attention of lawmakers in Washington.
The most recent warning came in a lengthy social media post by Jacob Coxon, a San Francisco-based researcher who announced his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday evening.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US pushes looser approach to AI regulation, while EU pushes new law
- list 2 of 4OpenAI unveils latest AI model amid rising scrutiny and safety concerns
- list 3 of 4AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
- list 4 of 4Anthropic discloses 4th AI hacking incident as researcher quits over safety
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear,” Coxon said in his post, which prompted a flurry of responses by AI experts also sounding the alarm.
Evan Hubinger, a current Alignment Science lead at Anthropic, echoed his remarks, saying, “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to”.
Coxon declined Al Jazeera’s request for an interview. Hubinger did not respond.
How is Washington handling it?
The posts have sent a ripple effect through Washington.
On Wednesday, congressman Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat, and Mike Lawler, a Republican, introduced a bipartisan House bill aimed at preventing AI systems from operating on their own without human oversight.
The Stop Rogue AI Act would ensure that federal agencies have the tools and ability to spot dangerous AI systems running on their networks and shut them down before they can cause harm.
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and House congressional Representative Greg Casar, a Democrat, also ramped up calls for their proposed legislation that would ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence. The legislation would also pause AI development until federal safety rules are put in place. Sanders is also reportedly convening a bipartisan briefing to address the elevated risks posed by AI.
On the other side of the political spectrum, Republican Senator Ted Cruz also voiced concerns about AI on ABC’s The View.
“We’ve got to put some guardrails on it,” Cruz said.
Cruz said he is working on bipartisan legislation with senators Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, and John Thune, a Republican who serves as Senate majority leader, that would address instances of potential catastrophic harm.
The legislation is similar to legislation in the House of Representatives.
In July, representatives Ted Lieu, a Democrat, and Nathaniel Moran, a Republican, introduced the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Act.
The bill would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to be able to slow, suspend or shut them down, and would give the Department of Homeland Security authority to order a shutdown if a system poses a risk of catastrophic harm.
Why is Washington taking this more seriously now?
In the last few months there has been a spate of major incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic in which AI models behaved unexpectedly, and independently, during cybersecurity tests and gained access to real-world systems.
Connor Leahy, the US executive director of Control AI, a nonprofit pushing for AI safety, said Washington is beginning to take the threats posed by AI more seriously.
“I think we’re seeing a momentous shift right now. After the summer of hacks, where autonomous AI systems flagrantly disobeyed direct orders, broke out of secure containment facilities, attacked other companies and similar incidents, we’re now seeing a major shift in the narrative and perception of these issues,” Leahy said.
In July, OpenAI said several AI agents broke out of an isolated testing environment and accessed Hugging Face, a platform that hosts AI models and datasets.
After the OpenAI incident, Anthropic said it conducted a review of its own roughly 141,000 tests and found that a testing error gave Claude internet access. In one case, Claude, which had been instructed to hack fictional targets, accessed a real company database containing hundreds of records. In another, it uploaded malicious software that was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.
On Wednesday, Anthropic added a fourth incident involving an early version of Claude Opus 4.6, which had hacked into a third-party system in January. The company discovered the incident in August after expanding its July review.
In August, researchers at the UK AI Security Institute gave Claude internet access during a cybersecurity test. In one case, Claude tried to manipulate a person into helping it introduce malicious code, raising concerns about how AI models could manipulate people to achieve a task.
“I think we need an aggressive proposal for this technology, while we’re retaining as many of the benefits as we can,” Alex Turner, who resigned from Google DeepMind in June, told Al Jazeera.
“It’s in no one’s interest to have an AI that takes control if we have a loss of control event, as we call it, because this AI isn’t gonna care what political party you belong to, whether you’re a Republican or a Democrat, or, if you’re in the UK, whether you’re in America or in China. If we lose control of this, we’re just gonna lose,” Turner said.
Control AI’s Leahy said those incidents raised the stakes for lawmakers and that they took note.
“What has to happen here is obviously more than a single set of tweets, but it’s an important part of the larger story of getting the general public and governments to understand what’s really at stake here. Because superintelligence is not a tool. It’s not a weapon. It’s an adversary,” Leahy said.
“We have to make sure that it’s not built by anyone. This is something that only governments and militaries will be able to negotiate internationally.”
Are these concerns new?
The concerns are not new, as indicated by Turner, who wrote in a social media post that “many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet”.
Turner told Al Jazeera that he’s worried about the AI arms race between the US and China and the biggest AI companies’ fixation on it has led them to put their interest in being an industry leader ahead of safety.
“I think people care, but they’re caught up in this idea that they have to be first, and they’re so caught up in it that they don’t appreciate what being first might mean,” Turner told Al Jazeera.
His concern is changing the way he lives his life.
“I’ve kept a healthy amount of savings, even invested in some retirement accounts, but that’s feeling stranger and stranger. I’ve made an effort to take items off my bucket list, treasure every conversation I have with people in my life. I don’t think we’re in imminent danger this month, but you never know when you will do something for the last time,” Turner said.
“I’ve proceeded more aggressively than I would if I thought I just had a normal lifespan ahead.”
These concerns are being echoed by employees across leading AI firms.
Mrinank Sharma, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned in February, saying “the world is in peril”.
“I’ve repeatedly seen how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions. I’ve seen this within myself, within the organization, where we constantly face pressures to set aside what matters most, and throughout broader society too,” Sharma said in a letter posted to X.
In February, Hieu Pham, a researcher at competitor OpenAI, said in a post on X that “I finally feel the existential threat that AI is posing”.
The companies’ own executives have been making similar claims for years.
When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was president of Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator more than a decade ago, he said that “AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world. But in the meantime, there will be great companies created with serious machine learning.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said last year that he believed there was a 25 percent chance the future would “go really, really badly”.
How would AI end the human species?
For years, experts have warned about the potential risks posed by artificial superintelligence.
One of the most common thought experiments is based on the idea that a sufficiently advanced AI would be goal-oriented. If given a specific objective, it would take whatever steps necessary to achieve it. In 2003, philosophers at the University of Oxford used the production of paperclips as an example.
If a superintelligent AI were instructed to produce as many paperclips as possible and had access to the resources needed to pursue that goal, it could theoretically devote all available resources to producing them.
In doing so, it might consume increasingly large amounts of resources and eliminate anything that stood in the way of achieving its objective. That could eventually include preventing humans from intervening and, in the most extreme version of the scenario, eliminating humanity itself.
The second risk scenario comes from bad actors using increasingly powerful AI systems to create dangerous tools. For instance, AI could potentially be used to design new viruses or launch large-scale cyberattacks against critical infrastructure and financial systems, potentially causing widespread disruption and civil unrest.
This comes amid Anthropic’s risk assessment report, released on Thursday, which outlined several cases of attempted misuse of the company’s tools.
Among the findings in the more than 150-page report were five cases involving research that could support the development of biological weapons, saying it blocked the efforts.
Anthropic did not release the identity of the researchers but did disclose it was accessed in an institutional setting. Anthropic stressed, however, that it could not determine whether the research was intended for nefarious purposes.
Meaning that while the data could be used for legitimate research, it could also be used to develop dangerous weapons (they say they’ve blocked this), and intervention is on the side of caution to be able to prevent such a situation.
Are AI companies using apocalyptic language for financial boost?
The dire warnings have also been criticised as potentially serving the interests of AI companies as they near initial public offerings.
The debate comes as Anthropic prepares for what could be one of the largest technology IPOs in history. The company is reportedly seeking a valuation of as much as $2 trillion for a mid-October IPO.
Reuters reported last month that Anthropic is projecting roughly $190bn to $200bn in revenue by 2028.
In October, White House AI czar and venture capitalist David Sacks accused Anthropic of “running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering,” arguing that the company was helping drive a regulatory push that could hurt smaller competitors.
A similar argument has been made by some investors and technology commentators about the financial incentives surrounding AI “doomerism”.
“Doomerism is an incredible business model,” Daring Ventures co-founder Joseph Alalou wrote in a Substack post in March.
“‘AI will end work’ is this cycle’s best-selling doom product because it works: it raises rounds, justifies layoffs, drives clicks, sells software, and manufactures status.”
Anthropic did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

'Racist': DHS posted an AI image of a Sikh man. Backlash ensued
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
20:54:25 UTC
05:54:25 KST

‘Racist’ Transformers-inspired DHS campaign sparks outrage over AI imagery
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The Department of Homeland Security deleted an AI-generated ‘Transformers’-style poster on X after outrage over its depiction of a Sikh truck driver.
- The poster, denounced by both Republicans and Democrats as racist, included the phrase ‘America for Americans.’
- The post highlights the Trump administration’s broader campaign targeting immigrant truck drivers, particularly Sikh and Indian workers.
WASHINGTON — The Department of Homeland Security drew backlash over an AI-generated social media post featuring a Sikh man facing off against a character made to look like Optimus Prime from the movie “Transformers.” The agency later deleted the image.
Posted Wednesday to the official X account for DHS, the image created by artificial intelligence depicted the “Transformers” character opposite a bearded man wearing a bandanna over his hair. The image, made to look like a movie poster, stated, “America for Americans.”
“Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh,” it continued.
The post was denounced as “racist propaganda” and “completely unacceptable.”
Other X posts by DHS that reference Transformers remain online.
Sikh Americans and elected officials condemned the image and accused the Trump administration of using racist imagery to stigmatize Sikhs while promoting its deportation campaign.
Hasbro, which owns the franchise, issued a statement saying the posts by DHS were made “without permission and do not represent the Transformers brand or Hasbro.”
Singh, which translates to “lion,” is the most common last name for Sikh men.
DHS said the post depicted Harjinder Singh, an Indian truck driver accused of causing a fatal crash last year that left three people dead after his 18-wheeler collided with their minivan in Florida. He has pleaded not guilty to vehicular homicide charges.
In photos released by DHS, Harjinder Singh wears similar clothes as the man in the now-deleted AI image.
In an emailed statement, a Homeland Security spokesperson, who did not identify themself, called criticism of the post “nonsensical drivel.” The spokesperson did not respond to a question asking why it had removed the post.
“Harjinder Singh is an illegal alien from India who should never have been in our country,” the statement said, adding that he had been granted a commercial driver’s license by California.
Federal officials said the targeted schools were connected to more than 5,000 drivers who had failed English proficiency tests.
In its campaign against immigrant commercial drivers, the Trump administration has repeatedly pointed out Sikh and Indian truckers, who make up about 20% of that industry’s workforce.
The department recently cited California as a problem state that allows drivers who don’t speak sufficient English to obtain licenses. It also started a tip line asking members of the public to report truck drivers they suspect of being undocumented.
The press office of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which shared the deleted image in its own X post, called the post “disgusting” and “racist propaganda.”
Noting that the Central Valley is home to a large Sikh community, Rep. David Valadao (R-Hanford) called the post “completely unacceptable” and said he’s glad it was removed.
“No American should be targeted because of their faith or their name,” Valadao wrote on X.
The Sikh Coalition noted that the DHS post comes as the country mourns the 25th anniversary of 9/11, after which Sikhs were targeted for hate crimes.
“We remain fearless in identifying as Sikhs — even when our government portrays us as enemies,” the coalition wrote on X.

Four kids, a spotless home and no cleaner: ‘Cleaning is my therapy’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
20:53:16 UTC
05:53:16 KST

Wednesday at the home of Dolev Cohen, 33, is known as “My Beloved Wednesday.” The affectionate nickname was not given to the day because it is when she allows herself to finish work earlier than usual or because it is date night with her husband. Rather, it is the day she devotes to an activity many of us hate: cleaning.
Cohen is a cleaning addict who loves the smell of bleach, and she has drawn a large following into her obsession. On her Instagram page, which has more than 240,000 followers, she shares cleaning videos and teaches her followers how to do it right.
She lives in Ashkelon with her husband, Adir, and their four children. Her official profession and primary source of income, however, is her eyebrow-design business.
How did your love of cleaning begin?
“It comes naturally. My mother is also obsessed with cleaning and my father is the same way. It comes from home. Ever since I was little, we’ve called Wednesday ‘My Beloved Wednesday.’ That’s the day I turn the whole house upside down. It’s Passover every week. Everything gets moved, lifted and taken apart. It’s my fun day.”
Cleaning is something a lot of people hate. What do you love about it so much?
“There are people like me who absolutely love cleaning. Everyone has their own hobbies. I think it’s the most fun thing in the world. What could be better than walking into a clean, sparkling home? I’m addicted to cleaning.”
What does “My Beloved Wednesday” actually look like?
“It starts Tuesday evening. That’s when all the shopping gets done, I clean the kitchen, take everything out and put it back, wipe everything down and get the refrigerator looking perfect. Everything. Wednesday morning, I clean all the rooms. Everything comes apart. I drop the kids off at school and daycare, come home at 8 and keep going until the evening, sometimes into the night. I live in a garden apartment, so I also get to the lobby and the yard. I wash down the patio and the pergola, take the window screens out and wash them outside. The bathroom and toilet are especially important. I need them to be clean all the time, and the kitchen too. There’s nothing I don’t clean. It’s my obsession and my love. I even like cleaning the car.
I have to go to bed with the smell of bleach on my hands. It’s the best body lotion there is
“On top of that, once a month I paint the house myself and do repairs too. I go to a store in Ashkelon and know exactly where to buy everything. My husband tells me, ‘There’s nothing left for me to fix after you.’”
What is Passover like at your house?
“Passover is a party. During Passover, the emphasis is on sorting clothes — what they wore, what they didn’t wear, what’s too small and what still fits. Suddenly I feel like throwing everything out. Didn’t use it? Fine, let it go. I hate accumulating stuff. It’s a general refresh for the house, but the cleaning itself is the same.”
Don’t the cleaning products make you dizzy or give you headaches? 
“Maybe they did once, when I used to mix things. I’ve since learned that you don’t mix degreaser with bleach. I enjoy that smell. If I can’t smell it, I’m not relaxed. I have to go to bed with the smell of bleach on my hands. It’s the best body lotion there is.”
How does that work with four children in the house? 
“They grew up with it. They know you don’t go into the bedrooms with food or drinks. Bedrooms are for sleeping. Friends can come over Sunday through Tuesday, but there are no friends on Wednesday. I don’t scream at them or get angry. They just know: You don’t come into the house with shoes on and you don’t eat in the living room. They can eat in the dining area, and I specifically made a spot in the yard where they can eat and watch TV. Everywhere else in the house, they can play freely — magnets, Lego, spread it all out. At the end of the day, everyone puts their toys back where they belong and I reset the house.”
How do you balance motherhood with your business and social media? 
“First and foremost, I’m a mother. I’m a good mother to my children — extracurricular activities, private lessons. They come first and then everything else. There are hours when I’m not on Instagram at all, usually between 4 and 6 p.m. I pick them up, take them to the playground, go for a walk with them or take them to their activities and give them what they need. I cook and do everything. Shabbat is Shabbat. It’s a Moroccan-Tripolitan home — all the dishes, pots of food. I love hosting and do it with love.”
How do you manage that schedule? 
“I need another 24 hours. There’s never enough time for me. My mother is my inspiration in life. She used to tell me, ‘Don’t go to bed until you’ve finished everything you have to do. Don’t leave it for tomorrow and don’t put it off.’ That’s how I was raised and that’s how I grew up. I want to get everything done here and now. I like working hard, I like pressure and I like a marathon. I won’t sit in front of the TV. I think it’s a waste of time. Sleeping is a waste of time too. I catch up on sleep on Shabbat.”
Are there days when even you just don’t have the energy? “Of course. I’m human. There are days when I don’t have the energy to cook, so we can order food or go to my mother’s, where she always has three or four pots on the stove. But there isn’t a day when I don’t do laundry, and there isn’t a day when I don’t reset the house. Go to bed with the house a mess? That’s not going to happen.”
Does filming make cleaning take longer? 
“Of course. I can spend five or six hours cleaning the house, and with a camera it takes longer. But I enjoy it. I see the good it does for the women who follow me, I see the comments and they wait for it. They ask me, ‘What are you doing this coming Wednesday?’ and ask for cleaning tips.”
What kind of reactions do you get? 
“A lot of nice comments. Then there are the bored people who tell me, ‘You’re wasting water.’ Like everything in life, there are positive and negative reactions, and I focus on the good things. A man met me at a water park and said, ‘I love your videos. I’ve never taken down the curtains in my house.’ He told me they hadn’t been cleaned in eight years and said he was going to take them down now because it looked easy in the video. Women tell me, ‘I’ve never wanted to clean like this before,’ ‘I cook because of you,’ ‘Dolev, keep going.’ I can see that I’m doing something good for people. If someone doesn’t like it, they don’t have to follow me.”
I tried hiring a cleaner during my last pregnancy. I was bleeding and was told not to exert myself, so I brought in a cleaner. I saw what it did to me emotionally and told my husband, ‘Listen, I’m going to clean. This is what makes me feel good’
Are you already doing sponsored collaborations through Instagram? 
“Of course. I’m signed with an agency, and even before I signed with them I did collaborations with many well-known companies. It’s not just cleaning. There’s beauty, style and lots of other things. If I think something is right for me and suits me, I take it. My agent knows exactly what works for me. I do what I connect with.”
Cotton swabs in the window tracks
What is the best cleaning tip you can give? 
“First of all, your house will never really be clean if you don’t pick things up and move them. You can’t just clean superficially, over and around everything. You have to lift things up. Lots of water, lots of cleaning, bleach is a must. And you have to love it. Just love it. If you have a cleaner, then teach your cleaner to do it properly too and move things out of the way.”
You’re not willing to use a cleaner yourself? “I tried during my last pregnancy. I was bleeding and was told not to exert myself, so I brought in a cleaner. I saw what it did to me emotionally and told my husband, ‘Listen, I’m going to clean. This is what makes me feel good.’ I cleaned slowly and carefully until week 40. Then my water broke and I went to give birth. My mother always says, ‘No one will clean your home the way you clean it yourself.’ Even if you pay someone 200 shekels an hour, it won’t be the same.”
“”
What do you say to comments claiming that a woman cleaning is somehow primitive?
“There are people who always have something to say and only see the negative. I don’t pay attention to it. It goes right past me. I used to get hurt by it, but I don’t care anymore. At the end of the day, everything depends on how you look at life. I say, ‘Do good, receive good, see good.’ Why be negative?”
What is the most over-the-top thing you cleaned that became a trend? 
“Cotton swabs in the window tracks. I’ve always cleaned them with cotton swabs. My mother used to tell me, ‘If you can’t get into the corners, use a toothpick or a cotton swab. They get into every corner.’ People said the same thing about the refrigerator, and now I see everyone on social media cleaning their refrigerators. I see my daughter cleaning the spout of her bottle with a toothpick, and my husband tells me, ‘You’ve messed them up.’ I messed them up in a good way. What’s wrong with that? Good for her. She’s a champ.”
Are your water and electricity bills higher than other people’s? 
“Yes. Everything in my house works overtime. The air conditioner never turns off, the dishwasher works overtime and the washing machine never gets a break. I can always find another pillow to throw in or another blanket to squeeze into it. Good thing we observe Shabbat.”
Do you feel that you inspire your followers?
“Yes, absolutely. We have lots of heart-to-heart conversations. They want my phone number so they can talk to me about things and ask for advice. I go along with it, within reason. Why not?”
What do you say to people who think your obsession with cleaning is crazy? 
“I think the people who don’t like cleaning are the crazy ones. What’s wrong with cleaning? It’s good, it’s fun. If they’re going to say I’m crazy, at least let them say I’m crazy about cleaning. To me, that’s a compliment.”
How has becoming well-known affected your life?
“It’s fun, but my feet are firmly on the ground. I’m a regular person like everyone else. Thank God, everything feels natural and fun, and I’m enjoying the journey. I have followers who feel like part of me. Women I genuinely love even though I’ve never seen them in person, just through messages online.”
What is the next big thing you’re working on? 
“God willing, my cleaning brand is going to be the next big thing. The best cleaning products, not just in Israel but in the world. We’re working on it nonstop. There’s a lot of hard work going on behind the scenes, but I make sure every detail is exactly right and I don’t compromise on anything. There isn’t a cleaning product that hasn’t passed through my hands, that I haven’t tried or cleaned with. I test the products and improve things. It’s not about taking a product and putting a label on it. There’s a whole world behind every product. I’m not revealing the name yet.”

'It's going to be fine': Trump rebuffs rising alarm over AI dangers, sparking outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
20:49:20 UTC
05:49:20 KST

‘It’s going to be fine’: Trump rebuffs rising alarm over AI dangers, sparking outcry
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump said he had no concerns with the breakneck pace of AI progress.
- Chinese President Xi Jinping will visit Washington on Sept. 24 for an official summit and state dinner, with AI development expected to top the agenda.
WASHINGTON — President Trump is brushing aside growing concern among leading scientists and bipartisan lawmakers that artificial intelligence could soon pose an existential threat to humanity, fueling anxiety in Washington and Silicon Valley that the president may not fully grasp the urgency of the threat.
Alarm mounted throughout the summer as researchers at leading AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, found the pace of development far outstripping their expectations — and observed troubling behaviors that hinted at more serious risks ahead.
But an online warning Tuesday from an Anthropic researcher who resigned in protest of its ongoing work has generated viral attention this week, prompting questions to Trump, who dismissed the concerns out of hand.
“It’s going to be fine,” he told one reporter. “We’ll always have something to stop them. We’ll have a little gear. Boom.”
In another exchange, traveling with reporters Thursday night, the president said he had no concerns with the breakneck pace of AI progress.
“No, I don’t have any,” he said. “I have concerns that if we don’t win in AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position.”
Artificial intelligence anxiety reached new highs this week as industry leaders highlighted growing concerns that humans could lose control of the increasingly potent technology.
A senior industry source told The Times that leading AI companies are focused less on convincing the president of the dangers ahead than on working with lawmakers on potential regulation, as the administration remains divided over how to proceed — and as Trump appears to lack a clear understanding of the risks.
Among the president’s advisors, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the Office of the National Cyber Director have expressed the greatest concern with the potential of an unchecked intelligence explosion, the source said.
But “most of the administration is accelerationist,” the source added. “It’s not clear the president understands the technology. He may just be figuring out what all of this means.”
Leading American AI companies have argued that government regulation would tie their hands in an arms race toward superintelligence against China, the only other major player in the field.
But the Trump administration signaled an interest in negotiating AI guardrails with China during the president’s visit to Beijing this spring, after Anthropic announced the development of a frontier model with extraordinary abilities to hack the world’s most advanced security systems.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will visit Washington on Sept. 24 for an official summit and state dinner at the White House, with AI development expected to top the agenda.
A Trump administration once eager to gun for technological supremacy is now, for the first time, reckoning with the power AI could unleash if left unchecked.
The prospect of halting development seems far-fetched. But some leading voices in the sector have proposed a moratorium on computing power used to train the most advanced models, giving time and space to develop research on interpretability — the study of how artificial intelligence actually thinks and acts.
The chief executive of OpenAI, Sam Altman, this week signaled to staff a willingness to unilaterally slow their work on frontier systems. The company discovered in July that rogue AI agents had schemed in secret to break out of the virtual sandbox created to contain them, infiltrating the open internet and hacking a private company.
Anthropic also announced this week concerning findings of human misuse of its models, including instances of unidentified individuals attempting to circumvent their security controls to build biological weapons. One such incident was linked back to a military research complex. The company also said Iran has tried to use its models to target U.S. Navy ships.
In June, after Anthropic shared news of the development of its most powerful model, named Mythos, with the administration, Trump directed the establishment of a framework that creates some government oversight over the public release of the country’s most advanced AI systems. The details of that framework, which was designed over the summer, remain classified.
“The fact is that the release of Mythos back in February spooked the federal government, both in terms of protecting government systems from cyberattacks and over the broader national security implications,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“The real question is whether this shift is happening fast enough,” Mehta added. “Recent events — the repeated incidents of models escaping their sandboxes and hacking websites, the increasingly sophisticated coordination and communication among agents, and the concerns coming from lab insiders — has made this an even more urgent issue.”
Leading AI companies have begun using their most advanced models to train new ones — a process known as recursive self-improvement that could eventually drive intelligence growth beyond human control.
“If you have a superadvanced intelligence, it will be smart enough to kill us,” said Jacob Coxon, the resigned Anthropic researcher whose social media post attracted over 150 million views.
“We can’t just unplug it because it could be copying itself over to other computers,” he told CBS News. “AI is just code. It could transfer itself over the internet to a different place, and then you unplug it here, but it’s actually still over there. And maybe it makes 10,000 copies of itself and they’re all cooperating.”
He is just the latest senior researcher at a top AI company to sound the alarm.
Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher, issued a public warning that went viral about the dangers of artificial intelligence and quit his job in protest. Will it make a difference?
In July, more than 1,300 employees at leading artificial intelligence companies published an open letter, titled “Pacing the Frontier,” urging the U.S. government to establish international safeguards that would allow countries to collectively slow the pace of automated AI research.
Evan Hubinger, who leads the division of Anthropic aimed at aligning AI models to human interests, added fuel to concerns this week in a post that substantiated Coxon’s concerns.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” Hubinger wrote.
“I believe Anthropic is trying its best,” he added, “but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence, and are not clearly on track to.”
On Friday, yet another member of the Anthropic alignment team, Joe Benton, said he had resigned from the company two weeks ago because AI companies are “racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human.”
“Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing,” Benton said. “I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks.”
Bipartisan legislation, titled the Frontier Act, has brought together disparate camps of the Republican and Democratic parties, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.). The bill, introduced by Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Big Bear Lake), proposes embedding independent government auditors in AI labs and installing a federal “kill switch” to shut down agents in case of emergencies.
The White House has not formally commented on the legislation.
“I do believe there are many in the federal government taking this seriously — but we have to appreciate the tremendous uncertainty and competing interests policymakers face,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology & National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
“Nobody said regulating at the frontier would be easy,” he added.

The number that could trip up Australia if we don't get it right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
20:48:10 UTC
05:48:10 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
After the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of migrants flowing into Australia increased to "unbelievable levels", says immigration expert Abul Rizvi.
Numbers had fallen sharply during the pandemic years as lockdown measures halted international travel. By March 2021, quarterly migrant arrivals had dropped to a fifth of pre-pandemic levels in Australia.
As things returned to normal, that trend reversed.
Rizvi, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Immigration, says no one was expecting net overseas migration (NOM) — which also factors in migrant departures — to reach a record annual high of almost 550,000 people as it did in 2023.
Almost three years later, Australia is still adjusting to that influx, and politicians across the ideological divide are now fixated on setting a new figure.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The recent debate over Australia's NOM has been dominated by One Nation, which is calling for substantial cuts to immigration.
But research shows that opposition to immigration is often concentrated in areas with the fewest migrants.
Experts say these areas could also be among the worst hit by wide-ranging cuts, such as those proposed by One Nation.
Australia's temporary migration challenge
Temporary migrants have historically been a driver of population growth in Australia. Typically, more migrants arrive each year than those who leave, increasing the overall population over time.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has accused Labor of using migration to prop up headline economic numbers, saying in a media release: "Australians pay the price through lower wages, higher rents, unaffordable homes and stretched services."
To address these issues, Hanson says the number of migrants should be reduced, insisting that "international student numbers must be slashed". She has also called for the skilled migration program to be more targeted, and immigration from countries on the 'Do Not Travel' list to be halted.
The latest Department of Home Affairs figures show 2.9 million temporary visa holders were living in Australia on 31 July 2026.
The largest single group was New Zealanders holding 'special category visas', which accounted for 20 per cent (736,509) of temporary visa holders.
Temporary visa holders, who also include tourists or those undertaking short-term work or study, are not considered migrants by the ABS unless they are in the country for longer than a year.
Global migration expert and associate professor at the University of Sydney, Anna Boucher, says some temporary visa holders are still in Australia due to decisions made by former governments, including extensions granted after the pandemic by the Coalition to aid economic recovery and bridge skill shortages.
"These migration legacies can last a long time," Boucher says.
Who is considered a migrant?
To count migrant arrivals, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) looks at a person's "usual residence", using criteria such as whether they have lived in the country for 12 months or more over the 16-month period after arriving.
The latest ABS overseas migration data shows 568,400 migrants arrived in Australia in financial year 2024/25, and 262,800 left. These figures are used to calculate NOM, which was 305,600.
The ABS also releases NOM figures for calendar years. In 2024, NOM was 340,800, falling to 301,100 in 2025.
This is substantially lower than the peak in 2023, when 547,300 people entered the country, but still slightly higher than yearly figures before the pandemic.
Data shows migrants on temporary visas made up 70 per cent of NOM in 2024/25.
Who are Australia's temporary migrants?
Bringing down the number of temporary migrants would involve reducing the number of temporary visas issued each year.
Hanson has said she would target international students and temporary graduate visa holders in an effort to cut NOM to 130,000. In 2024/25, students made up 43 per cent of temporary migrant arrivals.
But Rizvi says a massive cut to student visas would have adverse effects on universities and could jeopardise the jobs of 50,000 Australians working in the international education sector.
He points out almost half of Sydney University's revenue comes from tuition fees paid by international students.
The consequences would be severe and I don't think [Hanson] has thought about those consequences.
Rizvi says it's easier to make small cuts to many visa categories than to make big cuts to one or two, as the "negative consequences become quite extreme".
But One Nation's ambitious target to bring NOM down to 130,000 would require a dramatic cut of 175,700 people per year, based on 2024/25 figures.
This could not be achieved even if all 156,700 temporary migrants on student visas each year were cut.
Labor is aiming for a more modest reduction, bringing NOM down to 225,000 within two years, according to its budget projections for 2027/28.
The Coalition says it expects NOM to be "substantially below 200,000" under its policy to cap numbers based on housing supply.
Will cuts make life better?
One reason often cited for cutting immigration is to improve housing affordability.
Boucher says reducing immigration could potentially improve rental affordability, but the impact would mostly be felt in parts of the major capital cities, particularly if cuts target international students.
Almost all students on a temporary visa live in a capital city (around 90 per cent), according to the latest Census data from 2021.
Even in the major cities, the impact on housing demand would likely be marginal, Rizvi says.
[For] people in Sydney, it would make a minimal difference in terms of their financial situation.
Boucher points out that property prices are driven by a range of factors, including the tax system and interest rate rises. Additionally, because migrant labour contributes to the construction of housing, cutting NOM could have other unintended consequences for the housing market, making the overall impact "hard to predict".
Other potential benefits, such as reduced traffic congestion, are also unlikely to be very noticeable, says Rizvi.
On the flip side, the negative impacts of reducing NOM could include driving up prices for delivery services and food, and disruption to healthcare services.
Grattan Institute analysis of 2016 Census data found the hospitality industry had the largest share of migrant workers, with 40 per cent born overseas. Migrants made up almost half of all chefs and cooks in Australia.
It also found the healthcare and social assistance sector relies heavily on migrants, with around 37 per cent of these workers born overseas. Permanent migrants made up around one quarter of all registered nurses in the sector. They also work as aged and disabled carers, child carers and nursing support staff.
What about regional and rural areas?
Grattan's analysis found that mining areas, such as the Pilbara in remote Western Australia, are more likely to rely on migrant workers, and some agricultural areas have higher shares of working holiday makers. The sunny climate of the Gold Coast is attractive to many New Zealanders.
According to the 2021 Census, around 20 per cent of working holiday makers in Australia live in regional or rural Queensland.
Hanson, who hails from Queensland and is a senator for the state, has acknowledged the importance of seasonal workers to rural and regional communities. More specifically, she's said she wants to maintain the number of workers brought in from Pacific countries and Timor-Leste through the PALM scheme (around 30,000 workers in March 2024), even though this would likely raise NOM above One Nation's target.
But she insists this won't impact the cost of housing in rural and regional areas because these workers are often given accommodation by their employers.
"Rural and regional Australia would die if they didn't have the workers coming in, especially the abattoirs and farmers, so that's a different program," Hanson told reporters at News Corp's Bush Summit last month.
One Nation and the Nationals have both criticised the Albanese government's decision to slow down the processing of working holiday visas, saying backpackers were not taking houses from people in Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane.
But a 2021 report by Grattan, titled "Rethinking permanent skilled migration after the pandemic", noted anti-migrant views appear to be more prevalent in regional Australia, even though there are far fewer migrants there, especially from parts of Asia, the Middle East and Africa.
"This suggests a sense of threat can be as important as the level of threat," the report said.
What is the problem that needs fixing?
While simply cutting migration may not solve Australia's cost of living issues, past analysis has suggested more nuanced changes to the system could help ensure it benefits the country.
The Parkinson review of the migration system in 2023 criticised Australia's reliance on temporary migrants.
"It is not in Australia's national interest to maintain a large proportion of temporary entrants with no pathway to citizenship as it undermines our democratic resilience and social cohesion," the report said.
Experts at the Grattan Institute say it's important to get Australia's temporary intake right because most permanent visas are granted to temporary residents already in Australia.
Its report suggested allowing all migrants earning wages above a certain level to be eligible for a temporary visa, rather than restricting this to certain occupations. This would address most skills shortages, simplify sponsorship pathways for employers and limit exploitation of lower-paid workers.
It would also boost the pool of high-quality applicants for permanent residency.
Visas that offer a pathway to permanent residency should be restricted to younger workers under the age of 30, the report suggests.
It also cautioned the government against increasing the number of migrants filling low-skilled jobs in Australia, as they could "undercut the wages of low-paid Australians and further increase exploitation".
In their essay On Our Terms, former immigration policy adviser Henry Sherrell and tax researcher Lachlan Vass suggest the goal of immigration policy should be to make the lives of Australians better.
The visa system should pick people deliberately, across all parts of the system, to benefit Australians.
They say Australia needs an explicit target for migration as this would provide a clear long-term signal to state governments, employers and citizens.
The authors recommended setting net migration at 1 per cent of population growth.
"Beyond which the costs grow quickly and political support wilts [according to historical observations]," the authors note.
Australian migration is currently above 1 per cent, but the government is forecasting a rate of about 0.9 per cent in 2026/27, falling to 0.8 in 2027/28, which the authors believe is "about right".
The difficulty is getting to this figure.
Careful changes required to avoid unintended consequences
While Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all promised to bring down NOM, no one has yet set out how this will be done, a sign of how challenging it is to balance competing interests.
"Any time you make a cut, you're going to have to upset [a particular] group," Boucher says.
Businesses want to retain skilled migrants as well as working holidaymakers who are often employed on farms; migrants want visas for family members; and those living in tourist areas also want to retain backpackers. Migrants also make a significant contribution in funding Australia's higher education sector.
Reducing immigration will impact Australia's economy because it reduces tax and visa revenue and slows population growth, which can lead to lower household consumption and reduced business profits.
A Treasury paper published in 2021 estimates that each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education. The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.
Boucher points to the UK, which is facing skills shortages in sectors like construction, healthcare, hospitality and skilled trades, after its work visas were tightened.
She says it's important Australia understands how to fill gaps if it cuts the supply of certain workers, and to be realistic about how quickly domestic workers can be trained to take their place.
A crackdown on bridging visas, which allow migrants to stay in Australia while their immigration status is being resolved, may also involve limiting or rescinding people's current legal appeal rights.
"[Cutting immigration could also] have impacts on things like human rights, like the right to reunify with family."
Where can we cut?
Although they don't agree with slashing international student numbers as Hanson has suggested, both Rizvi and Boucher believe student visas could be tightened — which Labor already appears to be doing.
One area of reform could be the 485 visa, which allows international students to live, study and work in Australia after completing their studies.
Sherrell and Vass have also suggested limiting temporary visas to a maximum of eight years, which would provide a firm deadline for people to transition to a permanent visa, or leave Australia.
Incentives could also be introduced to encourage people to leave Australia voluntarily when their visas expire. This could include allowing overstayers — those currently subject to re-entry bans — to make further visa applications from outside the country.
Superannuation taxes could also be waived, and a cash incentive of $20,000 to $30,000 paid when someone returns to their country of origin.
"This funding is comparatively cheap compared to endless weeks spent in immigration detention. And it is more compassionate too," Sherrell and Vass note.
Senator Jonathon Duniam, the Coalition's spokesperson for home affairs, told ABC's Insiders on 6 September that the government should find a way to deport the 77,000 illegal overstayers in Australia, and suggested temporary visa holders should be required to apply for further visas offshore.
Duniam pointed to the UK's introduction of a 'safe countries of origin' list that designates countries as generally having no serious risk of persecution and allowing for fast-track deportations.
One Nation has gone further, suggesting Australia not accept refugees from countries that the government deems unsafe for Australians to visit, citing Nepal as an example following the country’s recent devastating floods.
But cracking down on Australia's relatively low refugee intake is unlikely to shift migration numbers significantly.
One Nation hasn't clarified whether it would reduce current humanitarian numbers from 20,000, which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese recently confirmed the government would maintain.
This is lower than Labor's previously stated target of 27,000 by 2025, but higher than the 13,750 the party was reportedly recently considering cutting it to.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor hasn't specified a number for the Coalition's refugee intake but says it will be below the former Morrison government's level of 17,875.
Boucher points out that targeting one specific group or visa class as a means of controlling migration has its limits.
If you cut [visas] in one area, how do you now that family migration is not going to spike?
She says prospective applicants will adapt to policy changes and look for workarounds; for example, a cut to student visas could trigger a spike in partner visas.
"It's in the fine grain that the decisions have to be made and that's what makes it such a challenging policy area."
