How US leaders remembered the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:21:48 UTC
04:21:48 KST

How US leaders remembered the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks
Trump drew parallels to the US’s present-day war against Iran, while figures like Abdul El-Sayed called for inclusivity.
A quarter-century after the attacks on September 11, 2001, officials across the United States have taken part in tributes and memorials to honour the 2,977 victims and those who risked their lives as part of the rescue efforts.
The incident is considered the deadliest “terrorist” attack in US history.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trial for 9/11 accused, including Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, set for June 2028
- list 2 of 3Mamdani releases records on toxic air in New York after 9/11 attacks
- list 3 of 3Trump pays tribute to the victims of 9/11 at Pentagon ceremony
Four planes were hijacked. Two crashed into the World Trade Center, causing its Twin Towers to collapse. A third struck the Pentagon outside Washington, DC. And the fourth plummeted into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew rose against their attackers.
Through social media messages, public speeches and appearances at ceremonies, US leaders on Friday took different approaches to remembering the lives of the thousands who perished on the fateful day.
Here’s what they said:
US President Donald Trump
US President Donald Trump chose to stay in Washington, DC, to observe the 25th anniversary.
During the attacks, 184 people died near the capital when American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US military.
Trump opted not to attend a Friday ceremony at the World Trade Center site in New York, where all his living presidential predecessors were in attendance.
His vice president, JD Vance, travelled to New York instead. The ceremony at the World Trade Center has a policy of not allowing political speeches.
In his remarks at the Pentagon, Trump described what happened as “true evil”. He also paid tribute to those who died in the attacks.
“We will honour their lives, we will cherish their beautiful memories, and we will protect this country and its freedoms for every future generation,” Trump said.
The president also praised US troops as he appeared to link the 9/11 attacks with his administration’s war against Iran.
“We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory,” Trump said.
“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror – the Islamic Republic of Iran – will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he later added.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also spoke at the Pentagon, delivering his remarks shortly before Trump’s.
He warned the audience to practice “eternal vigilance” against what he called continued threats.
“There are still enemies who hate us. Every day, enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home,” he said.
He proceeded to seemingly use the 9/11 attacks as justification for the US-Israeli war against Iran, which started on February 28.
“Over the past six months, we have laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism,” Hegseth said, referring to Iran. “Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11.”
He went on to claim that the US military has destroyed Iran’s defences and that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for international trade.
Iran has stopped commercial traffic through the strait since the start of the war.
“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong, to hell, and tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong,” Hegseth said. “And we’re ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day. We control the strait. We will finish this fight.”
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attended the New York memorial service, alongside the city’s former mayor, Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the attacks.
Before the event started, Giuliani shook hands with the mayor, despite previously calling on Mamdani not to attend the event.
Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, had recently come under fire from some conservative politicians and victims’ family members who said his presence at the memorial would offend them.
A Change.org petition garnered more than 100,000 signatures from those who wished to express concern about Mamdani’s participation.
Like all politicians attending the service at the National September 11 Memorial, Mamdani was not permitted to speak.
Instead, the mayor released a video on social media remembering those who were killed and challenging the public to honour their memory by doing good works.
“Twenty-five years later, we have a sacred obligation to those who were stolen from us. To care for one another as they cared for strangers. To live lives worthy of the sacrifices they made. And to build a city worthy of their courage. A city where we run toward one another,” Mamdani said.
“That is how we’ll remember.”
On Tuesday, Mamdani also released a trove of previously undisclosed documents suggesting city officials tried to downplay – or even mislead – first residents about the dangerous air quality following the attacks.
US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took to the social media platform X to honour the lives lost during what he described as a “cruel act of terror”.
El-Sayed is locked in a tight midterm race in Michigan against his Republican opponent, former US Representative Mike Rogers.
Michigan’s open Senate seat is considered a must-win seat for Democrats, if they hope to take back control of the US Senate.
Rogers has sought to create controversy over El-Sayed’s past comments about the September 11 attacks. He has pointed to audio of El-Sayed reportedly saying, “9/11 scarred our country in profound ways, but what we did after 9/11 scarred millions of other people.”
During the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday, Rogers blasted El-Sayed, who is Muslim, for being sympathetic to terrorists. He also sought to highlight El-Sayed’s links to left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker.
“I never imagined that, 25 years after 9/11, I would be running against somebody who campaigns with Hasan Piker, who thinks America deserved it,” Rogers said. “Yep, but here we are.”
On Friday, however, El-Sayed used his social media post to push back against Rogers’s attacks.
“Nothing can justify the murder of innocent civilians. Nothing,” El-Sayed wrote.
He also called on Americans to help build a country that was “more inclusive, more empowering, more just” in tribute to the lives lost.
“They didn’t just attack America that day. They attacked the idea of America,” El-Sayed said of the 19 al-Qaeda hijackers who participated in the attacks.
“The notion of a nation brought together by ideals where it doesn’t matter how you pray or if you pray at all. A place where freedom and commitment to justice bind us, even if at times we struggle to fully realise it.”

The US Government Launched 3 Previously Unreported Investigations of Polymarket Trades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:21:34 UTC
04:21:34 KST

The US government launched at least three previously unreported investigations into trading on the prediction market Polymarket, according to documents obtained by WIRED through a Freedom of Information Act request.
Voting records from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates prediction markets, shed new light on how the government approaches these investigations. In early May, CFTC chairman Michael Selig approved an order allowing the agency’s enforcement division to launch a private investigation into potential insider trading on Polymarket event contracts related to pardons issued by former president Joseph Biden. The order granted permission to take testimony, obtain subpoenas, administer oaths, and require the production of documents in the course of the investigation.
The documents obtained by WIRED did not specify which trades were under suspicion, but the order came several weeks after an NPR report on a suspicious Polymarket trader who netted over $300,000 on pardon-related markets in the final days of the Biden administration. The trader correctly wagered that the former president would issue preemptive pardons to a number of prominent MAGA critics, including former US representatives Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, and US senator Adam Schiff.
At the end of May, Selig approved another investigation order. This time, the topic was “Iran event contracts” on Polymarket. As with the Biden pardon documents, the investigation order did not provide details, but it came two weeks after 60 Minutes aired a report on a network of suspicious Polymarket accounts that made $2.4 million on Iran-related trades, with a 98 percent win rate.
“If these investigations are being prompted solely by press reports of potential violations of the Commodities Exchange Act, that’s a significant sign of weakness in this regulatory scheme,” says Joseph Konizeski, a former chief trial attorney in the CFTC’s division of enforcement. The agency has come under fire in the second Trump era for its perceived friendliness to the prediction market industry.
In July, Selig greenlit a third investigation, this time focused on suspected insider trading on Google-themed Polymarket event contracts. In an email exchange included in the documents obtained by WIRED, Paul Hayeck, the acting director of the CFTC’s department of enforcement, noted that the investigation would focus on “additional individuals who may have engaged in insider trading related to Google’s 2025 Year in Search Ranking.” Hayeck wrote that the Southern District of New York is conducting a “parallel investigation.” He specified that the CFTC's investigation would be separate from the ongoing case against Michele Spagnuolo, a Google engineer accused of insider trading.
SDNY declined to comment. Google declined to comment. It pointed WIRED to a statement it released in June noting that Spagnuolo was no longer with the company. The CFTC did not respond to requests for comment and questions about the status of the investigations.
“While we do not comment on specific investigations, we regularly refer matters to law enforcement and support ongoing investigations as part of our commitment to protecting the integrity of our markets,” Olivia Chalos, deputy chief legal officer at Polymarket, told WIRED in an email.
The CFTC is also reportedly investigating Polymarket itself. The company, which had its flagship platform banned from the United States in 2022, was permitted to launch a US-regulated version with a narrower set of markets in late 2025. It recently underwent a fundraising round led by Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, which valued the company at $21 billion.
The CFTC has also launched investigations into potential insider trading on Kalshi, Polymarket’s archrival, in the past. According to The New York Times, Kalshi has referred at least 32 cases to the agency. The CFTC fined former US representative George Santos $35,000 for his behavior related to a Kalshi contract about whether he would attend Trump’s 2026 State of the Union address.
Kalshi issued its first-ever lifetime ban to Santos for violating its rules on market manipulation for the same behavior, and also fined him just over $71,000. Santos was not criminally charged.
So far, two arrests have been made stemming from Polymarket insider trading investigations. In April, federal authorities arrested a US special forces officer who prosecutors say used classified information to make more than $400,000 in profits on event contracts related to the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. And in May, Spagnuolo, who allegedly made over $1.2 million on insider trades, was arrested while traveling to New York. In both cases, the CFTC filed civil charges, and the Department of Justice filed criminal fraud charges. Both men are fighting back by arguing that Polymarket trades are a form of betting and not subject to commodities law.
It’s unclear if the Department of Justice has launched parallel investigations into the Iran War or Biden pardon contracts. The DOJ did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A former CFTC staffer tells WIRED that parallel criminal investigations are likely, “given the significance of the matters.”
Additional reporting by Maddy Varner.
Update 9/11/2026 4:15 pm ET: This story has been updated to include a response from SDNY.

Traveling to Kyiv during war: What you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:20:10 UTC
04:20:10 KST

Traveling to Kyiv during war: What you need to know
A person looks at the train schedule at the railway station in Kyiv, Ukraine, on June 12, 2024. (Danylo Pavlov / The Kyiv Independent)
Booking spontaneous trips within minutes using a single platform is a distant memory for those wanting to come home or visit Ukraine.
Over 20 million people have passed through the Ukrainian border in the first half of 2026, the Ukrainian State Border Guard Service revealed on Aug. 5, setting the year on track to be the busiest since the beginning of the full-scale war.
Yet reaching Ukrainian cities remains a complicated task since the complete shutdown of the country's airspace in February 2022, leaving only two options for travel: by road or by rail.
What was once a simple flight away is now a completely different type of odyssey. The Kyiv Independent explains the easiest ways to get to Kyiv during the war and what to consider when traveling.
Main routes
For those traveling from more distant locations, the easiest way to get to Kyiv is to first fly to Poland or Moldova and then take a train or bus. However, direct trains and buses are also available from dozens of cities across Europe.
Since the onset of Russia's full-scale war, most people have been heading to Warsaw as the first leg of their Kyiv journeys, owing to the Polish capital's large international airport and Poland's developed road and railway networks.
But with the full-scale war approaching its fifth year, Polish border crossings, train stations, and airports have become overloaded with travelers.
Recently, Moldova's capital, Chisinau, has become a substitute for crowded Poland. Its airport offers low-cost flights to destinations across Europe, as well as direct bus routes to and from Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.
Another popular alternative is Budapest. Like Chisinau, the city's airport is well connected and offers trains and buses to Kyiv and several other Ukrainian cities.
read also
Transport options
Due to the constant threat of Russian attacks, it is only possible to reach Kyiv by land. Despite the war, there are ways to travel comfortably and efficiently.
The daily Warsaw sleeper train remains the most popular and takes about 14 hours, depending on border wait times.
But since direct tickets between Warsaw and Kyiv sell out very quickly, the Polish border towns of Przemysl and Chelm have become important travel hubs. Travelers often use them as stopovers for trips from the airports in Warsaw, Krakow, or elsewhere.
A journey to Kyiv from Przemysl or Chelm usually takes around 10-11 hours. Traveling through these stopover cities sometimes requires buying separate tickets for the Polish and Ukrainian legs of the trip, however.
One complication of traveling via Poland is that Ukrainian trains do not use the standard European track gauge, so passengers have to switch trains before crossing into Ukraine.
Upon reaching the border, passengers must leave trains operated by European carriers and continue their journey with Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways), Ukraine's state-owned and sole passenger train operator.
Luckily, Ukrainian tracks extend to the Polish border towns of Przemysl and Chelm, meaning passengers can board a Kyiv-bound Ukrzaliznytsia train already there.
Traveling by train from Budapest entails similar challenges.
On the direct route, the train makes a technical stop at the Ukrainian border town of Chop, where it either swaps wheels to match the Ukrainian track gauge or passengers switch trains at border control.
On average, the entire journey from Hungary's capital takes around 18 hours.
On the other hand, Moldova uses the same tracks as Ukraine, allowing direct train service from Chisinau without additional stops. Direct sleeper trains take upwards of 17 hours and run daily to and from Kyiv.
While train travel may be more comfortable, bus travel offers greater flexibility in passenger capacity and departure times.
Companies like FlixBus, which operates double-decker buses, offer over 10 daily trips from Warsaw, with an estimated journey time of 13 to 18 hours. They also offer direct bus connections to Kyiv from other cities across Europe.
Another popular option for road travel is a smaller minibus that seats up to 10 passengers and offers more comfortable recliner seats, blankets, and even onboard amenities like Wi-Fi.
Companies advertising luxury travel operate these minibusses and have their own preferred border crossings, departure days, and stops along the way. Depending on these factors, journey time may last anywhere from 11 hours.
Buying a ticket
Planning ahead is crucial, yet it can be difficult during wartime.
Ukrzaliznytsia mostly opens ticket sales at 9 a.m. local time 20 days before the departure date, though some tickets may go live 30 days in advance.
Tickets for Ukrainian trains can be purchased on the Ukrzaliznytsia website or mobile app, but all international routes require identity verification through Diia — Ukraine's digital state system — or, for foreigners, identification via a bank account.
For foreigners who do not live in Ukraine and don't have a bank account there, buying international tickets online via Ukrzaliznytsia requires some additional steps.
They must first verify their identity through the app by submitting photos of themselves holding a passport and of their passport next to a security code generated by the app. Only then can they purchase the tickets.
read also
For some cross-border trips to Ukraine, travelers can also buy tickets on the websites of Ukrzaliznytsia's international partners, such as the Czech carrier RegioJet or Polish Railways.
Train tickets from Poland range from $50 to over $110 (about Hr 2,700 to 6,000), depending on the type of ticket and the timing of booking relative to departure.
Simple seats tend to be cheaper than sleeping berths, though the latter is much more comfortable for long cross-border travels.
Train tickets from Chisinau cost between $55 and $80 (roughly Hr 2,500 to 3,600), also depending on ticket class and booking time.
For those traveling from Budapest, a ticket to Chop costs less than $15 (usually under Hr 500), and the next train bound for Kyiv costs from $40 (Hr 1,815).
Bus ticket costs vary more depending on the carrier. FlixBus offers a trip from Kyiv to Warsaw "for as little as $54.98," but this requires advance booking.
Tickets for private minibusses tend to be more expensive, with some companies charging over $150 for transfers between Warsaw Airport and Kyiv.
Traveling in wartime
Travel during war changed dramatically, forcing both carriers and passengers to adapt. Wartime conditions can unexpectedly prolong travel time.
Before the full-scale war, an hour-long queue at the airport border control seemed tedious; it is now considered lucky to cross the Polish-Ukrainian border within two to three hours. Such unpredictability affects how travelers plan for connecting flights and trains.
Crossing Ukraine's state border requires a passport, but citizens of most countries across Europe, North America, and elsewhere can stay in Ukraine visa-free for up to 90 days.
Once in Ukraine, another unpredictable element complicates the journey — Russian strikes and air-raid alerts.
For trains, an air-raid alert means an emergency stop and mandatory disembarkation. Ukrzaliznytsia adopted these rules after Russian drones repeatedly struck civilian passenger trains. Passengers are often left standing in fields, sometimes in the middle of the night and without a shelter nearby.
Buses, on the other hand, are not required by law to stop during air raid alerts. However, the risk of a Russian strike is always present — another factor travelers must take into account when planning their journey.

Berk Kutay Gokmen
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, the deadliest such attacks in US history, was commemorated Friday with a ceremony in New York City.
The ceremony was held at the site of the former World Trade Center and attended by US Vice President JD Vance, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, as well as former Presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton.

The brief interaction between Giuliani and Mamdani was also noted by US media. Despite Giuliani’s previous calls for Mamdani to stay away from the Sept. 11 commemorations, the two shook hands and exchanged a few words during the ceremony.
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, attended a separate memorial ceremony at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.

Saudi Arabia shuts East-West Pipeline after drone attacks from Iraq, injuries reported
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:13:26 UTC
04:13:26 KST

Mohammad Sio
11 September 2026•Update: 12 September 2026
Saudi Arabia said Friday that it had shut down its East-West Pipeline after it was hit by multiple drone attacks originating from Iraq in the Riyadh and Madinah regions Thursday, leaving several people injured and causing damage.
An official source at the Energy Ministry, in a statement, said the attacks took place on Thursday morning.
The source said the oil pipeline was shut down “as a precautionary measure” following the attacks.
A number of people were injured and received medical care, the ministry said, without specifying the number of casualties or their condition.
Emergency and specialized technical teams responded immediately and took measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.
The ministry said any further developments will be announced in due course.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the attacks, saying the pipeline was targeted by several drones coming from Iraq.
It said the attacks caused injuries and some damage that authorities are working to repair.
Riyadh said it decided not to retaliate "at this stage" after Iraq’s prime minister requested that Saudi Arabia allow Baghdad to take measures to prevent attacks launched from Iraqi territory against the kingdom and neighboring countries.
Saudi Arabia said it supports the Iraqi government's efforts to prevent the attacks.
The kingdom stressed, however, that it reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security, facilities, citizens, and residents.
In response, Iraq condemned the attacks and rejected any assault that threatens the kingdom's security and stability or harms relations between the two countries.
Iraq orders investigation into attack
The prime minister's media office said Baghdad welcomes Saudi Arabia's decision to respond positively to Iraqi efforts to contain the situation, describing the move as reflecting Riyadh's concern for Iraq's security and stability and its commitment to bilateral relations.
Iraqi Prime Minister and Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Ali al-Zaidi ordered an investigation into the circumstances of the attacks and the parties behind them, according to the statement.
He also directed authorities to take legal action against anyone found to have been involved, stressing that the state would not tolerate activities that endanger Iraq or its relations with neighboring and friendly countries.
The government said it would continue working with regional and international partners to prevent similar attacks and uphold the principles of good-neighborly relations.
Baghdad reiterated that Iraqi territory and airspace "will not be a launching point for attacks against any country," stressing that its policy is based on respecting the sovereignty of other states and preventing Iraq from becoming an arena for regional confrontation.
Tensions between Riyadh and Baghdad rose sharply in late July after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted several drones launched from Iraq that were attempting to strike oil facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh region. Saudi Arabia blamed Iranian-backed militias and urged Baghdad to prevent Iraqi territory from being used as a launching point for attacks against the kingdom.
Iraqi authorities pledged to prevent unauthorized attacks against neighboring states and subsequently formed a joint security committee to develop measures aimed at preventing violations.
The dispute escalated again on July 29 when US and Saudi forces carried out strikes against sites belonging to the Iranian-aligned Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) in Iraq. The PMF said 20 members were killed and 32 wounded.
Saudi Arabia said the operation was carried out in self-defense following attacks from Iraq on its petroleum facilities.

Houthi advance in Yemen is about more than just the Red Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:01:07 UTC
04:01:07 KST

Houthi advance in Yemen is about more than just the Red Sea
Houthis were already able to disrupt shipping – their advance consolidates that power, and exposes Yemeni government weakness.
The rapid Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week is an astonishing military victory, but not quite the game-changer it is being portrayed as.
The group has been able to threaten the vitally important shipping route, but they have been doing so since 2023. This new victory consolidates that control, proving that Yemen’s government is not currently in a position to defeat them.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can the Houthis close the Red Sea after seizing the Yemen coast?
- list 2 of 3Why Pakistan is talking to Iran as the Houthi-Saudi fight escalates
- list 3 of 3Houthis control key shipping route after gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast
The prior Houthi control over the northern section of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, including the major port city of Hodeidah, has allowed the Iran-allied rebel group, for years, to first attack shipping linked to Israel and the United States – and then, in recent months, Saudi Arabian-linked vessels.
That control also damaged the global economy. Long before the US war with Iran and the transformation of the Strait of Hormuz into a tool to throttle international trade, Houthi attacks around Yemen had turned Bab al-Mandeb into a similar weapon, and led to bombing campaigns against the Houthis by the US, the United Kingdom, and Israel.
Houthi officials themselves have emphasised this, with one leading official, Abdulqader al-Murtada, saying earlier this week that the group did “not need control over Bab al-Mandeb, for the blockade [on Saudi ships] is already in place”. Al-Murtada could point to the Saudi ships that have avoided Bab al-Mandeb since the Houthis began attacking them in July, even before their latest progress.
However, the Houthi lightning advance makes it even easier for the group to disrupt shipping. They now have access to the Red Sea’s narrow entry point and several islands in it, allowing them to use shorter-range weapons and more easily reach vessels they want to attack and board, as well as potentially using sea mines to further restrict shipping.
Not going away
The increase in the Houthi ability to target shipping – even with the caveats outlined above – does have an impact on market sentiment. Oil prices have increased as traders price in the ability for Iran and its allies to disrupt shipping in Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, the two maritime chokepoints of the southern Arabian Peninsula.
However, the consequences of this advance are not limited to the increased ability of the Houthis to attack shipping, but to the increasing reality that the Houthi problem on the Red Sea is not going away.
For months, after Saudi Arabia backed a Yemeni government campaign against southern Yemeni separatist forces earlier this year, the mood had shifted in the country’s anti-Houthi camp.
The perception was that the Yemeni government, led by the Presidential Leadership Council, had finally gotten its act together. President Rashad al-Alimi repeatedly spoke of a unified military chain of command, allowing the military to overcome the divisions blamed for its inability to defeat the Houthis.
Yemeni and Saudi officials had hinted at an anti-Houthi campaign all year. The Red Sea coastline was a possible location: the largely flat geography suited the government, allowing Saudi Arabia to effectively use its air power; much of the population is not made up of the Houthis’ traditional support base; and prior Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping meant that there would likely be international buy-in for such a campaign.
The seizure of the Red Sea coastline has broken all of those narratives.
The momentum the Yemeni government thought it had, even at the start of this week when it claimed advances in al-Jawf, to the east of the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, is now gone.
After months of projecting unity, Yemen’s anti-Houthi camp is once again turning on itself, trading accusations of blame for the defeat.
Saudi dilemma
The message the Houthis have for Saudi Arabia is clear: ‘Your partners in Yemen can’t defeat us.’
Therefore, the potential Houthi argument is that Saudi Arabia has to make a deal with them and agree to their terms, including Riyadh funding public sector salaries, access to income from Yemen’s oil and gas reserves, and no restrictions on flights and shipping to Houthi-controlled ports.
The Houthis have an incentive to lock in their gains and raise the cost of escalation before Saudi-backed Yemeni forces can reorganise.
Their attacks on Saudi Arabia, escalating in the past week, have been damaging, and the group is promising more if Riyadh increases its military support for the Yemeni government.
The risk of any such intervention is clearly there for Saudi Arabia. But so is the risk of inaction. The Houthis have repeatedly demanded more concessions when they were in positions of strength.
With the Yemen war unresolved, the Houthis may decide to escalate again in the future, even if a deal is agreed now.
And so, policymakers in Riyadh could determine that it makes more sense to make a concerted effort to deal with the problem head-on now, rather than allow it to fester into the future.

04:01:00 KST

Dozens of newly declassified presidential briefing documents released Friday, marking 25 years since the Sept. 11 attacks, shed new light on U.S. intelligence about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida in the years and months before the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people.
The documents illustrate security analysts' tracking of bin Laden's movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to U.S. targets.
Proclaiming "an act of exceptional transparency,” CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the documents were the agency's single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs - the highly classified briefing prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.
The documents range from a February 1998 file - prepared for then-President Bill Clinton - entitled "Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning bin Laden and other terrorists to a Sept. 12, 2001, report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the U.S. Capitol.
Another, from just weeks before the attacks, details how al-Qaida's "flexible operational decision making and broad definition of acceptable targets enable the group to adjust plans to changing conditions.”
Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that probed the attacks from 2002 to 2004.

Traditionally, there are no political speeches at the Ground Zero commemoration. Victims’ relatives read their names, paid tribute to first responders and called for national unity.
The United States on Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks with a solemn ceremony in New York.
The anniversary was marked by commemorations across the country, including wreath-laying ceremonies, moments of silence, vigils and readings of victims’ names, as well as volunteer initiatives.
On 11 September 2001, hijackers from al-Qaeda, an Islamist extremist group, seized four commercial jets and crashed them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people.
US President Donald Trump attended a ceremony at the Pentagon rather than in New York, drawing criticism from some victims’ relatives and linked the post-9/11 “war on terror” to the current war in Iran.
"Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget. That's why we fight today," Trump said.
9/11’s legacy: Security vs freedom
The 11 September attacks left a lasting impact on many aspects of life in the United States and continue to shape the debate over the balance between security and freedom.
The attacks transformed US air travel, led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and prompted new federal surveillance and intelligence-gathering powers, as well as new banking regulations.
They also fostered a culture of individual vigilance, summed up by the slogan “if you see something, say something”, while a wave of patriotism encouraged some Americans to join the military, fire departments and police forces.
New York mayor attends 9/11 ceremony amid criticism
The September 11 attacks fuelled mistrust, prejudice and hate crimes against Muslims in the United States. Twenty-five years later, Muslim Americans have a growing role in public life, with Zohran Mamdani serving as New York City’s first Muslim mayor.
Mamdani attended Friday’s Ground Zero ceremony despite a campaign urging him to stay away, backed by former Mayor Rudy Giuliani and the right-wing New York Post newspaper.
A petition was signed by more than 100,000 people. It accuses Mamdani of links to individuals seen as dismissive of US institutions or extremist ideologies.
Mamdani was recently praised for releasing documents revealing what city officials knew about toxic air in Lower Manhattan after 9/11, which has been linked to cancers affecting thousands of New Yorkers.

The true crime writer fighting to solve decades-old Adelaide murders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

The Interview: Debi Marshall can't stop investigating murder
Debi Marshall can't bear the avalanche of true crime we're living through. There must be a reason to do it, she says, and that's the pursuit of truth and justice. But she understands the public's fascination with what she calls "the dark side". She can't shake it herself, despite her family begging her to stop, despite the toll she says it's taken on her life.
An investigative journalist and author of six true crime books — including Killing For Pleasure, on which the film Snowtown is based — Marshall's investigation into the so-called Family Court bomber Leonard Warick drew attention to him years before he was charged with multiple murders. She also chronicled the 1973 murder of baby girl Deidre Kennedy and her family's push to overhaul Queensland's double jeopardy rules, which they eventually achieved.
Marshall has promised her daughter she's finished writing true crime books. But there's one case she can't let go of — Adelaide's unsolved "family" murders — and she's fighting, along with the victims' families, to lift suppression orders she believes could lead to answers.
You've written about worrying whether you have crossed a line into "barbaric sensationalism" in your "quest to expose the truth", and that some days you question why you do the work you do, whether anyone cares. What keeps you doing this work?
It simply has to be done. It has to be written. I mean, there are so many unsolved murders in this country, sadly. And there's very few investigative crime journalists who are doing the work that I do. And when you speak to victims' families as often as I do, who reach out to me and ask for help, I just find it impossible to turn my back on them. And it could be a child murder; it could be serial killings.
So, as hard as it is on me personally, and it has taken a dreadful toll on me at all sorts of levels, I can't turn my back on it. I can't walk away. And I think it's the path I've chosen and the things that go with that, the nightmares, I regard them as something of collateral damage, but the older I get, the more I notice the toll it's taken on me.
I was recently reading writer Maggie Nelson's memoir The Red Parts. She said that while researching her aunt's murder she suffered from what she called "murder mind". She could write all day with "a certain distance", but "in bed at night I found a smattering of sickening images of violent acts ready and waiting for me". Would you describe what you experience as akin to murder mind?
Oh, absolutely. When you're writing or researching, your mind takes you to another place. You're focused on what you're doing, as you need to be, and it's only later at rest when the words and the images and the interviews and the thoughts come back sometimes in very distorted ways, but always in nightmares. And some of the nightmares I've had are unrepeatable.
My specialty, for want of a different way of putting it, is serial killers. So, when you're chasing serial killers, you need to be careful they don't start chasing you. But they do start chasing you in your dreams. And sometimes they catch you, which is awful.
Also, I'm dealing with lust killers. So, these people are opportunistic. They're the worst type of killer in terms of the public's fascination with them, but also the fear that they engender in the community, because you don't know where they are. They could be the boy next door and often are.
So, these people frequently visit me in my nightmares to the point where when my daughter was 12 years old, I was still walking her to school. It was only one block away my sister said, "you've got to stop doing this, it's not healthy". I was like, "I can't let her go because there could be someone waiting for her".
I mean, that of course is extreme. That was happening when I was writing the Snowtown book, Killing For Pleasure. When you're dealing with sexual torture, and cannibalism and dismemberment, to the degree that I was immersed in that particular story at that time, there's no respite from it.
Do you think over time you've gotten better at balancing, I guess, the statistical probability that your daughter's probably very safe compared to what you know from what you have investigated?
No. I have three grandchildren who are all under five. And I just about have a heart attack when they open the front door on their own. Because I know how quickly these things can happen. I know how quickly children can be snatched. And just because we think we're safe in our front yard, trust me, we're not.
I wrote a book, called Lambs to the Slaughter, on a guy called Derek Percy, who was an opportunistic child killer. And he wrote of his sadistic fantasies. I think that he murdered nine children in the 60s.
I know they were different days. But it was just that quick and that opportunistic and it can happen to anyone, anytime.
In 2022 you published the book Banquet: The Untold Story of Adelaide's Family Murders about the chilling abduction, sexual abuse and murder of five teenage boys and young men in Adelaide between 1979 and 83. You've investigated the murders and the rumours linking these crimes to Adelaide's elite. You're still working on the cases, of which four of the five remain unsolved. Do you believe they can be solved?
Absolutely. They not only can be solved, they should be solved and they should have been solved a long time ago. There was suppression sitting around names of people who were either police witnesses, informants or suspects and I'm in a battle royale right now working with some of Australia's senior legal figures, who are equally as appalled as I am that these suppressions remain in place, to try to get those suppressions lifted or at least one of them lifted.
What's involved in this battle to get these suppression orders lifted?
These are orders that are almost 50 years old and there's no court case within cooee. So, they were put on in the administration of justice, or part of that was in the administration of justice, to protect the integrity of a trial. Well, there is no trial that we know of, but South Australia Police recently made a public statement that they would not support the lifting of these suppressions. In the meantime, we've got victims' families sitting out there praying for justice and passing the baton of grief to yet another generation, which is just so unacceptable.
So, the lawyers are investigating how and if we get that suppression lifted. I, along with the lawyers and the Commissioner for Victims' Rights in South Australia, are representing the victims' families in this matter. We've started a GoFundMe crowdfunding called "Adelaide's 'Family' Murders: Help Lift Suppression Orders". We need that to cover running costs and also in the event that we will have to pay the legal costs of any person who challenges the lifting of the orders. If we win, the money will go to the Homicide Victims Support Group.
If you are successful in getting the suppression orders lifted, what's next?
What's next is the image or images, depending on how many we can get lifted.
How many are we talking about?
Well, there's a few, but some of them are not particularly relevant to what I'm looking at.
The family members of these young men have waited decades to see some kind of justice. You know what they're going through. You pursued the killer of your partner Ron Jarvis, and finally saw him sentenced 22 years after the crime. What did that wait feel like?
I'm always reluctant to compare what I went through with Ronnie with what the victims' families go through because to lose a child, whether they're an adult or not, must be incomprehensibly heartbreaking. To lose a partner was bad enough, but to get justice, it's just the most extraordinary thing.
In my case, to be able to visit Ron's grave site and say, you know, we got him, we finally got him, but it's taken 22 years, darling, but here we are.
In Ron's case, he was a marijuana dealer, I didn't know that until very late in the day, and he was murdered not long after that. I remember someone saying to me once, well, he's not exactly an innocent victim, is he? I guess the general public would look at it like that.
But when you're in the thick of it and you're in love with someone who's murdered, it certainly doesn't feel like that. It just feels like an enormous heartache that you carry with you forever.
I was in my early 30s, and I was on my own for a very long time after that because I was just too heartbroken to re-partner.
How do you clear your heart and your mind of all the horrors that you see in your work? Where is your happy place?
When things get really too bad for me I'll trot off and see a psychologist. But the other part of me is I'm blessed to have been born with an optimistic, happy nature so that if things get really grim, I throw a party. I love to dance and sing and drink beautiful wine and travel and I have a gorgeous little family and special friends.
True crime is everywhere these days. Why do you think it's so popular?
People are just fascinated by the dark side. What makes a person tick, pulling back that veil, looking into a human soul that is so tortured and so dark, that is endlessly fascinating. And that's part of the reason I do the work as well. Was it nurture or nature? Did something happen to them in their childhood? If it did, does that excuse their behaviour?
For example, we've got the situation with James Vlassakis at the moment, the youngest of the Snowtown killers. His parole was agreed and then, they went into this legal argy-bargy and he's still behind bars waiting to see whether they'll let him out of the gates.
He has done his time in terms of his sentence, but now it becomes a moral issue for many people. Well, yes, he has served his sentence, but does that mean he should be released?
Do you consume many true crime podcasts or books?
No, look, I don't. And my daughter, who is herself a journalist, a few years ago begged me, "mum, please stop writing this stuff, please, it's enough". And I sort of did make that promise, but I'm not sure that I won't break it one day.
It sounds to me like you're not quite finished, especially with the family murders.
I'm certainly not finished with the family members and my daughter knows that. She accepts that one. I think she just doesn't want me to go back into that darkness.
I divorced about a year ago and with my lovely ex-husband I used to just sit up at night, pretty much every night, particularly when I was doing a book or TV series or whatever, and ruminate on the cases with him. And he hates true crime. He's a builder. He's a bloke who likes to get his hands dirty and make something constructive.
Even though he was incredibly supportive, he never really understood why I was so fascinated with that. He supported me through it, but one night he said, "Deb, can you stop talking about this? Let's have some peace in our household, some fresh air from this". And I get that, you know, because it does become all consuming.

Hastie emerges as genuine conviction politician

analysis
Genuine conviction politicians cut through in the age of large language models
People who lead us in public life can often sound like one of those dead-eyed "large language models" many are so worried about.
Politically-optimised LLMs jerry-rigged to flesh-and-bone "neural networks". Sprouting reasonable-sounding nonsense.
All that's missing is a silly name like Llama or Rufus.
This column has no real understanding of how AI works. But the way LLMs are fed on data in Silicon Valley's dark satanic mills reminds one of how the French force-feed ducks and geese to expand their livers for foie gras. It's illegal to produce this artery-clogging delicacy in Australia because the ducks really don't like it.
But as with AI, we're allowed to import foie gras in whatever quantities we fancy.
One Nation's failed super sell
Politicians feed their personal internal LLMs with polls and focus groups and by watching how voters react to the things they and their colleagues do and say. Then then hold up the mirror to the audience, hoping they like what they see.
As with any circular self-fertilising system it pays to keep your guard up for when these political AI machines make stuff up. Or worse still, hallucinate.
Barnaby Joyce springs to mind after this week declaring on 7.30 that he "was not Jesus Christ". And that he should therefore not be asked too many questions about One Nation's latest superannuation policy.
The uncharitable interpretation of this — certainly one that Treasurer Jim Chalmers suggested — is that Joyce was bluffing his way around the fact that he didn't know the details. An interpretation, by the way, that some Liberals privately agree with.
There's a strong view that One Nation's policy was leaked by someone inside the Coalition which was preparing to announce a very similar idea.
But we've digressed somewhat. Back to politicians who sound like automated simulacra of intelligence and meaning.
Hastie launches blistering assault
Sometimes you get a flash of lightning. An insight into someone being more genuine and honest.
This week raised the possibility that Andrew Hastie might be an example after he launched a blistering public assault on Pauline Hanson for calling him a "traitor" in a social media cartoon.
The former SAS veteran who served three tours in the Middle East slammed Hanson as a "lying coward" for failing to take responsibility and deleting the film, which called him a traitor eight times. He said her accusation was an attack on all veterans.
"The question I have for Senator Hanson is: are you calling them traitors as well? Because if you are, just own it. You don't get to redefine ANZAC. You don't get to redefine the profession of arms."
The row between Hastie and One Nation continues to rumble, but it's generated plenty of online heat.
Tassie senator Jacqui Lambie, another veteran, was equally scathing of Hanson, who by Friday was telling everyone to take a "chill pill".
As of late yesterday the offending video was still pinned to the top of her social media feeds.
Hastie's fightback — which has been buttressed by a string of Coalition voices — is both targeted and deliberate. The MP for Canning knows he has a difficult fight on his hands keeping his southern Perth-based seat in the face of a resurgent One Nation. And he's long ago decided that rather than work with Hanson — as some Liberals have advocated — he wants to take her on directly.
It's all complicated by the fact that Hastie is up against it given WA's insular media ecosystem is largely arrayed against him over the Ben Roberts-Smith case. So it's a bold experiment and we'll have to wait to see if it works.
But the unique thing about what Hastie is doing is that he's fighting fire with fire against Australia's most prominent populist. It's part of an ongoing transformation over recent months.
Loading
Remember when we made big cars
A year ago Hastie was making headlines with a fairly hokey social media campaign that was harking back to a distant past, a sepia-coloured Hills Hoist idyll. Remember when we made big cars. Economists — inside and outside the Coalition — shook their heads in disbelief.
Then Hastie learnt the hard way what it means to be burnt by the flaming pit of hell that is online engagement.
Originally pitching himself as a libertarian against political censorship, Hastie was against the tide of Labor's post-Bondi anti-vilification legislation. After switching to a more centrist view that there should be limits on saying terrible things about minorities, Hastie was excommunicated by many of his previous boosters, outraged at this transgression.
In response, Hastie has been busy trying to build support from different constituencies.
The question for Hastie, and those who want him to lead the Liberal Party, is whether he can make his momentum last.
There's no way to know at this point and there are many examples abroad of how such an approach has failed. Particularly in the United States where Donald Trump tore down column after column of Republican opponents.
Hanson is no Trump, but it's a dangerous fight. In the US, Republicans who couldn't beat Trump either joined him or quietly faded away, though there are some exceptions.
At the very least, Hastie has established that he's an institutionalist, with a clear set of values and that he's prepared to defend them, even if it's uncomfortable and may upset his own base. But that's what genuine conviction politicians do.

Meanwhile, the Greens splinter
Which brings us to the Greens, who were quietly having their own internal meltdown this week.
The surprise is that it happened on an issue of core business; the question of whether to support a new method for generating carbon credits from turning land that was earmarked for logging into national parkland. For many in the environmental movement opposition to this idea was hard to understand. Why die on this remnant old-growth forest covered hill?
But for others, including Bob Brown and Christine Milne, it was selling out the environmental movement to neoliberalism.
In the end the Greens partyroom voted six to five to support the government's policy. Three Greens then dissented on the Senate floor, the first time anyone can remember such a thing happening at such scale.
In most other political parties the sight of 27 per cent of the party room crossing the floor would trigger a leadership spill. It's not clear that's what will happen this time. But one does have to wonder.
Either way, it's a tough business being a political leader. Not something you'd want done by Claude or Gemini or Grok.

Germany's election and the UK's sanctions signals political warfare

analysis
Political warfare is on display with Germany's election and the UK's sanctions
The complexity of the differing forms of warfare being employed in conflicts around the globe these days has seen analysts increasingly try to organise them under the headings of 'kinetic' and 'economic' warfare.
Kinetic warfare is the sort that involves shooting things at each other. Economic warfare employs weapons like sanctions.
There's been an escalation in both sorts this week: a resurgence in missile exchanges in Ukraine and the Middle East; and new rounds of sanctions employed against Israel, Iran and Cuba.
The US House of Representatives is also scheduled to vote next week on sweeping new tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and gas, though it is unclear whether the vote will proceed or not.
There have also been developments which represent both kinetic and economic warfare: notably the Iran-backed Houthis gaining control of the strategically crucial city of Mocha on the Red Sea coast of Yemen, just 50 kilometres from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Saudi Arabia has been getting around the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz on its eastern flanks by shipping oil via pipeline to its west coast, in order to ship it out through the Red Sea.
Far-right party triumphs in Germany
The spectre of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait coming under more lethal Houthi fire sent a shudder through world markets on Thursday night.
But the new player that has erupted on the warfare block this week is political warfare.
That is, shifting internal politics within countries which are changing the geopolitical landscape.
The conspicuous latest examples of this came in an election in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, and the equally important shift by the UK government of Andy Burnham in its position on Israel.
The success of the far-right Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party in winning 44 per cent of the vote in the state election — while the ruling CDU's vote halved to just 17.2 per cent — has shaken national German politics, even though the rise of the AfD has been underway for some time.
As this week ends, German media is widely reporting that the position of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in mortal danger, because — like former UK PM Keir Starmer — he has proved both an ineffective communicator, and a disliked leader. He has not been able to fend off the rise of the AfD, after pledging he would see the party's vote halved.
The pressure is also only going to continue on Merz, and on German politics, with two more state elections due next weekend in Berlin and another state that was once part of the old East Germany: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
The result saw fiery clashes in the Bundestag in Berlin, in which Merz conceded that voters had spoken "pretty clearly" in the state election last weekend with a result that had shocked his CDU party "to its very foundations".
"They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," Deutsche Welle reported him saying.
"We must try, myself included, to reach people more effectively, in the full range of their emotions."
However, a more combative chancellor hit back at the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel, likening the AfD's "remigration" policy — the mass deportation of irregular migrants and foreigners who are required to leave the country — to "nothing other than ethnic cleansing based on skin colour and origin".
AfD's policy makes even right-wing parties anxious
Merz said there was agreement within his governing coalition that many people without a right to remain permanently in Germany should be deported.
"But we distinguish carefully between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, who are welcome in Germany, and those who do not have a permanent right to remain and who must leave our country again," he said.
The AfD's remigration policy is only one of the policy positions which leave many in Germany, and in Europe more broadly, deeply anxious … even right-wing parties in other countries.
Le Monde described the AfD's victory as "particularly embarrassing" for Marine Le Pen's Rassemblement National (RN).
RN had been part of a coalition in the European Parliament with the AfD until 2024 when it broke away "after ambiguous statements by the German party about the role of the SS during World War II and disagreements over remigration".
But it is the AfD's hostility to Ukraine and calls for closer ties with Russia which is of greatest concern in Europe.
Germany, Europe's largest economy, has been the major European backer of Ukraine under Merz, who has also been overseeing the biggest rearmament of his country since World War II, under the perceived threat coming from Russia.
As the former head of MI6, Sir John Sawers, told the Financial Times this week, "it's been a real testament to European support and solidarity that we've kept the Ukrainians going".
But he acknowledged that with changes in the wind in the politics of Germany, France and Italy in the next year, this could significantly change.
The more prosaic issue of gas supply may have a major role to play in the political warfare over Ukraine in coming months.
Europe currently holds its lowest gas stocks in 20 years. With about one third of the world's LNG supplies knocked out by attacks on Qatari production facilities, and facing another bleak winter, the pressure in Europe to start buying more gas from Russia will be intense, including in Germany where the AfD explicitly advocates for this to occur.
Ukraine will need all the friends it can get as European support wobbles, which is why the recent UK move to announce a defence deal with Ukraine, and now a deal between Canada and Ukraine to provide military support in the form of military drones and air defence interceptors, is so significant.
UK takes more assertive stance
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has been the poster boy this year for the call for Middle Powers to take on more active independent roles in world affairs.
This week has seen another shift in the UK's international position which reflects that trend.
The UK likes to still think itself as a 'Great Power' but it is at best a middling one these days, even it does still possess nuclear weapons.
But under new prime minister Andy Burnham, and his foreign secretary Ed Miliband, the UK is taking a more assertive position on foreign policy issues, this week releasing legislation for tougher sanctions against Iran, and most notably announcing trade sanctions against West Bank settlements in Israel.
The importance of the West Bank move is not just about the actual trade sanctions. It lies in the upgrading of the language the UK is using about the actions of the Netanyahu government in the West Bank.
Loading...
Just as Merz attacked the AfD in Germany for a policy he says amounts to ethnic cleansing, Miliband accused Israel of doing the same thing in the West Bank.
What is more, he made explicit the view that the UK regards Israel's occupation of the entire West Bank as unlawful — adopting the findings of the International Court of Justice — rather than continuing with the almost 60-year-old claim that it is just temporarily "occupied".
It is a particularly big turnaround for a party that was defending itself against claims of antisemitism only a few years ago.
Whether the trade sanctions can be implemented by the UK, or the other 11 countries who also indicated this week that they would impose similar measures, is yet to be seen.
Commemorations of the 25th Anniversary of the terror attacks of September 11, 2001 have seen a number of analysts observe that Al Qaeda had eventually been contained.
But those threats have been replaced with state-sponsored terror, notably from Iran and Russia. And Europe has been confronting the cost of the mass wave of refugees that era of terror unleashed.
Along with the transformation of the United States from global policeman to global disruptor, middle power countries are having to write their own rules rather than just hiding behind America in this new world.
Unfortunately, it is not clear whether Australia has yet mastered the dexterity to engage in this new era of political warfare.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

====================================================================================================

A human set a new mathematical record. Then AI came for it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

On the last day of August, a human mathematician kicked off a flurry of advances on one of the most famous problems in number theory — and was almost instantly superseded by AI.
Julia Stadlmann of the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign reported a new record in the quest to solve the twin prime conjecture, which posits that there are infinitely many pairs of prime numbers that are just two numbers apart (3 and 5 are twin primes, for example, as are 17 and 19). It was the first such advance in more than a decade.
It’s a “fiendishly difficult problem,” says mathematician Kannan Soundararajan of Stanford University, who says he admires Stadlmann’s persistence and courage. “It was really quite impressive.”
Within three days, an AI startup called Axiom Math had built on Stadlmann’s approaches to best her effort. Within two hours of Axiom’s announcement, both records were surpassed by OpenAI, which just five days later claimed to have solved another of math’s biggest puzzles.
“It’s a David-versus-Goliath story where the human gets the gold,” says Kevin Ford, Stadlmann’s postdoctoral mentor at Illinois. For three days, at least.
The rapid-fire series of events has sent mathematicians’ angst over AI skyrocketing. In the view of many researchers, some AI companies are not only subverting professional norms but also undermining researchers’ pursuit of knowledge. “What we are seeing here is a consequence of some very deliberate choices to abandon any pretense of gaining human understanding … and using AI tools for the sole purpose of achieving a benchmark,” Terence Tao of UCLA, a Fields Medalist and probably the most influential blogger in mathematics, wrote on mathstodon.xyz.
Chasing pairs
Prime numbers, those that can be divided only by one and themselves, are of seemingly endless fascination to mathematicians, who have long puzzled over where along the number line they appear and why. The twin primes conjecture, which has been wrestled with since at least the 19th century, is widely believed to be true but still unproven by number theorists. An easier version of the problem asks not whether there are infinite pairs of primes with a gap of two but whether there are infinite pairs of primes that all have the same gap of any size.
In 2013, mathematician Yitang Zhang, now at Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou, China, proved that answer is yes: Some gaps must repeat infinitely many times. Mathematicians don’t know that a gap of two does, but Zhang showed that a gap of some number less than 70 million does, thus setting the first record for the “small prime-gap bound.”
Mathematicians quickly took turns lowering that number. The lower they can push it, the closer they are to solving the twin prime conjecture. By the middle of 2014, massive collaborative efforts had brought the bound down to 246, meaning pairs with some gap size equal to or less than 246 must repeat infinitely. That is where the record stood for a dozen years.
Stadlmann began working intensively on the problem about two years ago, after finishing her doctorate under James Maynard at the University of Oxford in England. (Maynard had helped set the previous record, and won the Fields Medal in 2022, in part for his work on prime gaps.) Stadlmann took on the formidable task of trying to better integrate the more recent techniques with Zhang’s earlier efforts.
Both approaches use a “sieve” method, which partially filters out composite numbers using various weights, for example filtering out multiples of 2 more strongly than multiples of 3. Paradoxically, this idea of partial filtering offers a better idea of the distribution of primes than a complete filter would. Stadlmann determined the optimal weights by piecing together regions of high-dimensional space where the different approaches prevail. She had to calculate the volumes of those regions with only a rough idea of what the regions look like.
“It goes beyond finding a needle in a haystack,” says Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal.
By early summer 2026, Stadlmann had managed to move the world record down from 246 to 240. With time, number theorists agree, her methods could have done better. Unfortunately, she did not have time.
In mid-August, Stadlmann began hearing rumors that OpenAI was planning to announce a big new result on prime gaps. Ford told her: “Drop everything you’re doing and put this result on the math preprint archive. Get it out there. Even if it’s improved the next day, you’ve got the record at least for a day.”
As it turned out, the record lasted three days. It may be the last time the record will ever be held by a human.
After Stadlmann posted her result online, researchers at Axiom Math, who had been checking the proofs published in 2013 and 2014, shifted their energies and incorporated her new ideas into a theorem-proving AI. Over the next three days, pulling all-nighters, researchers at Axiom got the bound down to 212, a good estimate of what Stadlmann might have achieved with more time and computing resources.
Meanwhile, OpenAI had been working on a closely related problem that asks for the largest gaps between primes instead of the smallest ones. The team had been using it as a benchmark to showcase the problem-solving abilities of its newest large language model, GPT-6 Astra. According to OpenAI computer scientist Sébastien Bubeck, the team was also exploring the small gaps problem, a sort of add-on because mathematicians at the company were interested in it. Astra got the record down to 186, OpenAI reported in a paper that accompanied the model’s release on September 3.
Bubeck says that OpenAI does not intend to push their work on the prime-gaps problem further. “Our goal is not to preemptively strike and capture all the results possible,” says Bubeck. “Our strategy is to empower the mathematician.”
But controversy in the math community swiftly ensued.
Math for understanding
No one disputes the idea that AI can be a stunningly useful mathematical tool. “Last week, I did a proof in two hours that would have taken me a month before,” Granville says. AI can sift through the vast literature faster than a human, identify dead ends more quickly, and try many more combinations of ideas.
But AI also brings many questions: Who will have access to these tools? How much will they cost? What’s the best way to make sense of machine-generated proofs, which can be filled with “AI slop” that humans can’t immediately understand? How will the culture of the field change if a computer can swoop in and make someone’s work immediately obsolete?
Though Stadlmann says she doesn’t feel mistreated, many mathematicians were upset that OpenAI was working on the same problem as Stadlmann without informing her. Typically in mathematics, academics will stand back if others, particularly less senior researchers, are already at work on a problem. Alternatively, they might reach out to collaborate. “I do not see that OpenAI carefully considered how they treated her,” Granville says.
OpenAI says that they were in touch with Maynard, but that they did not contact Stadlmann directly.
Mathematicians are now in the process of digesting OpenAI’s paper and the strategy that made the new record possible. “I am not so much interested in the exact number, but I am very interested in the mathematical ideas,” Stadlmann says.
It’s this pursuit of ideas that mathematicians worry will be lost when AI is let loose on unsolved puzzles. For problems like these, notes Tao, who collaborated on previous small prime-gap efforts, the value is not in the answer, but in what comes out of the struggle. Along the way, mathematicians develop techniques, new ways of thinking about problems and a deeper understanding of mathematics as a whole, which cannot be conveyed by a single number like 186.
“I love the process of problem solving,” Ford says. “Banging our heads against the wall and getting frustrated, and all of a sudden seeing the idea that works.” He worries that as AI takes that away, talented young people will decide not to enter the field. Future researchers may be discouraged from pursuing problems for which a machine can beat them to the answer. “That would be massively detrimental,” he says, “not just to math but to science in general.”
