Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:52:23 UTC
00:52:23 KST

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi takes a group photo with AI company leaders including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei at the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi on February 19, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
A dramatic resignation from AI company Anthropic this week where a researcher accused it and OpenAI of “gambling with our lives,” threw fuel onto the fire around AI safety.
As governments from California to the U.K. scramble for a political response to the issue of whether AI can be made safe, three experts told POLITICO that to make real progress, laboratories, governments and international bodies must first get on the same page about testing.
The steady flow of revelations that AI labs failed to contain models they were testing, allowing them out into the world where they lied, hacked and coordinated with each other, has heightened urgency to address core questions of how governments or other bodies can or should guarantee that AI is being developed and deployed safely.
Advertisement
Lawmakers, campaign groups and developers alike are calling for new laws and international treaties on AI. “It’s a wake-up call to the United States Congress, to parliaments all over the world, that we’ve got to do something immediately to stop the uncontrolled growth of AI,” U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders told BBC’s Newsnight program Thursday.
The experts POLITICO spoke to want to see an overhaul of the existing approaches championed by developers, testing AI agents en masse rather than one at a time, and for the industry to submit itself to more old-school auditing like the nuclear sector.
Getting the basics right
This year’s heightened AI anxieties started when OpenAI admitted that during internal testing, its own AI agents autonomously gained access to the internet and had hacked fellow AI company Hugging Face, where they thought they would find the answers to the assignments they’d been set.
OpenAI wasn’t the only one: copycat confessions from Anthropic and Meta AI drove home the breadth of the problem, and even the U.K.’s taxpayer-funded AI Security Institute admitted to errors in evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI agents that saw near misses with agents targeting real people and organizations.
Developers and testers alike say they’re working to avoid the mistakes of the past, for example making sure models can't access the internet and deploying data monitoring to detect unexpected activity by the AI being tested.
Another relatively simple concept would be requiring AI companies to report safety incidents, whether or not during testing.
Advertisement
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”
“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”
Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.
“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.
Out of alignment
Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.
The concept of the alignment of AI models or agents — i.e. making sure AI systems do what they're told by human users and don’t go off-piste — has been one of the cornerstones for AI safety in the industry’s eyes.
Advertisement
AI companies like OpenAI champion alignment as the best way to make AI safe. In last week’s release of new model GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI called it “our most aligned model … more likely to operate within the boundaries set by the user and implied by its environment.”
Others view alignment as one of the main obstacles to AI safety, seeing it more as a Band-Aid that gives the semblance that models are being made safe.
“The wider problem is that alignment has become a stand-in for all of AI safety,” said Andrew Strait, former head of societal resilience at the U.K.’s AI Security Institute.
Boyan Milanov, senior research scientist at the AI Now Institute, said alignment will “never be reliable enough to replace proper safety.”
The investigations into the Hugging Face incident showed AI agents were aligned with their own objectives, not those of their human creators. Former OpenAI researcher and whistleblower Daniel Kokotajlo told the London ControlAI event that the incident was an “example of misalignment: in no way, shape, or form were these AIs trained or instructed to do this sort of thing.”
The sector seems stuck on alignment. AI researcher Jacob Coxon, the researcher who relit the AI safety debate this week with his resignation from Anthropic, also said that “attempting to speedrun alignment should require extraordinary confidence that there are no better trajectories available.”
Advertisement
Alignment is “significantly insufficient when we talk about agents interacting with each other and in potentially adversarial environments like the open web,” said Strait. The focus on alignment has also led to the sector “drastically under-resourcing” other aspects of safety, said Strait.
He said his concern is that the industry is racing to deploy agents “while treating the infrastructure needed to contain their behavior as something we can catch up on later.”
“The people whose websites, businesses and public services those agents interact with have not agreed to be part of that experiment,” said Strait.
Old but gold
An old-fashioned approach to safety standards is an alternative to the industry’s preference for alignment. Calls for AI to defer to existing safety engineering practices from sectors such as nuclear safety, civil aviation or medical devices stretch back years.
In these other sectors, there is the concept that an overall system will include fail safes to ensure that if one element of the system fails, either something else kicks in or the system shuts down.
The problem with AI is that it’s still highly unpredictable. “It can fail in very weird ways. There are a lot of attacks against AI that don't fit traditional frameworks,” said Milanov, and so any safety engineering approaches should “evolve to take AI into account.”
Advertisement
There is a fundamental issue here, said Russell, speaking alongside OpenAI whistleblower Kokotajlo at the ControlAI event, that even AI’s creators don’t really understand it. Developers “tell us that we, the human race, cannot protect ourselves with such rules because they, the developers, do not know how to comply with them. Obviously, this is a fallacy,” said Russell.
Milanov pointed to another issue with how models are built. AI developers train their models to resist answering questions on topics such as chemical, biological and nuclear risk, he said, whereas the “real solution” is controlling the data that models are trained on so the models don’t know how to give instructions to build a biological weapon.
Regulation, regulation, regulation
Pushback is needed against AI labs creating their own safety standards, said Milanov, as OpenAI has again called for this week. Instead, new regulation should “force them to adhere to existing standards that we already have now,” he said.
There is some regulation in the works at the U.S. state level. California Governor Gavin Newsom signed two bills on AI safety testing Wednesday. Anthropic had already backed the bills, but OpenAI added its support just before Newsom gave his approval.
The bills mark a small step for formalizing testing: they create a registry and ethical rules for external auditors and ways to check the credentials of organizations touting for testing work.
Outside of the U.S., the EU has an AI Act in force that means companies must work to combat “systemic risks.” The U.K. government abandoned its initial plans for an overarching AI bill last year, but some U.K. lawmakers are taking that fight back up. This week one British MP introduced a bill to prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence, another wrote to the U.N. and OECD begging them to do more at the global level.
Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic’s public willingness to back new regulation could be heartening, although Strait noted “the test is whether they accept independent scrutiny, enforceable obligations and decisions that go against their commercial interests.”
“We should not keep releasing systems with unresolved, serious safety failures and asking society to absorb the consequences,” Strait said. “Safety testing needs to give the public a basis for trusting these products, and regulators the evidence and authority to act when that trust is not warranted.”

What remains of America’s 9/11 memory - and what is disappearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:52:21 UTC
00:52:21 KST

History, as Israelis know all too well from our own challenged historical accounts, is fungible. As politics change and stories pass from one generation to the next, and feelings are considered, even the basic facts can be reinterpreted. The story of 9/11 is no different.
And while September 11 is not being scrubbed from the record, demography, schoolhouse inconsistency, partisan fights over marking the anniversary, and a shift in public language all point to fading lived memory – and, in some institutions, a softer or redirected story. Memorials still stand, names are still read, and most adults still say the day remade the country. What has changed is the kind of memory. In some circles, the retelling of the event has shifted from shared shock to contested history.
The initial reason 9/11 may feel different 25 years later is because of who is alive to remember it. More than 100 million Americans were born after 2001 or were too young to form a memory of that morning.
History vs lived experience
“We’re teaching a generation of students now for whom 9/11 is history, and for some, it’s ancient history like the Vietnam War or the Korean War or World War II,” Joshua Rovner, an associate professor of foreign policy and global security at American University’s School of International Service in Washington, who has taught courses on 9/11 since 2001, said in USA Today in September 2025.
YouGov, a British-founded public-opinion and market-research firm that runs online polls, conducted an August 2026 survey of 1,098 US adults and found that 46% first learned of 9/11 from the news – but among 18- to 29-year-olds, 37% learned it in school, and 6% said they had not heard anything about it. Older Americans still carry “where I was” memories. Younger ones often do not. For many, it is an annual date, not a constant presence.
Politics and war have taken a toll on 9/11 memories. The attacks are now bound up with two long wars, trillions of dollars, thousands of soldiers dead, and security that was never totally achieved. Pew’s 2021 review found 69% saying the US mostly failed to achieve its goals in Afghanistan. A Washington Post-ABC poll that same anniversary year found more Americans saying 9/11 changed the country for the worse (46% ) than for the better (33% ). The brief post-attack unity, “trust in government at 60% in October 2001,” per Pew, collapsed to 24% by 2021.
On the 20th anniversary of 9/11, Newsweek quoted University of Florida political scientist Stephen Craig. “Today, 9/11 is ‘a source of substantial political tensions,’ not the rally it was when [president George] Bush hit ~90% approval,” Craig said. “The post-9/11 ‘rally round the flag’ was short; the longer polarization predates and outlasted it.”
Schools have not filled the gap with a national story. There is no uniform curriculum assigned to teach about 9/11. Only 14 states, including New York, Texas, Illinois, and California, explicitly require September 11 in social-studies standards. In the other 36, the topic is discretionary – left to districts and teachers. An article by Jeremy Stoddard and Diana Hess, professors at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, in The Conversation’s September 2021 issue, describes an “anniversary-only” pattern.
“Teaching 9/11 as a memorializing event on the anniversary also generally avoids deeper inquiry into the historic US role in the Middle East and Afghanistan. This includes, for example, arming mujahedeen fighters against the Soviets in Afghanistan in the 1980s and aiding Iraqi president Saddam Hussein in the war against Iran also in the ’80s.”
They suggest teachers take a more “in-depth approach to explore how US actions contributed to the formation of al-Qaeda, which bombed the World Trade Center in 1993 and later carried out attacks on US embassies in East Africa as well as on the USS Cole, a Navy ship fueling in Yemen, in the years leading up to 9/11.”
In some schools, 9/11 lessons have taken a progressive spin, tilting towards Islamophobia, the Patriot Act, and American foreign-policy guilt. The result is inconsistency – and a vacuum in which conspiracy content and social-media fragments can stand in for a shared account.
Changed media reporting
Anniversary journalism in 2026 illustrates the same split over emphasis. While most high-profile news still calls 9/11 a terrorist attack and still cites the death toll, a smaller set of prominent pieces treats the attacks mainly as the opening of a story about Muslims, surveillance, and civil liberties.
Asma Khalid’s August 18 Atlantic essay, “Islamophobia has corroded American values,” links the 25th anniversary to America’s 250th and moves quickly from 2,977 dead to the Transportation Security Administration, watchlists, and current anti-Muslim rhetoric. PBS NewsHour’s September 1 “Settle In” episode with Rozina Ali, timed to the anniversary, centers on the FBI and post-9/11 surveillance of Muslim families.
The Washington Post reported on August 28 that Canada’s CBC had a policy of not labeling specific attacks as terrorism and made an exception for 9/11 only after public criticism. USA Today’s Susan Page package still named 9/11 the worst terrorist attack in US history, then devoted a major section to liberty versus security – the Patriot Act, Section 702, Snowden.
The New York Daily News asked whether the country is safer and quoted critics of a sprawling surveillance architecture. CNN’s coverage of the fight over Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Ground Zero put families’ objections beside the mayor’s account of post-9/11 surveillance of Arab American communities. While none of these pieces deny the dead, some “soft-soap” the language, referencing “those who lost their lives” versus “those who were killed.” Several relocate the moral center of the anniversary from the hijackings to the response.
Agreement that the day mattered does not produce agreement about how to mark it. Thirteen percent of Democrats said Americans focus too much on 9/11; 43% of Republicans said the country focuses too little. Republicans backed a national 9/11 holiday 62-43 over Democrats. Democrats said Muslims have been treated worse than people of other religions since 9/11 by 72-28 over Republicans.
Threat perception has cooled even while the “changed us completely” number holds. Gallup’s October 2025 crime poll finds Americans worry about identity theft (69%) and scams (53%), while 41% of parents in August 2025 feared for a child’s safety at school, numbers well above the 36% who in 2021 said they worried about becoming a terror victim (down from 58% recorded in a Gallup flash poll on the night of September 11, 2001) and unlike fall 2001, when nearly half said they were less likely to fly and about a third were less willing to enter skyscrapers or large crowds.
Language and media play a huge part in how this story is told. Commemorative and official speech often prefers “lost their lives,” “died,” or “lives were stolen” to “killed in attacks.” King Charles and Queen Camilla’s April 2026 note at the New York memorial, as quoted by the BBC, read: “We honour the memory for those who so tragically lost their lives on 11th September 2001. We stand in enduring solidarity with the American people and in the face of their profound loss.” Mamdani, quoted in USA Today’s August 25 identification story, said, “We honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day.”
Memorial English is not a conspiracy, but over time, using only the softer verbs, plus curricula that skip perpetrators and ideology, can leave students with tragedy without agency: a disaster that “happened,” not an attack that was planned.
Outsourcing memory
So, the accurate charge is not that America has erased 9/11; it is that the country is outsourcing memory to an anniversary ritual while arguing over the caption. The dead are still named. The towers have been rebuilt. What is at risk is the harder sentence: that nearly 3,000 people were murdered in a terrorist attack by al-Qaeda, that the ideology did not vanish, and that remembering the victims and ensuring that America remains vigilant and secure are lessons we can’t afford to forget, erase, or hijack with conspiracy theories.
What is worthy of a school assembly in September, what gets a curriculum unit on wars and the dangers of unchecked and well-funded terror, and which verb a generation hears first – that’s what will keep the memory intact. As will telling our personal memories, which you, our readers, have shared to help preserve the history of that infamous day.
The writer’s memories of that tragic day: America must never forget
Tears streaming down our faces, my friend Anita and I met at the supermarket in Dobbs Ferry, New York. Food shopping seemed like the logical thing to do on a bright September morning with the sky so blue it looked like a painting and your world was falling apart.
The only planes overhead were teams of fighter jets – an unlikely sight in the Westchester suburb north of Manhattan. We shopped as though we were expecting a winter storm, but in truth we didn’t know what we were expecting. Communications were down – we couldn’t reach our husbands who worked in lower Manhattan by phone, and we were worried.
Anita’s husband worked on Wall Street near the Trade Center. Mine was an accountant at St. Vincent’s hospital. The newscasters on TV and radio were no help, being at a loss for putting the news puzzle together. We only knew that it appeared someone was attacking America using large jetliners as missiles.
At first it seemed like an accident – a plane somehow flew into a building, but by the time the second Trade Center building had been struck, it was clearly something more. The building of the World Trade Center, where I had once worked on the 62nd floor in the New York State Tax Department, was burning top-down like a cigarette.
Were our husbands alive? Were we to be the next target?
I filled my tank with gas in case I needed to drive to Canada with the two younger children. I spent time saying Psalms. It soothed my soul just enough to try and think clearly. My eldest son, at Yeshiva University High School in Manhattan, managed to get an open line. He told me he was stuck in New York. Public transportation, trains, buses, everything had stopped. Cars were gridlocked. Ash was blowing across the East River and into the Hudson, and as we watched, the news went from horrific to horrendous.
The first building came down, shooting debris through the streets, sending chunks of building into revolving doors of lower Manhattan, trapping my brother and many others in buildings nearby and covering everyone within miles with ash. Firefighters stood helplessly at the scene.
Like most news stories, the attacks on 9/11 unfolded in layers. Layers that affected every person in the US. But especially those of us in New York. Life simply stopped.
My ex-husband got stuck overnight on emergency duty in the hospital, an accountant on emergency duty, waiting for victims of the mass casualty, victims that never came. We were scheduled to sell our house – the closing set for September 13. The buyer, Rodolfo (Rudy) Hermano, was the catering manager for Windows on the World, the famous restaurant on top of Tower One.
It took a day or two to get the courage (and the phone lines) to call our lawyer. How does one even ask the question – did our buyer survive the blast that killed approximately 170 staff and patrons reported to be in the restaurant that day? His story is below.
On Friday, I baked challah and brought some to the shiva home of Rena Speisman, the mom of Hayley, who was in my son’s class. Her husband, Bob, a 48-year-old diamond industry executive, was a passenger aboard American Airlines Flight 77, the hijacked aircraft that was flown into the Pentagon.
While I was not directly affected, there were very few degrees of separation for my family from the tragedy that hit America just 23 miles down the Hudson from where we lived. My school chum Devorah suffered the loss of her uncle Abraham Zelmanowitz, known by the family as Avreymel.
Although he worked in the North Tower on Floor 27 for Blue Cross/Blue Shield and could have made it out alive with the rest of his colleagues, he chose to stay behind and try to help his co-worker and friend Ed Beyea, a paraplegic confined to a wheelchair. He sent Ed’s aide Irma Fuller out of the building to safety and assumed his care. FDNY Capt. William Francis Burke Jr. stayed to try to help the men in the stairwell, but the three men perished together when the building collapsed.
Abe Zelmanowitz’s DNA was identified in August 2002 – almost a year after 9/11. I attended the funeral on August 5, 2002. The casket, covered by a small parochet, was the size of a shoebox. Avreymel was buried in the Mount of Olives Jewish Cemetery, near his parents’ graves.
This selfless man, Avreymal Zelmanowitz is just one of so many who are being remembered on this 25th anniversary.
The morning the windows went dark: Rudy’s story
Rodolfo “Rudy” Hermano and his wife, Cathy, both worked busy jobs in hospitality. Rudy was in catering sales at Windows on the World, the acclaimed restaurant on floors 106 and 107 of the World Trade Center. Cathy was assistant director of catering at Hilton New York.
Parents of two young children, the dual-career couple had a “commuter date” each morning on the 6 a.m. Metro-North train from Irvington to Grand Central Station, where they caught up on events of the week. But on September 11, 2001, Rudy – usually perpetually early – was late.
He skipped the commute that would have put him on the 107th floor with his catering team and drove instead, planning to visit his mother in a Brooklyn hospital after work.
Jackie Sayegh, a bubbly colleague one desk away, used to tease him: “Rudy, this is not a hotel. Stop coming early.” That day she came in early anyway, so she could take Friday off to see her new husband in Atlanta.
Driving down the West Side Highway, Rudy reached the 168th Street exit when traffic stopped dead, and cars were forced off the road. Only emergency vehicles were waved through. He pulled into a neighborhood coffee shop and stood at the counter as a television behind it showed the first tower fall.
“To my left was a postman,” Rudy recalls. “He was in uniform, and I was in a suit. People were dressed casually, and I wasn’t. Then when I saw the towers on fire, and the first one collapsed, the man looked me up and down and said, ‘Do you know anyone there?’ And I said, ‘That’s where I work. Up there.’ The postman just looked at me with big eyes, and I really didn’t know what to say. We were buying a house. Did I still have a job?”
He tried to reach Cathy, who had taken their usual train, and left a voicemail she saved until very recently: “Something’s happening in the World Trade Center. I’m listening to 1010 WINS news. Airplane hit. I’m calling the office, it’s busy. It must be my building. I am not there.”
Hermano had been at Windows only about 10 months.
“The office was a family,” he said in a recent interview with the Magazine. Jennie Emil – whose brother David’s company, Night Sky, operated Windows and other restaurants – was not there that day. Jay Magazine, the catering sales manager, had booked that morning’s risk management client seminar for 100 attendees and was upstairs. An NYU nutrition intern, Orasri Liangthanasarn, newly hired as a second assistant, had come in early to catch up on her work. The captain, banquet manager Jupiter Yambem, and two or three servers were on the floor.
“Within our catering family, Jay, Jackie, Orasri, Jupiter, our servers, and so many others did not make it out. They were among some 75 staff who were trapped.”
A YouTube video, “Windows on the World, 9/11 Untold Story,” tells the behind-the-scenes story of that day. According to the video, around 8,000 people were inside the North Tower when the plane struck. The vast majority managed to escape, but not the 1,344 people above the impact zone.
Ken Womack, author of The Restaurant at the End of the World, said, “One of the great miracles of 9/11 is how many people survived and were able to get out of the Trade Center. But that wasn’t the case if you were on the 92nd floor or above in the North Tower. During the initial attack, sheetrock and other wreckage collapsed in the stairwells, virtually cutting them off.”
In one heartbreaking scene in the video, using real audio from that day, assistant general manager Christine Olendar begs the police for help. “What are we going to do for air?” she cries. The police assured her help was on the way. It wasn’t.
According to Rudy, within a week the small group of Windows on the World survivors gathered at Jennie’s apartment and hugged everyone who walked in the door. Rudy went to memorials and house prayers for immigrant families he had barely had time to know.
Greg Hein, who had referred Rudy for the job and was director of catering, was on his way in. When he came up from the subway into the concourse, people were running out, shouting, “Go out!” He didn’t know what was happening. He ran outside, looked up, saw the fire – and then the explosion as the second plane hit. Debris came down. He ran across the street to St. Peter’s [church] and huddled by the fence with his briefcase over his head, watching pieces of the aircraft fall around him.
He kept going back to Ground Zero to help. The dust wrecked his lungs. He died two years ago of those breathing complications. He was younger than Rudy.
“Fortunately, within a few months, I was working again,” Rudy recalls. “At the time, if you remember, the world stopped. There were no jobs in New York. I was lucky. In January, I bumped into an executive chef at the Regency I used to work with. He said, ‘So what are you doing?’ I said, ‘I really don’t know.’ Then he said, ‘I’m going to arrange for you to work with us at the Marriott in Stamford.’”
The Hermanos are moving again – this time to Santa Fe. Before Rudy left New York, he extended his stay for a reunion on September 11 with the surviving catering staff of Windows on the World. Twenty-five years later.
The ‘Magazine’ shares: Where were YOU when America was attacked?
No matter what country they lived in, people who lived through September 11, 2001, have deep and disturbing memories of exactly where they were and what they were doing on that crisp, beautiful morning when America was attacked.
Jennifer Abrahamsen, teacher, Sloatsburg, New York:
“I left school on my prep period to make a deposit at the bank. When I got to the bank, there was video of the towers burning on the television screen. I returned to school, and nobody in the building knew what was happening. You would be surprised how cut off from the outside world schools can be. I told the women in the main office what I had seen on TV. A television was turned on in the school library.
More and more teachers found out, and finally children of parents who worked in the Trade Center were called individually to the guidance office, and a family member was located to bring them home. Once all of those students were with family, an announcement was finally made during the last period of the day to tell the students about the attack on the World Trade Center. The principal at the time likened it to when US president John F. Kennedy was shot (on November 22, 1963).
One of my eighth-grade students raised his hand at the end of the announcement and told me he was scheduled to be at a party at Windows on the World that weekend. He asked if there would still be a party.”
Major “A.” in the IDF combat reserves, drafted since Oct. 7 (aliyah in 1984):
“I was working in Rochester, New York, at a tech firm, sitting at my desk. Every single person in the office got up from their desk and went into the break room to watch it on television. I saw it was a terrorist attack, watched for about 15 minutes, and went back to work. Because as an Israeli and an IDF veteran, I knew the only way to deal with terrorism on a community level is to clean up and get back to work; otherwise, the entire society is permanently paralyzed in trauma.
Meanwhile, for the next several months, people came to work and watched television all day long and didn’t get anything done; then they would rush home and sit in front of the television and watch… Exactly the opposite of what we are trained to do here in Israel. I ended up having to do the jobs of most of my coworkers while they sat in the break room all day long for months on end. They were frozen and addicted to witnessing the trauma over and over again. This is why we Israelis continue to thrive despite the horrific things that our enemies do to us.
Rachelle Ben David, Karnei Shomron resident (aliyah in 1982):
“I had been teaching in Kedumim, and when I got home, my friend called me and told me to turn on the TV. I watched as the second plane flew into the World Trade Center Tower. I knew people who lost friends and neighbors in the towers. A friend I taught with in Kedumim had a brother who was in the towers on the 70th floor when he heard a boom. Being Israeli, as soon as he heard a boom, he ran for the stairwell and flew down all the stairs. He survived.”
Edna Krausz, Jerusalem (aliyah in 2025)
“I had no idea anything had happened at 9:30 a.m. on September 11. Before opening my gift store in New Rochelle/Scarsdale, New York, I ran to grab a coffee at Starbucks. The grim faces around me told the story that was unfolding on the radio, and I listened with horror to what was transpiring. As I opened my shop, Inspiration Gallery, suddenly streams of people came through the door – apparently looking for inspiration… and hugs.”
Edna summarized, saying she gave out a lot of hugs that day. “It was solid comfort,” she continued. “I was amazed at how people reach out to other people. We don’t know what to do – so we seek God’s comfort in whichever way we can get it.”
She recalled, “A friend of mine had a daughter working on a high floor in the towers. The employees were told to stay in place. This girl, Lisa, said, no. She was familiar with terrorism and had been in the building during the first World Trade Center bombing. She ran for the stairwell and made her way out. I believe that people like this were getting a message. God communicated directly to their souls. As we say each day in the Amida (silent prayer) – ‘You grant our soul knowledge.’”
Elaine Strasberg, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2013):
“Tuesday morning, heading to my Israeli dance class on the Lower East Side, I was driving into Manhattan from Queens, going over the Williamsburg Bridge at 8:45 a.m., listening to the Nachum Segal music show on the radio. Traffic was exceptionally slow. When the program ended at 9 a.m., I switched to the WINS news station and heard about an explosion at one of the Twin Towers. I looked out the window and saw the smoke coming out of the tower. As I kept listening to the theories of what was happening, I saw the second plane hit the second tower!
Then I understood why traffic was hardly moving. We were not allowed to enter Manhattan and were diverted back into Brooklyn. When I got home and turned on the TV, I saw the collapse of the second tower. Of course, we stayed glued to the TV, hearing of the Pentagon and the plane crash in Pennsylvania.
My friends who had already gotten into Manhattan for the class were stuck there for the entire day and didn’t get home until late that night.”
Nahum Zak, Boca Raton, Florida:
“I was at the post office in Kew Gardens Hills, New York City, picking up the Palm Pilot I bought on eBay when I heard the radio report behind the teller saying a small plane (that was the first report) flew into one of the towers. The teller and reports seemed to think it was an accident.
“I remember thinking there’s no way someone flies by accident over NYC airspace into the No. 1 terrorist target in the state.
“It was the worst day of my life.
Yael Harris Resnick, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2013):
“Everyone has their own memories of that tragic day 25 years ago. Mine started early that morning around 6:45 a.m. when I woke up to my own tower falling, an eerie foreboding of what was about to happen in NYC about two hours later. I was very newly pregnant with my first baby, and I was bleeding. A lot.
“It was also my first day as a kindergarten teacher in New Jersey, just across the bridge from NYC, in a new school. There were kids counting on me. Little did I know at the time just how much they would need the loving support of their teachers. I put my own dread aside and promised that as soon as my obstetrician’s office opened, I would call to make an emergency appointment.
“You know how the rest of the day went for NYC and the world. I don’t need to describe the horror, the confusion, the relief, the pain. Despite the urgency of global catastrophe, personal catastrophes do not cease to exist. It was difficult due to traffic jams and the chaos of the day, but I managed to be squeezed in for an appointment. It was my first. The one where they check for a heartbeat. Miraculously, there was one. There was also one extra sac that was empty. No heartbeat. One tower down.
“I cannot describe the emotions of a moment like that. Lumped together with that devastating day, all I could do was be thankful, so thankful for that one strong little heartbeat fluttering inside me.
“Twenty-five years later, that little heartbeat has grown into a beautiful young lady. This summer she married the love of her life and was the most beautiful bride. It can’t be a coincidence that she is obsessively connected to all things 9/11 (especially the musical Come from Away) even though she hadn’t yet been born. And that she is now studying on the mother/baby and ultrasound ward at Shaare Zedek hospital to be a nurse, a gentle, old soul, present and nurturing when mothers receive news just like I did on that September 11, 25 years ago.”
Tsivya Fox-Dobuler, Ramat Beit Shemesh (aliyah in 2002):
“We lived in Far Rockaway, Queens. My ex-husband was on a train heading into Manhattan when he saw the first plane hit the Twin Towers. After years in Israel, he knew instantly it was terror, not an accident, so he got off, crossed the platform, and came straight home.
“I was teaching five-year-old boys at yeshiva that morning. My assistant walked in late and white as a ghost; a few minutes later the vice principal canceled playground on the most beautiful day of the year. I still didn’t understand until Mrs. Katz, whose kohanim sons were members of Hatzalah, looked like she’d seen death itself. After school I walked to the bay in Bayswater. People were lined up watching the towers burning in the distance, and Israelis who had lived nearby for years were suddenly saying they wanted to go home to Israel.
“The silence for weeks afterwards was almost worse. We lived 15 minutes from JFK Airport; for five days no civilian planes moved, only F-16s circling. My ex-husband had always said one day we would want to leave America and wouldn’t be able to. That week we believed him. A week later, we walked through Ground Zero. Clothes in a Gap store were still perfectly folded under thick ash. The smoke rose in straight pillars for months.
“A neighbor was saved because her elderly father, who never asked her to stay home, begged her not to go to work that morning. Our hazan (cantor) from shul was in Tower Two – obediently staying in place as he was advised to do – when a coworker grabbed his hand and forced him down hundreds of steps; they stepped outside seconds before the tower collapsed.
“On Yom Kippur, when he reached the words ‘who by fire,’ he collapsed on the floor, and the whole shul stood in silence, sobbing with him. For weeks, no one in Far Rockaway left their houses until NYC mayor Rudy Giuliani got on television and said it was time to start living again.”
Matti Led, Fair Lawn, New Jersey:
“I was at my desk in Brooklyn, a high school student, staring out the window, wondering why the clouds over Manhattan were so dark. Our principal interrupted class to break the news to us. We thought he was pranking us. A bunch of students ran down to the pay phone to call their parents who worked at the World Trade Center. Lots of kids were crying as they waited and tried to call their parents.
Later, as I took the B68 home through “Little Pakistan” (a Muslim neighborhood on Brooklyn’s Coney Island Avenue), I looked at the passengers on the bus and wondered if any of them were terrorists. Walking home from the bus stop, there were tiny shreds of paper (from the WTC blast) all around me.
“The reality only hit me when I actually saw videos of the planes hitting the towers.”
Tania Hammer, Talpiot, Jerusalem (aliyah 10 years ago):
“I was living in Far Rockaway and could see the Twin Towers across the way. I taught at Hebrew Academy of the Five Towns, and ran to a shop to pick up some supplies when I saw the first plane hit. We thought it was a terrible accident, so I went back to school. When the second plane hit, parents went berserk and converged on the school to grab their children. It was very chaotic, but the teachers couldn’t leave, and we tried to do some therapy with the children that stayed.
“Then we heard the Pentagon was hit, and I became anxious. My sister, a tax lawyer, was scheduled to work at the Pentagon that week. I had to call my sister. I tried and I tried but I couldn’t reach her. Nobody knew what exactly was happening. Eventually my sister picked up. I asked if she was okay, and she said, ‘Yes, why?’ She said she had stayed home to let a plumber in. That’s when I burst into tears.
“She said, ‘Why are you crying?’ and I said, ‘Turn on the radio.’ She turned on the radio and screamed, ‘Oh my gosh.’ There was no way she would have stayed home ordinarily. I told her, ‘Do you know what’s happening? Hashem saved you by sending a faulty toilet!’
“I had a cousin who worked on Wall Street, but every road was closed. He was covered in asbestos and dust from head to toe. He lived in Queens and couldn’t reach his wife or children, so he just followed the crowd and ended up on the Staten Island Ferry to his wife’s cousin’s home. She opened the door and screamed when she saw him. He told her, ‘It’s me, Jeff!’ She thought he was a monster. She was able to reach his wife. And then he had to find his way home. On foot. He must have walked a billion miles that day.
“Last time I went to New York, I visited the Ground Zero Memorial. It’s very well protected, and it offers different things to view, to see, a place to pray.”
Chaim Lauer, Arnona, Jerusalem (aliyah in 2021):
“I was getting on a bus to come into Manhattan. I heard about the first crash while waiting for the bus. On the bus, another passenger had a radio and said the second tower was hit. I said out loud, ‘We are at war!’ The other passengers looked at me as if I were crazy. Most did not understand that we were… and still are… at war.”
Florence Schleifer, Karnei Shomron (aliyah in 2011):
“I lived in Baltimore, Maryland, and was working as a kindergarten teacher in a boys’ yeshiva. My daughter Chanina lived on the Lower East Side. She was taking her two- and three-year-old to play group when they heard a huge boom. They were able to see the Twin Towers from where they were standing – the smoke, the fire, everything.
“My daughter stood on the street as people looked in shock, screaming, ‘Oh my God, a plane just accidentally flew into the World Trade Center!’ Chanina looked at the crowd and exclaimed, ‘That’s no accident. That’s terrorism.’
“Chanina called my husband, who contacted me at school, and then we found out about the plane that flew into the Pentagon. The principal announced, ‘Everybody’s getting picked up.’ As far as we knew, we were sitting ducks. Planes are flying, we’re near Washington, and we’re a boys’ school with hundreds of little Jewish boys.
“Meanwhile, in Israel, our daughter Shira, who lives in Jerusalem’s Har Nof, was having her first baby and was in the hospital. Suddenly the medical staff came into their room and said, ‘You’re American?’ They said, ‘Yeah. They said, “There’s an attack in America,” and they turned on the TV. Our grandson was born after a while. His birthday is 9/11.
“My two granddaughters, after witnessing the crashes firsthand in New York, worked with therapists to process what they had seen. They had them drawing pictures of big buildings on fire and planes flying into buildings.”
Schleifer ends her recollection on a positive note: “And after they made aliyah and grew up – both girls became soldiers in the IDF!”

Technofascism is already here; Big Tech built it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:51:36 UTC
00:51:36 KST

Technofascism is already here; Big Tech built it
Vienna-based philosopher Mark Coeckelbergh talks about Palantir’s fascist-leaning manifesto in interview with Tehran Times
TEHRAN – Mark Coeckelbergh, Professor of Philosophy of Technology and Media at the University of Vienna and a member of the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, has become one of the most prominent voices warning against the alliance between Big Tech and authoritarian politics.
His recent article “Technofascism: AI, Big Tech, and the New Authoritarianism” (AI & Society, 2026) examines how figures such as Peter Thiel and Palantir CEO Alex Karp are shaping a post-democratic worldview built on surveillance, militarization, and elite rule.
Coeckelbergh has also traced Karp’s intellectual shift from an early interest in the Frankfurt School to the reactionary politics now associated with Palantir, and has called for a “quiet revolution” toward digital humanism, grounded in education and a stronger democratic knowledge base.
Several of Coeckelbergh’s books have been translated into Persian, including “AI Ethics”, “The Political Philosophy of AI”, “Why AI Undermines Democracy and What To Do About It”, and “Communicative AI,” co-authored with David Gunkel.
Tehran Times spoke with Professor Coeckelbergh about technofascism, Palantir’s ideology, and the prospects for a more democratic, humane use of artificial intelligence.
Below is the full text of the interview:
For an audience hearing “technofascism” for the first time, how would you explain it in simple terms, and how is it different from ordinary authoritarianism?
Sometimes “fascism” is used very loosely, just as a way to say that certain views are undesirable. But I use it in a very specific academic sense, to describe how current technologies are leading to a new form of authoritarianism. The old kinds of authoritarianism we’ve seen historically — fascism, Nazism — had certain features, and we see some of them coming back today. But now, with AI and digital technologies, there is a new possibility for total surveillance and what’s called “algorithmic governmentality,” where ordinary citizens may not even know they are under surveillance, and where authoritarian governments have new tools to crack down on their own citizens.
There are also new myths. In the past, the Nazis had their own myths; now tech people fabricate new ones. These days they’re often based on a very specific kind of Christian thinking — Peter Thiel, for example, talks about the Antichrist, about a coming apocalypse, in the way many tech figures do. It’s a very particular use of religious narratives to support their own views.
We also see a strongly anti-democratic strand of thinking currently in Silicon Valley. I mentioned Peter Thiel — the Palantir manifesto, for instance, shows clear anti-democratic tendencies. Thiel doesn’t believe in democracy. There’s also a glorification of war, which is typically fascist, and figures like Curtis Yarvin, who argue against democracy and have links to people like Thiel.
So, I think a constellation is forming in which Big Tech has gained much more power, combined with these new narratives and myths. Classical fascism also had a form of corporatism — a close connection between big corporations and the state — and we see that again today. These big tech corporations essentially want a post-democratic, post-liberal model in which CEOs and other tech elites decide what happens — effectively taking over the state. Before that full takeover, there is the close collaboration we already see in the US between Big Tech and the current administration, the Trump administration.
You mentioned Peter Thiel. I’ve read your Medium article criticizing the Palantir manifesto and the views of Alex Karp and Peter Thiel. If Palantir, as you argue, is part of Thiel’s response to violence and disorder, what kind of society is he ultimately trying to build through technology?
He’s trying to build an authoritarian society led by a small elite — a tech elite that leads humanity into a new stage of technological development, one in which people like you and me have no say. For him, democracy is a problem — a bug — that needs to be solved through authoritarian means. I’m genuinely worried that people like Thiel currently have a great deal of influence, not only on the American government but increasingly on European governments too. We’re seeing a tendency toward a more authoritarian use of technology, toward militarization, and toward a more generally aggressive kind of politics that fits that picture.
Let’s talk about Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir. Karp came to Frankfurt intending to study with Jürgen Habermas and was influenced by that intellectual environment. Do you see a connection between that background and the thinker he has become?
I think Karp kept a keen interest in social and political theory, but he really moved from an environment that was more liberal and left-leaning toward an ideology that is clearly right-wing, reactionary, and potentially fascist. He changed direction there. I think the dangerous thing is that this ideology, as expressed, for example, in the Palantir manifesto, carries a lot of influence because Palantir sells its products to many Western governments. In this way, both the ideas and the underlying tendency toward mass surveillance and the oppression of people can spread. That poses a real risk for many countries around the world, including Western ones.
Palantir presents itself as a company serving ordinary people — the welder, the truck driver, the soldier. What do you think this image is meant to emphasize?
I think it wants to sell security technology in the broad sense, and military technology, and to do that it has developed an ideology that says you need more militarization and more control in order to gain security. So naturally it promotes these values — security above all — in order to sell its products and to wield influence, both in the US and elsewhere. This may appeal to many people, but they forget that the technology will be used against them in the first place.
Karp argues that democratic countries need technological superiority to compete with their rivals. Where do you draw the line between deterrence and an AI arms race?
The way he frames it — that we need to be better prepared and tougher militarily — rests on a worldview that divides the world into friends and enemies, which is itself a typical authoritarian and fascist way of thinking. He wants people to buy these products in order to make themselves stronger against their enemies, so to sell them, he paints a picture of a chaotic world where enemies could attack at any time.
The message to a country is: you’d better prepare and buy this kind of security and military technology to strengthen yourself. A fascist worldview includes the idea that you should try to be the strongest and defeat your enemies, and I think that’s how this ideology plays out here.
The AI arms race fits into that: for Karp and many others in the US, the Chinese, the Russians, and other powers are seen as enemies or potential enemies in that race, and whoever wins gains dominance. That’s the kind of world — one of clear friends and enemies, where you need to establish dominance — that he wants, and it’s the starting point of his approach for governments like that of the US.
I’ve read some of your other work, and if I’m not mistaken, you’ve connected some of these ideas to Plato and the Roman Empire. What can those older examples teach us about AI today?
What you see in the past is that technology has often been used to support centralized power. Technology has also often been developed as a result of warfare and military use, and military technology has sparked a lot of innovation.
But this also means that with AI, there is a big risk that when it is used for security or military purposes, it can create a world where there is not only more risk of war, but also a significant risk of totalitarianism. In such a system, as a citizen, you are always aware that the government or big companies know everything about you.
Basically, this leads to a situation where your freedom can be violated at any time, where a country might have more security at the cost of its own citizens. Although these militarization efforts currently do not lead to better security overall in the world, even if they enhance the security of the state or the company, they do not enhance the security of people.
Individual citizens can be subjected to surveillance in such a way that there is a lot of knowledge about them and, therefore, a lot of power on the part of governments and big companies.
So, in the end, it is not leading to security but to insecurity: to the feeling that at any time you might be arrested or you might be in trouble because of what you did, what you said, and so on.
This also fits with the view of some of these fascist and reactionary people. They love freedom; they like libertarianism in the U.S., but they want it only for themselves, for an elite. The rest of us, most citizens, have to deal with control, live under surveillance, and do what the government or the CEOs say. They want that kind of strong leadership, and they don’t want democracy.
As a solution to this situation, you’ve called for a “quiet revolution” toward digital humanism. What would that actually look like in practice, and is there any AI project or company you think is doing this right now?
The solution I propose is really about changing society by changing education — making sure there is a solid knowledge base and cultural foundation, so that it makes sense to use AI because that knowledge already exists and can guide the smart use of AI, and so that democracy can function, because democracy also needs a knowledge base. This is long-term work, however; it can’t be done quickly.
In the meantime, I think we do need to regulate these big companies. We need to make sure that some of their power is handed back to democratically legitimate institutions, back to civil society, back to democracy. If that doesn’t happen, this current tendency will only grow stronger in the future.
You’re now a member of the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. For an audience hearing about the panel for the first time, what is its role, why was it created, and how can it actually influence governments and companies for the better?
The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI was created by the Secretary-General as a way to build up scientific knowledge about AI as a basis for policymaking. In principle, its task is not to give policy advice directly, but to inform policymakers at the international level, at the UN, about the possible implications of AI — technical, economic, but also social and educational.
What’s really valuable about this panel is that it isn’t composed only of people from the West; it’s a broad panel with members from all kinds of countries, including the Global South. That’s a real advantage compared to many of the panels and advisory bodies I’ve seen in Europe or the US.
I think it can help us think about how to develop AI in a responsible and democratic way, not only within countries but also at the global level — what global governance of AI could look like, and what problems can be addressed at that level that can’t be handled by national panels alone.
If we really want more responsible AI, we need global cooperation, and I’d argue for global governance that goes further than cooperation between nations — a framework that transcends national governments and works toward minimal global rules for AI. That’s very much needed if we want to halt this power grab by Big Tech, and if we must prevent a global order where a few superpowers dominate other nations, reducing them to subordinate states or pushing them toward collapse, becoming failed states.
A global framework is needed for that. While that isn’t the direct aim of this panel, I believe that by building and sharing knowledge about AI and anticipating near-future developments, it can contribute to establishing a kind of global governance structure.
Given what’s happening in the world right now — so many conflicts, especially in the Middle East, and the US aggression against Iran — are you optimistic about the future, that resistance and education will lead to something better, especially considering that AI companies like Palantir are also involved in military technology, and that this worldview essentially means more war and more profit for them?
Yes — currently AI supports these aggressions and creates a situation of war and suffering for people, and I think in the short term I’m pessimistic that we can change that. We don’t currently have a global framework, nor an effective way to stop certain states from taking aggressive action against other states. So in the short term, I’m pessimistic. But in the long term, through better, more effective supranational institutions, but also through better education, and through helping people imagine a world beyond their own community, beyond their own state and the ideologies that frame their political world — if we manage that, I think in the long term I am optimistic that we can move toward more cooperation, more global ways of thinking, and more peaceful ways of thinking. That’s not going to happen anytime soon, but I think we should stay optimistic, because there are many people today, both in the West and elsewhere, who want change and who want peace. We have to stay optimistic and work with the people who want peace and want to improve the situation.

IN BRIEF: Key statements by Bank of Russia’s Governor Elvira Nabiullina

00:51:29 KST

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia decided to keep the key rate at 14% per annum, noting that current price pressures have increased in recent months.
TASS has compiled the key statements Bank of Russia Governor Elvira Nabiullina made at press conference following the regulator's board meeting.
Key rate
The Central Bank discussed maintaining the rate in detail today: "And, perhaps, the difference compared to the previous meeting is that we did not substantively discuss cutting the rate."
The scope for future rate cuts will be clarified in October.
High inflation expectations limit the room for cutting the key rate: "This is one of the factors limiting the scope for further key rate cuts and requiring a very cautious approach from us."
Maintaining the rate will foster moderate growth in domestic demand "so as to prevent the escalation of second-round effects."
Monetary policy is now expected to be tighter, the current scope for cutting the key rate is smaller than anticipated in the first half of the year.
"Every additional ruble" of state-driven demand stimulus moves the Central Bank further away from cutting the key rate.
The Central Bank does not plan to keep the rate at a level the economy cannot sustain for long: "If the rate level is, so to speak, unsustainable, it will quickly lead to a cyclical downturn -- that is, to rising unemployment, falling real incomes, and a drop in underlying inflation below the Central Bank's targets."
Rising prices and the fuel market situation
The acceleration of price growth during the summer months was driven primarily by the fuel market situation: "This is a one-off factor, but we see it affecting the prices of a broader range of goods and services."
According to the regulator, the situation in the fuel market will gradually stabilize: "We base this on the measures being taken by the government and by companies with government support -- they are implementing all necessary and possible measures to restore lost capacity and safeguard it."
Inflation and the ruble exchange rate
Under its baseline scenario, the Central Bank expects a sustained decline in inflation to resume "as the effects of the temporary contraction in production capacity fade, provided that aggregate demand growth remains subdued."
Inflation expectations remain high: "We need more data to assess the scale and duration of these effects and their impact on underlying inflation."
Pro-inflationary risks in the Russian economy have risen: "And they continue to predominate."
The Central Bank is not considering raising the inflation target, calling it "extremely detrimental."
Moderately tight monetary conditions must be maintained to prevent a one-off acceleration in inflation from turning into "a sustained trend."
The Bank of Russia’s objective is to ensure that today's rise in gasoline prices "does not turn into high inflation tomorrow."
The current ruble exchange rate is "very close to business expectations."
The pass-through of ruble exchange rate dynamics to inflation has slowed in recent years, and the exchange rate's impact on prices remains moderate.
Demand for imports is rising in Russia, a factor that contributed, among other things, "to some weakening of the ruble during the summer months."
Impact of UAV attacks
"As for the impact of UAV attacks on supply chains, the effect on inflation has so far been quite low -- negligible."
Budget
The Central Bank expects budget parameters to be clarified "by the end of September."
The regulator has not changed its estimates regarding budget parameters for the new three-year period.
National economy
Russian economic growth is moving in line with the Central Bank's forecast: "Overall, data for the first half of the year and indicators for the third quarter suggest that economic growth is tracking within our forecast."
The Central Bank assumes that lost economic capacity will be restored by the end of 2026: "Regarding the timeline for restoring lost capacities, we have not changed our assumptions. We anticipate that this recovery will take place by the end of the year."
Investment activity
Investment activity is "gradually recovering" following weak dynamics in the first quarter of 2026.
Labor productivity
Labor productivity growth "continues to lag significantly."
Lending and household propensity to savings
Lending, particularly in the corporate sector, has "accelerated again."
In recent months, the growth of retail lending has "remained quite moderate."
The household propensity to save "remains high."
Digital ruble
The mass launch of the digital ruble proceeded smoothly. Although there were specific technical issues, they were "promptly resolved."

Doctors held in Greece after music star dies during plasma treatment

- Plasma exchange is a complex, risky procedure meant for hospitals, but anti-ageing clinics operate in a legal grey area without clear regulations.
- Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis confirmed the clinic's activity was illegal and promised to re-evaluate the framework governing such treatments in Greece.
AI generated
ATHENS – Two doctors have been placed under arrest in Greece after a prominent music star died during a blood cleaning treatment, raising questions about private clinic licences in the country.
Giorgos Mazonakis, 54, died of cardiac arrest on Sept 9 during a plasma exchange appointment, a treatment used to remove harmful elements from the bloodstream.
Originally employed to treat disorders such as multiple sclerosis, plasma exchange has increasingly been used as an anti-ageing and longevity treatment.
Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said the framework governing anti-ageing clinics in Greece was a “grey area” that would be re-evaluated.
“Currently there is no framework,” he told Action24 TV. “This medical field has advanced rapidly, overtaking existing laws.”
Mazonakis was one of Greece’s best-known pop stars, with multiple hits and platinum albums to his name during a career spanning over three decades.
He was scheduled to stage a retrospective concert in Athens on Sept 20.
The doctors, who are a couple, deny any responsibility and insist Mazonakis lost consciousness before the treatment began.
Several officials have stated that plasma exchange is a complicated and occasionally risky procedure that requires a full medical team, and is not something that should be done at a private clinic.
“It is absolutely certain that the activity was illegal,” Georgiadis told state TV ΕΡΤ on Sept 11.
“It is forbidden to carry out (plasma exchange) outside a hospital environment,” he said, adding that the clinic had a pathology practice licence.
However, the suspects’ lawyer Nikos Agapinos told reporters that it was “a legal clinic with properly registered equipment”.
The couple were initially released after questioning on Sept 9, but detained on Sept 10 after police reportedly found discrepancies in their testimony.
It is believed that contrary to the doctors’ testimony, Mazonakis had already begun the treatment when he lost consciousness. AFP

El Nino raises risk of wetter autumn, flooding across UK: Met Office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:51:12 UTC
00:51:12 KST

Burak Bir
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
There is a greater risk of flooding and a wetter autumn average this year in the UK due to the El Nino effect, the country's weather agency warned Friday.
Strong El Nino conditions in the Pacific are putting the UK at greater risk of a wet and stormy autumn, the Met Office said in a statement, citing its latest seasonal outlook.
"Current evidence suggests conditions later this autumn and into early winter may be more unsettled than is typical for the time of year," it noted.
The statement noted that the chances of a warm and wet autumn for the UK are around one-and-a-half to two times higher than would normally be expected due to El Nino, adding that an increased likelihood of windy conditions also emerges later in the season.
El Nino is a natural climate phenomenon that occurs when sea-surface temperatures in parts of the tropical Pacific become warmer than average.
"The latest seasonal forecasts suggest an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions as we move through autumn, which would be consistent with the historical influence of El Niño events," said Met Office Chief Meteorologist Ian Lisk.
However, Lisk noted that El Nino is only one of several factors affecting the country's weather and does not determine exactly what conditions we will experience.
"We will continue to monitor developments closely and update our forecasts as confidence in the outlook evolves," he added.

Egypt seeks de-escalation in Bab el-Mandeb, freedom of navigation

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo supports “full de-escalation, not escalation” in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and freedom of navigation, warning that Egypt’s Suez Canal losses from navigation problems in the area reached nearly $11 billion.
Abdelatty made the remarks Thursday evening during an extensive briefing with representatives of foreign media, attended by Anadolu’s correspondent, in which he reviewed Egypt’s position on several regional and international developments.
The Egyptian minister’s comments come amid renewed tensions around Bab el-Mandeb as Yemen’s Houthi group moves toward the strategic maritime area and attempts to control it.
“We spoke about Bab el-Mandeb and freedom of navigation there, and we are for full de-escalation and not escalation,” Abdelatty said.
“Egypt is the country most affected by any problem that occurs in navigation, and we approached $11 billion in net Egyptian losses from the decline in Suez Canal revenues,” he added.
Abdelatty said Cairo is in constant contact with Yemen’s legitimate government and is working to reduce escalation there.
Since late 2023, navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb has faced disruptions and attacks carried out by the Houthis against ships they said were linked to Israel or heading there, against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, prompting many vessels to change routes and avoid passing through the Suez Canal.
Abdelatty said Egypt is communicating with all regional and international parties to reduce escalation, stressing again that military solutions only lead to more tension and escalation.
On Gaza, Abdelatty reviewed Egypt’s intensive efforts to implement the requirements of the first phase of the Gaza agreement, which began on Oct. 10, 2025, and move to the second phase of US President Donald Trump’s peace plan, which started last July.
Egypt and its partners had achieved a major result by convincing Palestinian factions, led by Hamas, to agree to hand over their weapons in exchange for Israel’s withdrawal from areas it occupied in Gaza, along with the implementation of the remaining requirements of the first and second phases, he said.
Abdelatty said some first-phase requirements had not yet been implemented, foremost the entry of 600 aid trucks into Gaza daily.
“The most important point in the second phase was the handover of the factions’ weapons and Israel’s withdrawal from the Strip. Hamas agreed to that, but Israel did not implement its obligations,” he said.
He stressed the need to “halt all Israeli measures that undermine chances of achieving calm, foremost settlement expansion and land confiscation.”
Abdelatty said the continuation of these practices threatens prospects for establishing a Palestinian state and undermines chances for a just and lasting peace.
Palestinians warn that Israel is paving the way for the formal annexation of the occupied West Bank through illegal settlement expansion and attacks by the army and occupiers, undermining the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel, with US support, has been carrying out genocide in Gaza, killing more than 73,000 Palestinians and injuring over 174,000 others, while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.
On the war on Iran, Abdelatty said Egypt is continuing its efforts and contacts with various parties to push for de-escalation and prioritize diplomacy and dialogue.
He stressed the need to return to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding between Iran and the US signed in mid-June, describing it as an important path toward a comprehensive and sustainable agreement that would spare the region the dangers of a wider war and its serious consequences for energy and food security in the region and the world.
Abdelatty also stressed the need to “guarantee the security and safety of maritime navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring the flow of trade and international energy supplies.”
He said countries in the region are paying the price for escalation between Washington and Tehran.
“Some African countries now have a fuel crisis and a fertilizer crisis because of the war on Iran and its economic repercussions,” he said.
Abdelatty said Egypt will continue all efforts and contacts with all parties to return to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding and guarantee security and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
He also reiterated Egypt’s condemnation of any attacks on Arab countries as part of the US-Iran escalation.
The US and Iran have exchanged military attacks amid stalled negotiations over disagreements related to navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic passage for energy and goods supplies.
On Feb. 28, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing more than 3,000 people, according to Tehran, which responded with attacks on US bases in the region.
The Egyptian foreign minister also addressed regional security arrangements, stressing the importance of strengthening collective capacity to protect Arab national security.
He called for commitment to clear principles, foremost respect for the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states, good neighborliness, non-interference in internal affairs, adherence to international law and refraining from measures that could escalate tension or threaten regional security and stability.
Abdelatty said the Joint Arab Defense Treaty should be the core of any regional security structure.
On developments in Sudan, Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the preservation of state institutions.
He stressed the importance of continuing efforts to end the crisis and ease the suffering of the Sudanese people.
Egypt will continue pushing for political solutions and an inclusive Sudanese political process that shapes the country’s future, he said.
Abdelatty said Sudan’s unity and territorial integrity are a red line for Egypt, adding that Cairo will not allow any measures or steps that could affect them.
Since April 2023, the Rapid Support Forces have been fighting the Sudanese army over a dispute regarding their integration into the military, causing famine in one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, killing tens of thousands of Sudanese and displacing 13 million people.
On Lebanon, Abdelatty renewed Egypt’s condemnation of Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon.
He stressed the need for full and non-selective implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701, the extension of Lebanese state sovereignty over all its territory and the restriction of weapons, in a way that preserves Lebanon’s security and stability.
Israeli attacks on Lebanon have continued despite a US-brokered “framework formula” signed by Beirut and Tel Aviv on June 26, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied territory in return for the deployment of the Lebanese army there.
On Egypt’s water security, Abdelatty said his country’s foreign policy toward Nile Basin countries is based on cooperation, development, shared interests and mutual benefit.
Preserving Egypt’s water security does not conflict with the development aspirations of other countries, he said, adding that the Nile River must be managed according to international law, especially the principles of no harm, cooperation and consensus.
Abdelatty expressed Cairo’s complete rejection of unilateral measures that violate international law in the eastern Nile Basin.
Egypt will take all measures guaranteed to it under international law to protect its rights and the existential resources of its people, he added.

North Sea gasfield decision likely delayed until after Holborn and St Pancras byelection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:50:25 UTC
00:50:25 KST

A decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea is to be delayed until later this autumn, with the Greens accusing Labour of hiding their position before the crucial Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week.
However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season.
The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali in Keir Starmer’s former seat.
Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis.
After his selection, Polanski said Labour has “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”.
“They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding.
“Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse. We have a climate crisis but Labour is taking the side of fossil fuel corporations, and the voters have a clear choice in this byelection between action on climate change or shortsighted rowing backwards.”
The delay also means Andy Burnham could avoid controversy over Jackdaw at the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of the month.
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said delays in approving Jackdaw would mean it takes longer to increase UK domestic production in the North Sea.
In a letter to the prime minister published on social media, Bowie asked Burnham to confirm “suggestions that you are about to delay the decision on the Jackdaw gasfield until after the conference recess and Holborn and St Pancras byelection”.
He added: “If this is the case, it would be nothing short of you placing the interests of the Labour party before the interests of Great Britain.”
A separate decision is also pending on the Rosebank oilfield project.
Environmental campaigners have called for both projects to be abandoned, while the US president, Donald Trump, has urged the prime minister to open them.
Labour’s manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, but the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank are seeking environmental approval for existing licences.
Last week, a spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”
The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.
Under the process, the energy secretary gives her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which then later issues a formal approval.
Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, and Fahnbulleh has since been considering her response.
Campaigners say the fields would produce as much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced.
Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian firm Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.

Lawmaker, formerly from Zelensky's parliament group, jailed for 9 years over 2020 graft case
Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court on Sept. 11 sentenced lawmaker Oleksandr Yurchenko to nine years in prison for bribery in a six-year-old case, the Anti-Corruption Action Center watchdog reported.
Yurchenko, then a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People parliamentary group, was in 2020 accused by Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) of soliciting bribes.
This marked one of the first high-profile corruption investigations involving Zelensky's allies, coming only a year after Zelensky and his party's decisive victories in the 2019 elections.
The court found Yurchenko guilty of bribery and, in addition to the prison sentence, ordered the confiscation of his assets and barred him from holding certain public offices for three years.
Yurchenko can appeal the verdict, which will enter into force in 30 days.
The lawmaker was exposed in a sting operation in August 2020. Through an intermediary, Yurchenko was said to solicit bribes from an undercover NABU detective.
Specifically, the lawmaker asked for $13,000 for himself to propose legislative amendments and $200,000 to bribe other lawmakers, according to the investigation.
Yurchenko was expelled from Zelensky's parliamentary group in the wake of the 2020 scandal, with the president publicly commenting at the time that each official must know that "if you took a bribe, you will go to prison."
The case also drew scrutiny toward then-Prosecutor General Iryna Venediktova, who initially blocked bribery charges against Yurchenko before giving in to public pressure and authorizing them on Sept. 17, 2020.
