Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:22:12 UTC
00:22:12 KST

This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: September 11, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
For this update, we have added over 6,000 names to our database. This spike is not related to the current situation on the frontline, but rather to the fact that we have mass-processed posts about missing soldiers and added those whose deaths have been confirmed through the Probate Registry and other sources.
Important note: as before, we do not count those missing in action. All these added people have died and are either buried or recognised as deceased in the absence of a body. These are the same kinds of records as the rest, we simply use a public missing-person post as a source for the soldier’s full name and details, and then check whether their death has been confirmed.
In the data we’ve collected, there are still relatively few fatalities recorded for 2026: right now, we have only 6,600 records of Russian military personnel with known dates of death who died this year, and since the last update, we added 631 people. For comparison: in 2024, we know of 95,600 deaths, with 1,692 added in the last two weeks; 59,700 deaths for 2025, with 3,613 added. In other words, the losses for this year make up a very small portion of our update.
Why are the recorded losses for this year so low in comparison? There are several reasons, but they all come down to one: the nature of the war has changed. Combat operations are being conducted in a strip known as the “grey zone” or “kill zone”, evacuating bodies from this territory is virtually impossible until full control is established, and the front is moving at an increasingly slower pace.
A backlog is also accumulating on our end: there are so many obituaries that we do not have time to process them all.
But the main reason for the lag in our numbers is that the death of any given individual is being registered with a growing delay. And to show how this happens, we selected one of the lists published by the Ukrainian project “I Want to Live” (“Khochu Zhit”).
The project posted this leak on April 17. The post claims that the 5,007 names are inmates recruited into the Russian army “in one of the months of this year.” We verified that at least 4,000 men from this list actually exist, and from then on we worked specifically with this shortened version of the leak.
The first check showed that almost all of these people were alive as of January 1, 2026.
On April 26, we cross-referenced this list for the first time with the Probate registry and state databases. This check revealed that 118 people had died in 2026.
Here is the result of the next check on May 20: the number of confirmed deaths increased by 80, with the majority of them occurring between January and March.
The third check, about a month later, already showed 352 dead. The trend continued: the people from the “I Want to Live” list were dying in January-March.
We did the latest check just before publishing this update, on September 10. Now, there are already 807 people on the list of the dead, which is one in five out of the 4,000.
In the first three months of 2026, 682 people died, or 84.5% of the known losses: 81 in January, 316 in February, and 285 in March. And only 125 people (15.5%) died in May–August.
In our database, built from publicly available verifiable sources like obituaries, only 112 of the 807 people are present (that is one in seven). It is obvious that public information about deaths appears even later than the official registration of death.
It is evident that over time the graph grows “upwards”, meaning we are mostly recording the deaths of people who actually died back in winter and early spring. Naturally, the data we’ve collected cannot be exhaustive, and we expect that information about the dead from this list will continue to be added. We do not expect to see the final picture of these losses for another two years.
How can it be explained that people from this list suddenly began dying en masse in the winter of 2026? First, there is no doubt that these people definitely died in the war. From obituaries, we know they were assigned to various military units: for example, the 254th Motorised Rifle regiment, the 15th Motorised Rifle brigade, the 5th Motorised Rifle brigade, and others. This means it’s impossible to tie these losses to a specific military formation. Nor is there data about particularly fierce battles in January–March: the intensity of combat operations did not decrease, but neither did it increase.
The simplest explanation: these people were indeed recruited over a short period of time (not necessarily within one month, as “I Want to Live” claims), assigned to assault units after brief training, and thrown into battle. The relatively small share of deaths after March suggests that the majority of these servicemen were either killed, severely wounded, or found a way to leave the assault troops. And new reinforcements came to take their place.
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By September 11, 2026, the death of 7,656 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 231,300 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 234,600 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

UK expanding settlement sanctions to Golan Heights, E. Jerusalem

Breadcrumb
UK to expand settlement sanctions to occupied Golan Heights, East Jerusalem
The UK government intends to include the illegal Jewish settlements in the occupied Golan Heights of Syria and East Jerusalem in the sanctions regime it is imposing on the settlements in the occupied West Bank, The New Arab has learned.
On Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that the UK is preparing to ban the entry of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank into British markets. He confirmed that financial and banking service transactions with these settlements would also be prohibited, alongside additional sanctions on settlers and contributors who support settlement activity in the West Bank, acknowledging that the region is facing ethnic cleansing committed by settlers he described as "terrorists".
However, the foreign secretary did not mention at the time the Israeli settlement movement in the Golan Heights, which Israel occupied by force during the June 1967 war.
Informed sources at the British Foreign and Commonwealth Office stated that these measures "will also include Israeli settlements in the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem". The New Arab has also learned that the relevant ministries have begun working on establishing the sanctions regime so that it encompasses all illegal Jewish settlements in the Golan and East Jerusalem.
British markets import wine produced in the occupied Syrian territory, a practice that anti-settlement activists in the UK have long demanded be banned.
Since occupying the Golan Heights in the 1967 war, Israel has established 34 settlements, housing 30,000 settlers. According to international law, these settlements are entirely illegal. The Israeli government announced in December 2024 its aim of doubling the number of settlers in the occupied Golan Heights, clearly stating that its long-term goal is to settle 100,000 residents there by 2030.
Anti-settlement activists welcomed the expansion of the British sanctions regime to the occupied Golan, noting that it reflects "consistency" in the government's policy toward settlement activity.
In statements to The New Arab, Chris Doyle, Director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding (CAABU), described the move as a “very good and highly significant step”, noting that successive British governments "have long declared that it (the Golan) is also an occupied territory". The CAABU head also warned of the "massive impact" of illegal settlement activity on the Syrian population in the Golan Heights.
Doyle added that including the Golan settlements in the sanctions confirms "the British government's desire for its positions to be consistent”.
Regarding the inclusion of East Jerusalem settlements, Doyle said it should not be taken for granted because, according to international law and resolutions, East Jerusalem is part of the occupied West Bank. Israel, however, considers East Jerusalem separate from the occupied territories, Doyle highlighted
The UK's intention to extend the sanctions regime is expected to unsettle the administration of US President Donald Trump, who in March 2019 recognised Israel's claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan.

UK lawmakers throw out Bill to legalise assisted dying
- UK MPs rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying for terminally ill adults by 286 votes to 270 after emotional debates and long parliamentary struggles.
- The proposed law would have allowed adults with less than six months to live to end their lives with medical and expert approval.
- Opponents celebrated the vote, calling it a protection for vulnerable people, while campaigners called it a devastating setback and vowed to continue pushing for change.
AI generated
LONDON – British MPs on Sept 11 rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying in a knife-edge vote and blow to campaigners in favour of the controversial procedure that is legal in a host of countries including Canada and Switzerland.
Plans to legalise assisted dying have had a long, emotional and ultimately stalled passage through Parliament, with protesters on both sides of the debate regularly demonstrating in Westminster.
Lawmakers in the House of Commons had taken the historic step to back a separate but identical Bill legalising the practice for some terminally ill adults in 2025, before that was scuppered in the unelected upper House of Lords.
The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was reintroduced this parliamentary session, but MPs struck it down after hours of impassioned debate on Sept 11, with 286 voting against and 270 in favour.
The Bill would have allowed adults in England and Wales who have been given less than six months to live and can clearly express a wish to die to opt to end their own lives.
They would need the approval of two doctors and an expert panel to make the decision.
Mixed reactions
Campaigners against assisted dying celebrated the result, with Gordon Macdonald from the Care Not Killing group calling it a “decisive vote”.
He said MPs had “over the last 24 months seen through the pernicious pretence that this draft legislation was safe and wouldn’t put pressure on vulnerable people to end their lives prematurely”.
Disability rights campaigner Philip Friend, 80, told AFP he was relieved.
“We were really worried about this Bill,” he said, adding opponents saw it as “very dangerous because it didn’t have the safeguards, it didn’t investigate coercion”.
“It was a very, very scary place.”
But outside Parliament, campaigners hoping for the law change wiped away tears and comforted each other.
“This is a devastating setback for dying people,” said charity Dignity in Dying, adding that “this issue is not going away”.
Rebecca Wilcox, the daughter of Esther Rantzen – a high-profile television personality who has a terminal diagnosis – told AFP she was “completely devastated”.
“My mum just described this as a tragic day,” she said, noting one British newspaper had called the previous parliamentary blocking of the Bill “a vandalism of democracy”.
“We will come back and we will do it again and we will still fight in the same dignified, measured way,” she vowed.
Neutral PM
New Ipsos polling in late August indicated sustained backing for assisted dying among British adults aged 16 to 75, with two in three supporting the draft legislation.
Ahead of Sept 11, new Prime Minister Andy Burnham had said he would sit out the vote, so as not to “unduly influence the debate”.
Since becoming the country’s leader in July, Burnham has relaunched his years-long push to improve social care for the elderly and vulnerable, and has supported prioritising palliative care.
The controversial draft assisted dying legislation passed in a landmark vote in the House of Commons last June.
But it was torpedoed by more than 1,200 amendments in the upper House of Lords, which was accused of obstructing and delaying the Bill.
Earlier in 2026, lawmakers in Scotland, where health is a devolved issue, rejected a Bill to legalise assisted dying.
Lawmakers in the self-governing British dependencies of Jersey and the Isle of Man have already approved assisted dying legislation, but the moves are awaiting royal assent. AFP

How a 19-year-old officer defied orders and joined the Six-Day War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:19:10 UTC
00:19:10 KST

In September 1967, three months after the Six-Day War, stories began to emerge that the war itself had left untold. Behind the headlines about the great victory were countless personal stories: split-second decisions, acts of heroism, mistakes, loss and incidents that sounded as though they had been written for a movie.
One such story appeared 59 years ago this week on the front page of Yedioth Ahronoth. Its protagonist was a 19-year-old female officer whose identity was not disclosed. She boarded a half-track without permission, went into battle with an armored unit, disappeared as far as the IDF was concerned, survived an anti-tank shell strike and, when the war was over, was sentenced to 35 days in military detention.
Six days later, the young woman had a name and a face: Second Lt. Anat Kirshner of Netanya. Before long, her story and photograph had appeared in newspapers around the world.
The war caught her on a bus
Kirshner came from a longtime Netanya family. She was a graduate of Tchernichovsky High School and a former member of the Scouts youth movement. Even her name carried a military legacy: Her father, Ezra, who had been a commander in the Irgun, named her Anat in memory of David Raziel, the organization’s commander, who was known by the alias “Maj. Gen. Ben-Anat.”
She served in an armored brigade made up of reservists. Around Israel’s Independence Day in 1967, she completed officers’ training and was sent on leave until she was due to report to her new unit in the IDF Southern Command.
On the morning of June 5, she was due to report for duty in the south. She boarded a bus and set out for her new unit. Midway through the journey, regular radio programming was interrupted. An excited announcer reported that war had broken out.
Anat later said she engaged in a brief “soul-searching.” She decided that at that moment she could be of greater use to the IDF in the unit she already knew. At the first stop, she got off the bus, turned around and headed north, back to the armored brigade.
A helmet, trousers and a half-track
By the time she reached the unit, only about 15 minutes remained before the force was due to depart. The commotion of war was all around her: Engines were running, soldiers were loading equipment and commanders were trying to get the vehicles moving.
One of the soldiers gave her a pair of trousers and a helmet. Anat put them on and climbed aboard one of the half-tracks.
The commanders spotted her and ordered her to get off immediately and report to the unit to which she had been assigned in the Southern Command. It was an explicit order. Anat simply did not obey it. Amid the chaos, no one checked whether she had actually left. The soldiers sitting with her in the half-track chose to remain silent, and the armored column set off with the young officer still aboard.
During the night, the half-tracks and tanks advanced toward the Jordanian border in the Jenin area. By morning, Jordanian forces began firing artillery and mortars at the convoy. In the half-track carrying Anat, one of the soldiers stood up. His steel helmet slipped from his head, and seconds later he was hit and fell. He was the brigade’s first fatality.
The shelling intensified. Soldiers were killed and wounded, and Anat jumped over the side of the half-track and ran with the troops to take cover behind a stone wall. The sights overwhelmed her. She burst into tears but managed to regain her composure and began helping bandage the wounded. One of them, whose hand had been severed, refused to let her treat him. He feared the sight would shock her.
When the battle ended, Anat discovered that Eitan, the brigade’s operations sergeant and one of her close friends, had been killed and that his body was lying by the roadside. She took a gold chain from his body and continued with the force. Her clothes were stained with blood, so she changed into Jordanian military fatigues found in a captured army depot.
'I didn’t want to die'
Later, the unit left one of the cities it had captured and came under heavy shelling. The half-track Anat was riding in was struck by an anti-tank shell. She and another officer jumped out. The officer was killed, while Anat emerged unhurt.
She ran with the surviving soldiers toward a nearby hill. This time, she could no longer hold herself together. “I didn’t want to die,” she later recalled. She went into shock and began to cry.
It was the soldiers around her who helped her recover. They told her that having her in the half-track helped them cope with the horrors they were witnessing and continue fighting. If her presence was helping them hold on, they told her, she had to pull herself together as well.
Anat calmed down and returned to duty. For three days and nights, she barely slept. She continued with the unit, watched forces blow up a bridge over the Jordan River and was then sent north with the brigade to the Golan Heights. At one point, exhaustion finally overcame her. She fell asleep inside the half-track and did not realize that the unit was taking part in the battles to capture the Golan Heights. She woke only after the fighting in the area had ended.
While she was fighting, the IDF was looking for her
No one in the Southern Command knew where the officer who was supposed to have reported for duty on the first morning of the war had gone. At the headquarters of the IDF’s chief women’s officer, concern mounted as attempts to locate her proved unsuccessful. According to the newspaper report, throughout the war no one could even bring themselves to call her parents and ask whether they had heard from her.
Only several days after the fighting ended did military personnel call the Kirshner family in Netanya. Her parents were horrified. Until then, they had no idea their daughter was considered missing. Her mother remembered Anat’s deep attachment to her former unit and called the armored brigade. They reassured her: Anat was alive and well.
On the eve of Shavuot, her mother left home and walked along Herzl Street in Netanya. Suddenly, she saw her daughter coming toward her, dressed in the Jordanian military fatigues she had worn during the fighting. Their reunion in the street was emotional. At home, Anat told her parents and sisters everything she had been through.
Her mother was angry. Not because she had gone into battle, but because of her lack of discipline.
From the battlefield to military detention
Several days later, Anat returned to her unit in the Southern Command. This time, a military policewoman was waiting for her.
She had been absent without leave, ignored an explicit order and participated in battles she was not authorized to take part in. She faced disciplinary proceedings and was sentenced to 35 days in military detention.
Before long, the young woman who had survived shelling, treated wounded soldiers and traveled with armored forces from Jenin to the Golan Heights found herself changing clothes once again, this time to enter a military prison.
Her mother called the commander of the armored brigade. According to the article, he tried to reassure her, saying: “Mrs. Kirshner, you can be proud to have a daughter like that.”
Senior military officials also apparently understood that the case was more complicated than an ordinary disciplinary offense. On the recommendation of the IDF’s chief women’s officer, Col. Stella Levy, Southern Command chief Maj. Gen. Yeshayahu Gavish decided to reduce her punishment. Within about a week, Anat was released from prison and returned to service as an officer in an IDF unit in the Gaza Strip.

Polish MEP takes axe to Ukrainian Nazi-linked memorial (VIDEO)
A Polish MEP has taken an axe to a memorial honoring Nazi-linked Ukrainian nationalist paramilitaries responsible for massacring Polish civilians during World War II.
In a video posted on X on Thursday, Grzegorz Braun can be seen repeatedly striking a stone obelisk in Bialystok, near Poland’s border with Ukraine, which commemorates members of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
The UPA was the armed wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), a WWII-era ultranationalist movement led by Stepan Bandera which collaborated with Nazi Germany. UPA fighters massacred tens of thousands of ethnic Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia, now largely in western Ukraine.
”The UPA monument in the Dolhobyczow municipality in Hrubieszow County is to be dismantled,” he wrote. “The obelisk offending the memory of the victims of the Ukrainian genocide against Poles should be removed... immediately after documenting the crime of Banderism,” Braun added.
Pomnik UPA w gminie Dołhobyczów w powiecie hrubieszowskim do likwidacji❗️
Obelisk obrażający pamięć ofiar ukraińskiego Ludobójstwa na Polakach powinien zostać usunięty profesjonalnymi narzędziami natychmiast po udokumentowaniu przestępstwa banderyzmu!#StopBanderyzacjiPolski… pic.twitter.com/8Q4QZ2z5vJ
According to Braun, local Poles feared Ukrainian retaliation if they removed the memorial. He said one proposal to dismantle it was met with the response: “We’re afraid they’ll set us on fire.”
The memorial stands over a burial site containing 41 UPA members killed in a clash with Soviet forces in February 1946. According to Polish records, a Ukrainian memorial was erected there without authorization in the 1990s. The stone monument honoring the UPA fighters was added later and has also faced questions over its legal status.
The site has repeatedly been vandalized. Unidentified people damaged inscriptions on the obelisk earlier this month, while the Ukrainian Embassy expressed “deep outrage” after another attack in July.
The OUN and UPA massacres remain a major source of tension between Poland and Ukraine. Warsaw recognizes the killings of predominantly Polish civilians in Volhynia, Eastern Galicia, and neighboring regions in 1943-1945 as genocide and estimates that up to 100,000 Poles were killed.
The dispute has intensified amid Kiev’s continued honoring of WWII-era Ukrainian nationalists. Vladimir Zelensky took part in the May reburial of OUN leader Andrey Melnik as part of efforts to establish a “Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians” and later granted a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.”
Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state honor. Warsaw has also warned it will not support Ukraine’s EU membership bid unless Kiev changes its approach.
Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik has meanwhile called for an end to free weapons deliveries to Ukraine, arguing that Warsaw has provided some $4.6 billion in military aid only to be repaid with a “Banderite pantheon of heroes.”
”Let’s stop being suckers for Ukraine!” she wrote on X.
Russian President Vladimir Putin weighed in last month, arguing that the neo-Nazi nature of the Ukrainian government has become so visible that even Poland’s strongly anti-Russian authorities can no longer ignore it. Warsaw, he said, faces an “obvious demand” from its population to confront the issue.
Public attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have also deteriorated. A July CBOS poll found 52% of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian migrants, against 42% in favor – the first time opponents had outnumbered supporters since tracking began after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev. Support has fallen from 94% in 2022 to 42% this year.
An August IBRiS survey separately found that 67% of Poles support deporting unemployed Ukrainian men of military age.

According to available information, the final sentence for MP Oleksandr Yurchenko is 9 years in prison. The court also imposed a three-year ban on holding positions related to the performance of state or local government functions, as well as confiscation of property. Until the verdict enters into force, the court left unchanged the preventive measure in the form of bail of more than UAH 3 million.
The court's verdict enters into force thirty days after its pronouncement, unless it is appealed in the appellate procedure
What preceded this
According to the pretrial investigation materials, the Member of Parliament, in veiled terms, asked to be given, through an intermediary, USD 13,000 in an improper benefit for submitting proposals to the draft law "On Waste Management" and USD 200,000 to bribe Members of Parliament – members of the relevant Committee – to vote for the proposals he had submitted.
In mid-August 2020, law enforcement officers recorded the MP's transfer and receipt, through an intermediary, of the first part of the agreed funds. The transfer of the second part of the funds was scheduled for August 26–27, 2020. However, the further execution of the special assignment was halted. The intermediary in the transfer of the improper benefit (the MP's unofficial aide) was notified of suspicion on September 10, 2020, and the MP – on September 17, 2020
The indictment in the case was sent to court back in August 2021.
Recall
In the autumn of 2020, the High Anti-Corruption Court ordered the detention, with the alternative of posting bail of more than UAH 3 million, of Member of Parliament Oleksandr Yurchenko, who was suspected of accepting a bribe. Later, bail of more than UAH 3 million was posted for the MP, and subsequently his electronic bracelet was removed.

Ukraine increases food exports in September, but remains at 40% of its capacity

Ukraine increases food exports in September, but remains at 40% of its capacity
Ukraine increased the volume of agricultural exports by road, rail, and the Danube River this month compared with August, but exports remain at only 40% of their full operational capacity as Russia continues to block the Black Sea, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry reported on Sept. 11.
Since the start of September, Ukraine has exported 630,000 metric tons of agricultural products, more than half of which was grain — 380,000 tons. While this fairs better than in August when Ukraine only exported 33% of its capacity, the alternative export routes to the Black Sea can only handle half the volume of seaports.
"Our task is to simultaneously expand alternative routes, support agricultural producers with financing and temporary storage of the harvest, and work on restoring full-fledged exports through seaports," Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said.
The blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports has sparked fears of a global food crisis as farmers struggle to send grain to customers in Asia and Africa. At the same time, there are concerns that Ukrainian farmers will lose money as grain prices fall and storage space runs out.
Last month, Kyiv predicted that it could lose 10.8 billion euros ($12.6 billion) from blocked agricultural exports.
To help farmers, the Agriculture Ministry has raised $12 million for free polymer storage sleeves for frontline farms to protect their grain from the elements. Other support includes expanding the state "5-7-9%" loan program, allowing farmers to borrow up to Hr 90 million ($2 million) each for operating costs at a fixed 10% interest rate.
As farmers continue to work under immense pressure, the pace of lending to the agricultural sector is increasing and could total an additional Hr 15 billion ($337 million) per month, reaching Hr 60 billion ($1.3 billion) by the end of the year, the ministry said. 
Ukrainian farmers need to raise at least Hr 80 billion ($1.8 billion) for the full autumn sowing campaign, which starts around now.
Ukraine previously asked the EU for 220 million euros ($255 million) to help cash-strapped farmers. While Brussels said it was considering the proposal, no decision has been made yet.
In the long run, without enough support, farmers may plant fewer crops, hampering an industry that accounted for 60% of Ukraine’s exports in the first half of the year.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance builds on a May 2026 European Commission initiative to develop a joint industrial ecosystem for unmanned aerial vehicles.
European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius emphasized the urgent need to adopt Ukraine’s battlefield experience, noting that drone design cycles and countermeasures must now be measured in weeks rather than months.

To counter this threat, the alliance will focus on establishing adaptable production lines capable of rapid expansion in the event of a wider European war.
Furthermore, the partnership aims to integrate Ukrainian battlefield technologies, such as the “Delta” intelligence system, while securing vulnerable supply chains for microchips, electronics, and explosives, Babel wrote. How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:12:05 UTC
00:12:05 KST

How 9/11 turned a terrorist attack into a generation of war
On the morning of September 11, 2001, Americans watched in horror as hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon and crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. Less than a month later, the US went to war in Afghanistan. Two years after that, it invaded Iraq.
What began as an attack by Al-Qaeda would come to reshape US foreign policy, the Middle East, and the way Islam was discussed around the world.
A quarter of a century later, September 11 still casts a long shadow over American public life. Al-Qaeda’s responsibility for the attacks has long been established, but the edges of the story remain blurred. Documents remained classified for years and only emerged piece by piece; lawsuits dragged on; questions lingered over who might have known more, who might have helped, and how far the web surrounding the hijackers actually extended. In the gaps between what was proven, what remained secret, and what was merely suspected, conspiracy theories flourished – but so did genuine political and legal questions that America has never quite managed to put to rest.
Nowhere has that shadow fallen more heavily than on Saudi Arabia; 15 of the 19 hijackers were Saudi citizens, and for decades, victims’ families, lawyers, and advocacy groups have pressed for greater disclosure about possible links between people associated with Saudi institutions and some of the attackers. The result is a peculiar political afterlife of 9/11. Even as Washington and Riyadh have remained strategic partners, questions surrounding the attacks have repeatedly resurfaced whenever the relationship with the kingdom comes under scrutiny.
Under former President Joe Biden, the issue returned to public attention when his administration ordered a new review and declassification of government records related to 9/11, following sustained pressure from victims’ families. The Saudi question also became entangled with a broader political reassessment of Washington’s relationship with Riyadh following the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
In that sense, September 11 left behind more than a settled account of a terrorist attack. It left a long political shadow – one that continued to affect how Americans view particular Arab states, their governments, and eventually, the Muslim world.
The architecture of suspicion
The more immediate consequence of September 11, however, was broader than the hunt for those responsible. The attacks changed the conceptual framework through which the US understood Islam itself.
After 9/11, the country needed explanations: Why did it happen, what produced Islamist violence, and how could another attack be prevented? The American system responded in a characteristically American way: It went looking for expertise. Government agencies poured money into universities, professional associations, and think tanks, demanding explanations – and quickly.
But there was an almost paradoxical mismatch between the question and some of the intellectual tools available to answer it. Many of the scholars being asked to make sense of Islam, political Islam, and jihadist violence built their expertise studying religion in a different context: Christianity in the US, including Christian fundamentalism and its relationship with political extremism.
To Grigory Lukyanov, a research fellow at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences and deputy dean at Russia’s State Academic University for the Humanities, the episode illustrates something larger about the American response to 9/11: Confronted with an unfamiliar threat and under enormous pressure to produce answers quickly, institutions reached for intellectual tools they already possessed.
“You needed ideas, you needed solutions, you needed an understanding of how to solve the problem,” Lukyanov said. “Money was given to scholars of religion, quick results were demanded, and existing analytical frameworks were transferred onto Islam.”
Islam increasingly became something to be categorized in security terms.
A movement classified as ‘moderate’ might be treated as a potential partner; one categorized as ‘radical’ could become a target of surveillance, sanctions, or counterterrorism operations, but the consequences quickly moved beyond policy and into everyday life. In September 2001, 28% of Americans said they had become more suspicious of people of Middle Eastern descent; in March 2002, 25% of Americans said Islam was more likely than other religions to encourage violence (now, 25 years later, it’s 51%).
For Lukyanov, the resulting distortions were almost built into the speed and structure of the response. “It is difficult to search for alternatives in counterfactual history,” he said. “The attack had happened. What could the United States do – simply not conduct a War on Terror? Retreat into something like the Monroe Doctrine, recoil from what had happened and accept defeat? That was almost impossible to imagine.”
The US of 2001 was at the height of its post-Cold War power, the Russian expert said. The Soviet Union disappeared a decade earlier; China had not yet emerged as a peer economic competitor; Washington possessed unmatched military, financial, and political reach. September 11 was therefore interpreted not only as a terrorist atrocity, but as a challenge to American global leadership.
“Not responding was impossible,” Lukyanov said. “The question is that the response was built on the experience, analytical frameworks, decision-making patterns and limitations that American political elites had at that moment.”
America’s road to endless war
If the securitization of Islam was one consequence of September 11, the most visible was measured in soldiers, bases, and wars. Yet here as well, 9/11 was less a beginning than an acceleration.
The US was hardly a newcomer to the Middle East in 2001. Its involvement expanded dramatically after the Cold War and the 1990-91 Gulf War. The US had troops and military facilities across the region, protected the Gulf monarchies, enforced no-fly zones over Iraq, supported Israel, and remained indispensable to Arab-Israeli diplomacy. By the end of the 1990s, American primacy in the region was difficult to contest.
“The United States began sinking into the Middle Eastern swamp long before September 11,” Lukyanov said. “There were essentially no other external players, and almost no major conflict or problem in the region could be resolved without the participation of Washington.”
September 11 was therefore not the moment America entered the Middle East. It was, in Lukyanov’s words, a crescendo – the moment an already extensive political and military commitment became something larger and far more difficult to control.
Less than a month after the attacks, the US invaded Afghanistan to destroy Al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government that had sheltered it. The initial campaign was remarkably swift. By December, the Taliban regime had collapsed. What followed was not. The US would remain in Afghanistan for nearly 20 years, its longest war, losing more than 2,400 service members as it tried to build a new political order. It ended in August 2021, with the Taliban sweeping back into Kabul.
Five years later, Taliban fighters patrol the capital in American-supplied Humvees, carrying American weapons and wearing American tactical gear. Around $7 billion worth of US-funded military equipment remained in Afghanistan after the collapse of the forces the US spent two decades building.
Destroying one enemy, creating another
Then came Iraq.
Unlike Afghanistan, the 2003 invasion was not presented as war against the organization that carried out the September 11 attacks. The administration of George W. Bush argued that Saddam Hussein’s regime possessed weapons of mass destruction (which were never found) and presented Iraq as part of a broader post-9/11 security threat. But by then, the invasion had already removed the Iraqi state’s leadership, dissolved much of its coercive apparatus, and opened a political vacuum at the center of the Arab world.
One consequence of the US invasion of Iraq can still be felt today, Lukyanov argues, pointing to the ongoing exchange of strikes between Iran and US forces across the region.
“It was the American invasion of Iraq, prompted by the 9/11 policies, that created the conditions for a geopolitical conflict in that country, escalating the geopolitical standoff between the United States and Iran,” Lukyanov adds. “It was precisely because of this that the United States significantly increased its support for Israel and its policies.”
Hussein’s fall destroyed a regime that brutally dominated Iraq for decades, but it also removed one of the principal Arab counterweights to Iran. Iraq’s long-suppressed Shia majority acquired unprecedented political power, while many Sunnis who occupied privileged positions under the old order suddenly found themselves marginalized.
The dismantling of the Iraqi Army and Baathist state structures left hundreds of thousands of armed and militarily trained men without a place in that order. Insurgency spread and sectarian violence followed. A new generation of jihadists that came into that landscape, now known as ISIS, built itself amid the occupation and the Sunni insurgency. By 2014, ISIS seized Mosul and proclaimed a caliphate across large parts of Iraq and Syria.
The friends America abandoned
The War on Terror did not only transform America’s enemies, it also transformed its friendships.
Across the Arab world, authoritarian governments quickly discovered the political value of becoming indispensable to America’s new struggle. Tunisia, Sudan, Yemen, Egypt, Jordan, and several Gulf monarchies expanded counterterrorism cooperation with the US, while governments increasingly presented domestic repression as part of the same fight against extremism. The distinction between jihadists and non-violent Islamist opponents could become dangerously elastic. Organizations that threatened the regime politically could be folded into a much broader security problem.
For aging authoritarian systems, the new order offered an opportunity. Lukyanov argues that some regimes came to believe that cooperation against a common enemy would buy them a kind of political absolution. “The War on Terror gave them the illusion that, by acting against a common enemy together with the United States, they would receive forgiveness for everything that had happened in the past.”
Few countries tested that proposition as dramatically as Libya.
Muammar Gaddafi spent decades as an adversary of Washington. But he was also an enemy of the jihadists seeking to overthrow him. After 9/11, this suddenly gave Tripoli and Washington something to talk about. Libya shared intelligence on Al-Qaeda and other Islamist militants with Western services; in 2003, Gaddafi renounced terrorism and agreed to dismantle his weapons-of-mass-destruction programs. Sanctions were progressively lifted, diplomatic relations restored, and in 2006, the US removed Libya from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
For a time, the bargain appeared to work. A ruler once treated as an international pariah reinvented himself as a counterterrorism partner. Washington, meanwhile, gained intelligence cooperation and the dismantling of Libya’s unconventional weapons programs without another war.
But there was a catch. Cooperation abroad did not require meaningful liberalization at home. Libya remained brutally authoritarian even as relations with Washington improved; elsewhere, the counterterrorism imperative similarly gave security states additional room to operate. In Egypt, emergency laws allowed thousands to be detained without fair trials, while Washington tolerated serious abuses by governments it relied upon for counterterrorism cooperation.
Then, a decade after September 11, the bargain began to come apart when uprisings began in Tunisia in late 2010, and Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali fled. In Egypt, Hosni Mubarak resigned after nearly 30 years in power. And in Libya, the reversal was even more extraordinary: Gaddafi – the former enemy who dismantled his weapons programs, shared intelligence on jihadists, and rebuilt relations with the West – faced an uprising of his own. NATO intervened against his forces, and in October 2011, Gaddafi was killed.
The political vacuum produced another irony, Lukyanov said. For decades, some Arab governments portrayed Islamism as one of the principal dangers from which their rule protected both their own societies and the West. Once several of these governments fell, however, Islamist movements proved to be among the best-organized political forces left standing. Ennahda won Tunisia’s first post-revolutionary election; in Egypt, the Muslim Brotherhood emerged as the dominant electoral force and its candidate, Mohamed Morsi, won the presidency. “In the end, in both Egypt and Tunisia, for example, movements that had provided Al-Qaeda with a social and political support base came to power,” Lukyanov said.
In the places where revolutions did not produce functioning political systems, the circle became darker still. Libya descended into fragmentation and civil war; Yemen collapsed into a regional conflict; Syria became the battlefield in which local rebellion, state repression, regional competition, and transnational jihadism converged. Groups linked to Al-Qaeda, and eventually ISIS, found new territory in the wreckage.
When the War on Terror came home
Six days after the attacks, Bush visited a Washington mosque and declared that “Islam is peace,” seeking to draw a line between the perpetrators and millions of ordinary Muslims. On the ground, however, the backlash was already well underway.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes surged from just 28 in 2000 to 481 in 2001 – a more than seventeen-fold increase. Another 49 assaults and 104 incidents targeting places of worship were reported in the first week after 9/11 alone. In Chicago alone, the number of reported anti-Muslim or anti-Arab hate crimes jumped from four in all of 2000 to 51 in just the three months from September to November 2001.
The effect was measurable within Muslim communities themselves; 57% of Muslim Americans said they had experienced some form of bias or discrimination since the attacks, and 48% said their lives had changed for the worse. Yet the response was not uniformly hostile; 79% also said they had experienced an act of kindness or support from friends or colleagues of other faiths.
The consequences went beyond the immediate backlash. The security architecture built in the aftermath of 9/11 also expanded the reach and militarization of law enforcement. By 2020, nearly 65% of the roughly 18,000 US law enforcement agencies had received military equipment through the Pentagon’s 1033 program, such as weapons, ammunition, and tactical armored vehicles.
“If we return to the question of how Islam and the Islamic world have changed, Islam as a teaching has not changed,” Lukyanov stresses. “Nor have the borders of Muslim states changed. What has changed, however, is the position of Muslim communities in Western countries and in countries outside Muslim-majority regions.”
A quarter of a century later, the legacy of 9/11 extends far beyond the attacks themselves. Not only the US, but the world around it changed: Wars reshaped the Middle East politics (though did not change the region’s borders), new extremist movements emerged, regional rivalries deepened, and Muslim communities in the West faced greater suspicion and scrutiny. In that sense, perhaps the most consequential story of 9/11 for the Muslim world is not what happened on that day, but what followed in response.

Following the success of the Buenos Aires and Lima stops, the international tour of the MEI—National Museum of Italian Emigration—continues in South America and arrives in Colombia. On September 14 at 6:00 p.m., the “MEI Experience Cube” will be inaugurated in Bogotá. This immersive multimedia experience, conceived by the MEI, uses images, testimonials, and audiovisual content to tell the stories of Italian emigration to various countries around the world. According to a press release, the installation will be on view through October 13, 2026, at the Italian Cultural Institute in Bogotá, located at Calle 35 No. 15-32, Barrio La Magdalena. The Colombian leg of the exhibition is hosted by the Italian Cultural Institute (IIC), in collaboration with the Italian Embassy, the Committee of Italians Abroad (Com.It.Es.) in Colombia, and ICSAIC, and under the patronage of the Italian-Latin American Institute (IILA). The MEI Experience Cube was created to share the heritage and story of the National Museum of Italian Emigration, based in Genoa, with the world through a format capable of adapting to the various host countries. An immersive journey that focuses on the individual and collective experiences of Italian emigrants, weaving them together with the history, culture, and development of the regions where they chose to live. In Bogotá, the narrative will therefore focus on the relationship between Italy and Colombia and the legacy left by Italians in the country, as illustrated through several particularly significant figures and events. To date, there are 11,634 Italians residing in Colombia. “With the Bogotá stop, we continue a journey that takes the National Museum of Italian Emigration beyond national borders to places where the Italian presence has left a profound mark,” says Paolo Masini, president of the MEI Foundation. “Each country allows us to tell different stories, but they are all part of the same great narrative: that of millions of Italians who, leaving Italy, built new lives and contributed to the growth of the communities that welcomed them. In Colombia, these ties are particularly significant, and the MEI Experience Cube allows us to showcase them through a contemporary, immersive, and accessible medium.” The Oreste Sindici Cultural Association of Ceccano, Roma Tre University’s Department of Architecture, and Professor Maria Margarita Segarra Lagunes, with “Vissi d’arte,” collaborated on the creation of the content. The experience was developed by Federico Basso for Opera Digitale. Media partners: Rai Italia and ANSA. Paolo Masini, president of the MEI Foundation, will be present at the inauguration, having traveled from Italy specifically for the occasion. Representing the Italian Embassy in Colombia will be, among others, Ambassador Giancarlo Maria Curcio, Second Secretary and IIC Regent Marina Zappettini, and Head of the Consular Chancellery Paola Orsini. Ambassador Curcio expressed particular satisfaction that the exhibition is being held in Bogotá and noted that it will certainly be visited with great interest not only by the Italian community in Colombia but also by the many Colombians who feel a close connection to Italy and are grateful for the contribution our compatriots have made to the country’s development.

As conflict engulfs Mocha, Yemen, health workers keep hospital open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:10:35 UTC
00:10:35 KST

“Our teams have been present in Mocha and the surrounding area since 2018. Our work focuses on improving access to paediatric and maternal healthcare, a lifeline for many women and children in an area where access to such care is a daily challenge.
In Mocha, we support the General hospital through the direct presence of MSF teams, as well as through broader support to the hospital and Ministry of Health staff. Outside the city, we also support maternal and paediatric healthcare in two healthcare centres in the region: Mafraq, east of Mocha, and Khawkhah, to the north. In these two facilities, our support includes funding, training, medical equipment, and supplies. We do not have permanent MSF teams based there.
The rapid evolution of the situation this week, including the swift advance of Ansar Allah forces and their control of most of the western coast, has had a major impact on both medical activities and the needs of people in recent days.
Just a few days ago, our teams in Mocha were preparing to reopen our former field hospital in the city to treat patients, including providing trauma stabilisation, in response to the fighting taking place east of Mafraq and the gradual arrival of displaced people in Mocha.
The rapid advance of Ansar Allah forces has fundamentally changed the situation. Within hours, the hospitals providing trauma services on the western coast were evacuated, while large numbers of people fled Mocha. 
We had already started providing water to displaced people arriving in the city, as well as finalising the setup of cholera isolation and treatment units in Khawkhah and Mocha. We were also increasing our ambulance fleet to refer critical patients to Aden, as hospitals there were at capacity.
The rapid advance of Ansar Allah forces has fundamentally changed the situation. Within hours, the hospitals providing trauma services on the western coast were evacuated, while large numbers of people fled Mocha towards the south and Aden, including healthcare workers from the city’s hospitals. The General hospital in Mocha was no exception.
Our team remained in Mocha, but we had to scale back and reorganise our activities and focus on one immediate priority: doing everything possible to keep essential medical services at the General hospital running.
So far, thanks to the commitment of Yemeni doctors, gynaecologists, nurses, and other healthcare workers, we have been able to maintain a minimum level of essential care, including deliveries, emergency care, and intensive care. As of today, around 30 healthcare workers remain present at the hospital. This may not seem like many, but their work is saving lives.
Our medical and humanitarian mission must be respected... Without these basic guarantees, we simply cannot do our job: treating people and saving lives.
When the city was taken, dozens of patients were still hospitalised in the maternity and paediatric wards. It was essential to maintain their care while continuing to receive patients requiring urgent treatment. On that day [Thursday 10 September], hospital teams cared for two patients who arrived in the paediatric and maternity emergency departments, performed two emergency caesarean sections, and continued caring for seven patients in intensive care and 10 babies in the neonatal intensive care unit, in addition to dozens of other patients and babies in the regular wards.
The situation remains extremely challenging. As of 11 September, almost all other healthcare facilities in the city had stopped functioning, largely because their staff had left. There is currently no possibility of referring patients, either within the city or to Aden.
The medical needs were already enormous before the latest escalation. They are even greater now.
We are looking for ways to reinforce our team in Mocha, but this is not straightforward. The situation remains highly stressful for both people and our teams. There were further bombardments overnight, and there is still considerable uncertainty about what may happen in the coming hours and days.
For us to continue providing care, our medical and humanitarian mission must be respected. Medical facilities, vehicles and staff must be protected so that people can safely access the care they need. This is also essential to allow patients in critical condition to be referred safely when the treatment they need is not available locally. Any threat to the medical mission puts the provision of essential healthcare at risk and may jeopardise our ability to continue working in Mocha. Without these basic guarantees, we simply cannot do our job: treating people and saving lives.
We do not know what will happen next. What we do know is that medical needs are enormous and go far beyond trauma care. We will continue to do our utmost to support the community and maintain access to essential healthcare for as long as we can.”

UN Security Council extends Sudan sanctions regime, arms embargo

15:10:15 UTC
00:10:15 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
11 September 2026•Update: 11 September 2026
The UN Security Council on Friday unanimously adopted a US-drafted resolution extending the Sudan sanctions regime, including an arms embargo, for one month until Oct. 9.
All 15 council members voted in favor of the short-term technical rollover, which maintains the existing measures while allowing more time for negotiations on potential changes to the sanctions regime.
US Ambassador Jeff Bartos said Washington welcomed the adoption, but stressed that a long-term technical rollover was “not an option.”
Bartos said the US wants to expand the arms embargo from Darfur to all of Sudan, broaden sanctions criteria to cover conflict-related sexual violence, kidnapping for ransom and attacks on humanitarian personnel, and strengthen the mandate of the Panel of Experts.
“The current sanctions regime is over 20 years outdated, and is insufficient to address the realities of the war today,” he said.
“That is why this council should expand the arms embargo across the entire territory of Sudan, expand the listing measures to include horrific actions such as conflict-related sexual violence, kidnapping for ransom, and attacks on humanitarian personnel, and strengthen the mandate and effectiveness of the panel of experts,” he added.
Sudan’s UN Ambassador Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed opposed any expansion of the arms embargo, arguing that it would undermine Sudan’s ability re-establish control, its right to self-defense and creates “unfair equivalence” between the Sudanese Armed Forces and armed groups.
The sanctions regime, established in 2005, currently includes an arms embargo focused on actors operating in Darfur as well as targeted travel bans and asset freezes.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and displacing millions.

Siberia’s Irkutsk region has introduced a record-high commission for military recruiters who successfully enlist foreign nationals and stateless persons into the Russian military, according to a directive signed by the regional governor on Thursday.
Under the directive, recruiters will now receive 1.5 million rubles ($17,800) for every foreign citizen they sign to a military contract. The new commission represents a fourfold increase over the past seven months, making Irkutsk the highest-paying Russian region for foreign enlistment incentives, according to the exiled news outlet Vyorstka.
Irkutsk previously offered a flat recruiter fee of 400,000 rubles ($4,700) per contract, regardless of the recruit’s citizenship. Vyorstka said the latest directive explicitly separates foreign citizens and stateless individuals from Russian recruits, while doubling the commission for enlisting Russians from other regions to 800,000 rubles ($9,500).
The move reflects a broader trend as regional governments scramble to meet military recruitment quotas. The Smolensk region recently raised recruiter payouts from 115,000 rubles ($1,300) to 1 million rubles ($11,900), while the Ryazan region hiked its commission to 805,000 rubles ($9,500).
Ukraine, which also allows foreign nationals to fight alongside its armed forces, previously identified more than 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries — excluding those from North Korea — who fought on the Russian side as of April 2026.
In a report published Thursday, Amnesty International said Russian recruitment efforts “frequently involved deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices.”
“Testimonies… describe contracts signed without informed consent, confiscation of passports, restrictions on freedom of movement, inadequate training and threats against those seeking to leave military service,” the NGO said, saying the practices “may amount to human trafficking.”

Get AI models ‘under control’, EU tells tech firms after hacks
- The European Union has urged tech firms to control their powerful AI models following hacks by autonomous AI agents, including breaches of Hugging Face and a German website takeover.
- The EU's AI Act enforcement began in August, allowing it to demand information, impose fines, and restrict or recall AI models if risks escalate.
- EU cybersecurity agencies have gained access to advanced AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6-ASTRA and Anthropic's Mythos 5 for testing and risk assessment.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Top tech firms need to get their powerful artificial intelligence models “under control”, the European Union warned on Sept 11 after a series of hacks by AI agents.
Fears over rogue AI have spiked after OpenAI technology operating outside human supervision hacked into Hugging Face, a repository of AI models.
And during an incident revealed last week, thousands of autonomous AI agents built by OpenAI defied their instructions and took over a German website.
Asked about reports that the hack was broader than suspected, an EU spokesman said: “It is high time for these providers to get their house in order and to make sure that they get their advanced models under control.”
The EU said earlier this week it was looking into the incident.
The 27-nation bloc has adopted comprehensive AI rules and its enforcement powers kicked in in August, which means companies must comply with the law or face fines.
“The AI Act is fully enforced. It’s not just a set of rules on paper any more,” spokesman Thomas Regnier said.
He added that the European Commission, the EU’s AI watchdog, has already demanded information from several companies – which he did not name.
“If it gets bad or worse, we can definitely evaluate models. We can require risk mitigation measures, and in extreme cases and where necessary, we can also restrict, withdraw, or even recall AI models,” he said.
The EU’s cybersecurity agency has received access to OpenAI’s latest models, including GPT-6-ASTRA, as well as to Mythos 5, the powerful AI model from rival firm Anthropic, which it is currently testing, Brussels said on Sept 10. AFP

MOSCOW, September 11. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia does not plan to keep the key rate at a level the economy cannot bear for long, the regulator’s Governor Elvira Nabiullina said, adding that this would push unemployment up and put pressure on real incomes.
"In any case, we will not keep the interest rate for a long time at a level that is, as they say, unbearable for the economy. Why? If the rate's level is unbearable, it will quickly lead to a cyclical downturn, which means growth of unemployment, declining real incomes, and a drop in underlying inflation below the Central Bank’s targets," she told a press conference following the regulator’s board meeting.
The Bank of Russia will ease its monetary policy and lower the key rate within the framework of its inflation-targeting policy, anticipating such a turn of events rather than waiting for it to unfold, Nabiullina noted.

Int'l Criminal Court feels Trump's squeeze as more states exit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-11
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

As the U.S. ratchets up pressure on the International Criminal Court (ICC), sanctioning two more high-ranking staff recently, a small but growing number of the global tribunal’s member states have announced their withdrawal.
The departures of Venezuela and Chad bring to five the number of countries to withdraw from the court in the past year, joining Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The surge in withdrawals comes as the ICC faces hostility from the U.S. and a leadership crisis after it ousted its chief prosecutor.
"Five countries have announced plans to withdraw from the Rome Statute, and we welcome more announcements in the future,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson told the AP.
The Rome Statute established the ICC in 2002 as the court of last resort to prosecute individuals responsible for the most heinous atrocities: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.
Based in The Hague, it takes cases when nations are unable or unwilling to prosecute crimes within their borders.
"The ICC regrets any decision to depart from the collective effort to end impunity for the most serious international crimes,” the court's spokesperson Oriane Maillet told the AP.
In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that the U.S. was launching a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court to U.S. sovereignty.”
Rubio said he would pressure the court's 125 member states to withdraw from the court, sanction organizations that work with it and ban staff from traveling to the U.S.
The Trump administration has already sanctioned a dozen ICC staff in retaliation for warrants the court had issued for Israeli war crimes in Palestine and investigations into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.
The Central African country of Chad specifically cited the United States in its decision to withdraw. Its Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Sabre Fadoul said in a statement that in a phone call with a U.S. official on July 23, "the American side expressed its concerns regarding the functioning of this institution and requested that Chad reconsider" its membership.
Four days later, Chad said it would leave the ICC.
Iva Vukusic, a researcher at Utrecht University, told the AP that the U.S. campaign will reveal how committed countries are to the court. "Are they willing to defend it if it costs them something real?” she said.
The State Department told the AP the U.S. would call on nations that "enjoy the benefits of the U.S. security umbrella" to reject the ICC.
It is not just pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump that is sending ICC members toward withdrawal.
Ruling military juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger blamed selective justice. The ICC had become an "instrument of neocolonial repression in the hands of imperialism,” the trio said when they announced their withdrawals last year.
A coup ousted Niger's democratically elected government in 2023. Since then, a military junta abandoned longtime partners and formed new alliances, including with Russia, where President Vladimir Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant for the war in Ukraine. Mali and Burkina Faso have undergone similar transformations.
"These countries are ruled by authoritarian leaders who want to avoid accountability for the harms they are inflicting on their own people,” Mel O'Brien, an associate professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, told the AP.
Burundi similarly accused the court of focusing too much on conflicts in Africa when, in 2017, it became the first country to withdraw from the ICC. The court opened an investigation into the East African nation earlier that year.
Most of the court's initial investigations were into African countries, though most requested the involvement of the ICC.
South Africa and Gambia also announced in 2017 that they would withdraw but later changed course.
A change of government can also bring a country back into the fold. Hungary announced it would withdraw from the court in 2025, but following the election of a new government, its parliament voted to remain.
The court also had an investigation in the Philippines when then-President Duterte said his country would withdraw from the ICC.
In 2019, the Southeast Asian country became the second to withdraw, but because withdrawal from the court is not retroactive, the investigation continued.
Duterte is now in ICC detention in the Netherlands awaiting trial on charges of crimes against humanity for deadly anti-drug crackdowns he allegedly oversaw while in office. Opening statements are set for November.
An investigation into possible crimes committed by Venezuelan security forces under former Venezuelan President Maduro will continue despite the country's announcement last month that it will also withdraw from the ICC.
In a statement, the country's Foreign Minister Felix Plasencia said the court had been "instrumentalized to deepen inequalities among peoples and disregard their right to self-determination and sovereignty.”
Venezuela is currently in the middle of U.S.-backed talks between the ruling party and the opposition.
Ukraine previously signed an agreement to give the court jurisdiction over crimes on its territory, following the outbreak of hostilities with Russia in 2014.
Joining the court was "Ukraine's way of saying that accountability for the gravest crimes cannot be optional, and that we intend to help build that system of justice,” Ukraine's Prosecutor General Andriy Kostin told the AP.
